title: Clean water scarcity: when there is water, but not water you can use
description: Most global water scarcity estimates only ask whether there is enough water. Jones, Bierkens and van Vliet also ask whether it is clean enough to use, and find that 55% of the world's people already face clean water scarcity at least one month a year.
tags: water scarcity water quality global hydrology climate change scenarios
text: When we say a region is “water scarce,” we usually mean that people want more water than the rivers can deliver. That is a question about quantity. But a river can be full and still useless if it is too salty, too loaded with organic waste, or full of pathogens. Edward Jones, Marc Bierkens and Michelle van Vliet at Utrecht University asked what happens to the global picture of water scarcity when water quality is counted as well (Jones et al., 2024). Their answer: more people are affected, and they are affected for more months of the year. 1. Water you cannot use is not available water Every use of water has a quality requirement. Drinking water needs to be much cleaner than water for cooling a power plant or irrigating a field. The study tracks three common kinds of pollution in rivers: Salinity, measured as total dissolved solids. Too much salt harms crops and makes water unfit to drink. Organic pollution, measured as biological oxygen demand (BOD). This comes mostly from untreated sewage, livestock and food industries. Pathogen pollution, measured as fecal coliform bacteria, a sign of contamination by human or animal waste. For each of these, the authors set a maximum concentration for each kind of use: domestic, industrial, livestock and irrigation. For organic pollution, for example, the limit is 5 mg/L for domestic water but 30 mg/L for irrigation. If a river is cleaner than the limit, its water counts as usable for that purpose. If not, it does not. 2. How do you add quality to a scarcity count? The study uses two linked global models. PCR-GLOBWB 2 simulates river flow, groundwater and human water use. DynQual follows pollution as it enters and moves through the river network. Both run at a 5 arcminute grid (roughly 10 km) and the analysis is monthly, from 2005 to 2100. The quantity part is a familiar ratio. Take the water people demand, subtract what groundwater pumping, desalination and wastewater reuse already provide, and compare the rest with what the river can give after leaving enough flow for the ecosystem. If demand is larger, the area is water scarce that month. The quality part uses a clever idea called dilution water. Suppose a town needs 60 units of river water, but the river carries twice the allowed amount of organic pollution. To bring that water down to the limit, you would need to mix in another 60 units of clean water. The town’s effective demand is now 120 units, not 60. Nobody actually dilutes water this way, but the idea turns pollution into a volume of water, so quantity and quality can be compared on the same scale. A place that looked comfortable on quantity alone can cross into scarcity once this extra water is counted. The authors call the quantity-only indicator WS and the combined indicator WSq. “Clean water scarcity” means scarcity measured with WSq. 3. The world today Averaged over 2005–2020, the results are: 3.8 billion people (55%) face clean water scarcity at least one month a year. Counting quantity alone gives 3.3 billion (47%). In any given month, between 1.7 and 2.6 billion people face clean water scarcity, compared with 1.0 to 2.1 billion on quantity alone. On average, pollution adds about 634 million people each month. 0.71 billion people (10.3%) face clean water scarcity in every month of the year, more than double the 0.32 billion (4.6%) counted on quantity alone. The last point is the most striking. For short, seasonal scarcity, quality adds about one-fifth to the count. For year-round scarcity, it more than doubles it (Figure 1). Dry seasons come and go, but pollution in many rivers stays all year. Figure 1. Share of the world population exposed to water scarcity in at least n months of the year, averaged over 2005–2020, counting quantity only (grey) and quantity plus quality (blue). The right panel shows how many times larger the clean water count is. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from the values in Table 1 of Jones et al. (2024). Where does quality matter most? The paper’s maps show that pollution creates scarcity in east Africa and large parts of China, often where there is enough water in the river. India suffers from both too little water and poor quality for much of the year. In Western Europe and North America, scarcity comes mostly in summer and is driven by quantity, but poor quality often makes it worse. Of the world regions, including quality changes the count most in Latin America and the Caribbean, the Middle East and North Africa, and East Asia and the Pacific. 4. The rest of the century To look ahead, the authors combine three scenarios of social and climate change with five climate models: SSP1–RCP2.6, a sustainable world with strong climate action; SSP3–RCP7.0, a world of regional rivalry, high population growth and slow development; SSP5–RCP8.5, a world of fast, fossil-fueled economic growth. In all three, clean water scarcity grows. The share of people facing it at least one month a year rises from 54–57% today to 56–62% by mid-century (2041–2060) and 56–66% by the end of the century (2081–2100). In numbers, that is 4.7–6.1 billion people by mid-century. By the end of the century the range is very wide, 3.8–8.2 billion, because the scenarios assume very different population sizes. The regional rivalry scenario (SSP3–RCP7.0) is the worst for both the share and the number of people. The regional picture differs a lot (Figure 2): Sub-Saharan Africa sees the largest change. Today about 26% of its people face clean water scarcity at least one month a year; by 2081–2100 this becomes 44–54%, depending on the scenario. Both quantity and quality drive the increase. East Asia and the Pacific is the exception. Its exposure falls slightly in all scenarios, and the paper shows that the fall comes mainly from improving river water quality, not from more water. North America and Western Europe increase most under the sustainable and fossil-fueled scenarios. This sounds odd until you look at population: those scenarios assume strong population growth in these regions (for North America, +121% under SSP5 by 2100), while the regional rivalry scenario assumes population decline. The increases are driven mainly by quantity, in summer. The Middle East and North Africa remains the most exposed region, with 77–85% of people facing clean water scarcity at least one month a year by the end of the century. Figure 2. Share of each region’s population facing clean water scarcity at least one month a year, for 2005–2020 (open circles) and for 2081–2100 under three scenarios (colored markers, slightly offset vertically so overlapping values stay visible). Values are means over five climate models. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from the values in Table 2 of Jones et al. (2024). 5. What the numbers leave out The authors are careful about the limits, and several of them mean the true numbers could be higher: Only three kinds of pollution are included. Nutrients, metals, plastics and many chemicals are not. Groundwater is assumed to be clean. In reality, arsenic, nitrate and salt make some groundwater unusable, so this assumption likely underestimates clean water scarcity. Only one hydrological model and one water quality model are used, so uncertainty from the models themselves is not captured. Future growth of desalination and wastewater reuse is not projected, because there are no good projections of how fast they will expand. The study measures physical scarcity only. Whether people can actually access water, and whether it is shared fairly, are different questions. The authors also note that their estimates sit at the high end of earlier studies. They argue that many earlier assessments underestimated scarcity because they used coarse units such as whole countries or annual averages, and because they ignored quality. 6. A few thoughts In practice, water quantity and water quality are often handled by different people, different models and even different agencies. This paper is a good reminder that, for the person turning on the tap or the farmer opening a gate, they are one problem. A river that is full but too dirty to use is, for that user, an empty river. The East Asia result is the most hopeful part of the paper. It shows that cleaning up rivers can reduce water scarcity as surely as building new supply. Wastewater treatment is usually discussed as environmental protection, but here it also works as a water supply measure. The paper does not report numbers for individual countries, so I cannot say what it implies for Korea. Korea sits inside the East Asia and Pacific region, and the regional averages hide large differences between countries. Still, the idea is easy to apply at home: a reservoir with a summer algal bloom, or a river reach just below a city’s treatment plant, can be short of usable water even when it is full. In an earlier post on water bankruptcy, we saw the claim that about 4 billion people face severe water scarcity at least a month a year. This study arrives at a similar number from a different angle, and it shows how much of that number comes from water that is there but cannot be used. Questions to think about Why does including water quality more than double the number of people facing scarcity all year round, but add only about one-fifth for scarcity in at least one month? The “dilution water” idea converts pollution into a volume of water. What are the strengths and weaknesses of this approach? If you were a water manager, would you spend the next budget on a new reservoir or on better wastewater treatment upstream? What information would you need to decide? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). Jones 등(2024)은 전 지구 수문 모델(PCR-GLOBWB 2)과 수질 모델(DynQual)을 결합해, 물의 양뿐 아니라 염분, 유기물(BOD), 병원성 미생물 오염까지 고려한 ‘깨끗한 물 부족(clean water scarcity)’을 2005년부터 2100년까지 월 단위로 평가했다. 오염된 물을 용도별 수질 기준까지 희석하는 데 필요한 물을 수요에 더하는 방식으로 계산한 결과, 현재 세계 인구의 55%(38억 명)가 1년에 한 달 이상 깨끗한 물 부족을 겪으며, 이는 수량만 고려했을 때(47%)보다 많고 1년 내내 부족을 겪는 인구는 수질을 고려하면 두 배 이상(4.6%에서 10.3%)으로 늘어난다. 미래에는 세 가지 사회·기후 시나리오 모두에서 이 비율이 금세기 말 56–66%로 늘고, 특히 사하라 이남 아프리카에서 크게 증가하는 반면, 동아시아·태평양은 하천 수질 개선 덕분에 오히려 감소한다. 지하수를 깨끗하다고 가정하고 세 가지 오염 물질만 다뤘다는 한계가 있지만, 물 부족을 줄이려면 물 사용 절감과 함께 오염 저감이 반드시 필요하다는 점을 보여준다. Reference Jones, E. R., Bierkens, M. F. P., & van Vliet, M. T. H. (2024). Current and future global water scarcity intensifies when accounting for surface water quality. Nature Climate Change, 14, 629–635. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-024-02007-0 The figures are original. The Python scripts that produce them are available on GitHub: Figure 1 and Figure 2.

title: Water bankruptcy: when a water crisis never ends
description: Kaveh Madani proposes a formal definition of water bankruptcy, a state in which a society has overspent its water for so long that some damage cannot be undone. A UN University report now argues that the world as a whole has entered an era of water bankruptcy.
tags: water bankruptcy water governance groundwater water security sustainability
text: We hear about a “water crisis” almost everywhere: a failed monsoon in one year, a city close to running dry, an aquifer that has been falling for fifty years. Kaveh Madani, the Director of the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH), argues that this word no longer fits many of these situations. In a recent paper in Water Resources Management, he gives the first formal definition of a term he has used for years: water bankruptcy (Madani 2026a). A UNU-INWEH report built on this paper goes further and declares that the world has entered an era of “global water bankruptcy” (Madani 2026b). 1. Why “crisis” is the wrong word A crisis, in the usual sense, is a temporary departure from normal. It has a beginning and an end: a severe drought, a contamination event, a flood. The goal of crisis management is to get through it and return to the old normal. Many of today’s water problems do not look like that. Lakes and wetlands have dried, groundwater has fallen for decades, land has subsided, and rivers no longer reach the sea. These are not short shocks that will pass after a few wet years. Madani lists four reasons why calling them a crisis is misleading: A crisis implies it will end. If a “crisis” lasts for decades, the system has not been through a crisis; it has failed. The word has lost its power. “Water crisis” has been used so often that it creates fatigue rather than action. Crisis management aims to restore the past. But a drained aquifer or a dried wetland cannot be restored on any realistic time scale. Crisis talk delays the admission of failure. It encourages promises that the problem is temporary, usually followed by new supply projects that treat the symptom instead of the cause. 2. The bank account analogy To explain the idea, Madani uses a simple analogy that has been widely quoted: Surface water is the checking account. Rivers, lakes and reservoirs are refilled every year or decade by rain and snow, our regular “income” from nature. Groundwater is the savings account. Many aquifers fill slowly over centuries or millennia. Like savings, they are meant for emergencies such as droughts, not for paying everyday bills. Bankruptcy comes when a society spends more than its income for so long that it also drains its savings. Then not every claim on the water, from cities, farmers, industry and nature, can be honored any more. Glaciers, snowpack, wetlands and soils are part of the savings too, which is why the shrinking glaciers I wrote about earlier are a sign of the same problem. 3. The formal definition According to Madani, water bankruptcy is a persistent condition in which two things are true: Insolvency. Over the long term, people take more water from rivers and aquifers than the system renews, and more than the safe limits for depleting reserves and stressing ecosystems. Irreversibility. The resulting damage to water-related nature, such as compacted aquifers, subsided land, dried wetlands, melted glaciers and lost species, cannot be undone without unacceptable costs, so the historical level of water supply cannot be restored. The second condition is what makes water bankruptcy different from financial bankruptcy. A bankrupt company can restructure and even grow beyond its old size. A bankrupt water system cannot return to its old baseline: the baseline itself has moved (Figure 1). Figure 1. Three states of concern in a human–water system, following Madani (2026a): (a) water stress, where the system is under pressure but still recovers; (b) water crisis, an acute shock followed by recovery; and (c) water bankruptcy, where long-term overdraft lowers the baseline itself. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic with invented curves. Madani also stresses two points. First, water bankruptcy is a property of systems shaped by people, not of nature alone. Second, it is not about how much water a place has, but about how it is managed. A wet country can go bankrupt if it overspends; a dry one can stay solvent if it lives within its budget. 4. The global picture In January 2026, UNU-INWEH published a report, Global Water Bankruptcy: Living Beyond Our Hydrological Means in the Post-Crisis Era, with Madani as lead author. It argues that while not every basin or country is bankrupt, enough critical systems have crossed these thresholds that the world as a whole has entered an era of water bankruptcy. Some of its headline numbers (Figure 2): Nearly three-quarters of the world’s population lives in countries classified as water-insecure or critically water-insecure, and about 4 billion people face severe water scarcity for at least one month a year. More than half of the world’s large lakes have lost water since the early 1990s. Around 70% of the world’s major aquifers show long-term declines. Groundwater supplies about half of all domestic water and over 40% of irrigation water. About 410 million hectares of natural wetlands, almost the area of the European Union, have been lost over the past five decades. Land is subsiding over more than 6 million km², almost 5% of the world’s land area, including densely populated areas where close to 2 billion people live. In some places the ground sinks by up to 25 cm a year. Over 1.8 billion people lived under drought in 2022–2023, and drought damage already costs about 307 billion US dollars a year. Figure 2. Selected headline figures from the UNU-INWEH report; the report gives them as approximate values, as labeled. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on numbers reported by Madani (2026b). The report highlights hotspots such as the Middle East and North Africa, parts of South Asia where groundwater-fed farming and growing cities are lowering water tables, and the American Southwest, where the Colorado River has become a symbol of over-promised water. Its examples include the shrinking of the Aral Sea and the drying of Lake Urmia in Iran, Madani’s home country, where the term water bankruptcy first entered public debate about a decade ago. 5. What changes if we call it bankruptcy? Naming the problem correctly changes the response. Madani suggests five principles for governing a bankrupt water system: Admit it honestly and early. Promising a return to past water deliveries is unrealistic and, in his view, unethical. Shift from new supply to less demand and fair reallocation. New dams, deeper wells, water transfers and desalination can help, but they cannot erase decades of overcommitment, and often take on “more debt from nature”. Protect what remains. Remaining wetlands, aquifers, rivers and glaciers are now a strategic reserve. Rethink development goals, including national ambitions for self-sufficiency in water-hungry crops. Share the losses fairly, with transparent rules, participation and safety nets for those whose livelihoods must change. Climate change, in this view, does not cause water bankruptcy, but it makes it worse: it reduces the “income” of rain and snow, raises the “spending” through higher evaporation and crop water demand, and makes the swings between wet and dry years larger. This fits the idea of human-made, or anthropogenic, drought discussed in my post on drought monitoring. 6. A few thoughts The concept is powerful because it combines two things that are usually discussed separately: the water balance (how much we take compared with how much is renewed) and the condition of the natural systems that produce the water. It also reminds us that admitting failure is not giving up. It is the first step towards realistic plans. There are open questions too. Where exactly is the line between a severe, long-lasting stress and bankruptcy? The definition deliberately sets no numerical thresholds, because they differ from basin to basin, and the paper calls for indicators to be developed. Turning the idea into something that can be measured and monitored will be a task for hydrologists. Korea receives plenty of rain, so the term may sound distant. But Madani’s point is that bankruptcy depends on management, not on how wet a place is. Groundwater levels, wetland losses and the balance between water rights and what rivers can actually deliver are worth watching through this lens. Questions to think about Think of a water problem in your country that has been called a “crisis” for decades. Would “bankruptcy” describe it better? Why or why not? In the bank account analogy, what would a “fresh start” look like for an over-pumped aquifer? Which indicators would you use to decide whether a river basin is water-bankrupt? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). Madani(2026a)는 수십 년째 이어지는 물 문제를 일시적 충격을 뜻하는 ‘물 위기’로 부르는 것은 잘못이라며, ‘물 파산(water bankruptcy)’을 처음으로 공식 정의했다. 물 파산은 장기간 재생 가능한 양과 안전한 한계를 넘어 하천수와 지하수를 끌어 쓴 상태(지불불능)이면서, 그 결과 대수층 압밀, 지반침하, 습지 소실, 빙하 손실처럼 되돌릴 수 없는 피해가 생겨 과거의 물 공급 수준을 회복할 수 없는 상태(비가역성)를 말한다. 지표수를 입출금 계좌, 지하수를 저축 계좌에 비유하면, 물 파산은 수입보다 많이 쓰다 저축까지 바닥낸 상황이며, 회복할 수 있는 금융 파산과 달리 기준선 자체가 낮아진다는 점이 다르다. UNU-INWEH 보고서(Madani 2026b)는 대형 호수의 절반 이상이 물을 잃고 주요 대수층의 약 70%가 장기 감소하는 등 세계가 이미 ‘물 파산의 시대’에 들어섰다고 보고, 실패를 인정하고 공급 확대보다 수요 감축, 공정한 재배분, 남은 자연 자본 보호로 전환할 것을 촉구한다. References Madani, K. (2026a). Water bankruptcy: the formal definition. Water Resources Management, 40, 78. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11269-025-04484-0 Madani, K. (2026b). Global Water Bankruptcy: Living Beyond Our Hydrological Means in the Post-Crisis Era. United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH), Richmond Hill, Ontario, Canada. https://doi.org/10.53328/INR26KAM001 The figures are original. The Python scripts that produce them are available on GitHub: Figure 1 and Figure 2.

title: The shrinking frozen reservoirs of the American West
description: The first complete count of glacier change in the conterminous United States, by Fountain and colleagues, finds that about a quarter of the glaciers have disappeared since the mid-twentieth century and a third of the ice is gone, weakening a natural buffer against late-summer drought.
tags: glaciers mountain hydrology water storage drought climate change
text: When we think of water storage in the western United States, we think of the large dams on the Colorado and Columbia rivers, or of the winter snowpack. Glaciers are rarely on the list. They are small, remote and few compared with those in Alaska or Canada. Yet a new study in PNAS by Andrew Fountain and colleagues shows why they matter, and how quickly they are disappearing (Fountain et al. 2026). 1. Why small glaciers matter for water Snow and glaciers both store winter precipitation and release it later. But they behave differently. Seasonal snow melts in spring and early summer and is usually gone by July. Glaciers last from year to year, and they keep melting in late summer, when it is hottest and driest and other water sources run low. Glaciers also act as a natural buffer. In a hot, dry summer they melt more and add more water to streams; in a cool summer they melt less. This keeps streamflow more even from year to year and supplies cold water that many alpine fish and insects depend on. As glaciers shrink, this buffer weakens, and mountain streams become more exposed to drought and warmer water. 2. The first complete count Surprisingly, nobody had measured the change of all the glaciers in the lower 48 states before. Individual glaciers have been studied since the late 1950s, but a complete inventory was compiled only recently. The authors compared two inventories: a historic one, taken from US Geological Survey topographic maps made between the early 1950s and the mid-1980s, a relatively cool period when glaciers were fairly stable, and a recent one, from aerial and satellite images taken around 2015. To estimate how much thinner the glaciers have become, they compared the old map elevations with modern elevation data from radar satellites and airborne laser scanning (lidar). 3. What they found The numbers are stark: The number of glaciers fell from 1,453 to 1,331. In total, 398 glaciers, about a quarter, disappeared. The net loss looks smaller only because some large glaciers split into several smaller pieces as they retreated. Glacier area fell by about 35%, from about 562 to 367 km², a rate of about 8% per decade. That is faster than in the Austrian Alps, Norway or the eastern Himalaya over comparable periods (Figure, panel b). Glacier surfaces dropped by about 11.6 m on average. The total ice volume fell by about a third, from about 19.7 to 13.2 km³. The lost ice, about 6.5 km³, is equivalent to about 5.5 billion tonnes of water. The smallest glaciers suffered most. Glaciers smaller than 0.1 km² lost about two-thirds of their area, while the largest lost about 15%. Figure. (a) Change in glacier area from the mid-twentieth century to about 2015 in the mountain ranges with at least 2 km² of glacier ice at the start, with ranges in Washington in blue and those in other states in red. (b) Rate of glacier area change per decade in the western United States compared with other regions, as quoted by Fountain et al. (2026) from earlier studies. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on numbers reported by Fountain et al. (2026). 4. Wet coasts versus dry interior The losses are far from even. Most of the ice is in the wet, maritime climate of Washington State, where the North Cascades alone hold about 89% of the remaining glacier volume. Glaciers there have lost about 29% of their area on average. Outside Washington, in the drier continental climate of the Sierra Nevada and the Rocky Mountains, glaciers have shrunk much faster, by about 52% on average. The Sierra Nevada and the Beartooth Mountains of Montana have lost about three-quarters of their ice volume. There is even one glacier that grew. After Mount St. Helens erupted in 1980, a new glacier, Crater Glacier, formed inside its crater. Between 2003 and 2015 it grew by 64% in area and thickened by about 100 m. 5. Small glaciers live by local rules One might expect higher glaciers, in cooler air, to lose less ice. In the wet Cascades there is a weak trend of this kind, but in the dry interior there is none. The authors explain this by the glaciers’ small size: most are smaller than 1 km², and their survival depends less on regional climate than on local terrain. Snow blown by wind or brought down by avalanches from the valley walls can matter as much as snowfall itself, and shade from steep cliffs protects ice from the summer sun. Many of these glaciers, in other words, are hanging on in sheltered spots in a climate that no longer favors them. 6. What this means for water The remaining ice, about 13.2 km³, is not much on the scale of a continent. By my own rough calculation, using the authors’ conversion from ice to water, it holds about 11 km³ of water, roughly four times the storage of Korea’s largest reservoir, the Soyang Dam. Its value lies less in its total amount than in its timing: it releases water in late summer, exactly when streams are lowest and warmest. That is why the shrinking of these glaciers matters for hydrology. With smaller glaciers, mountain streams will lose part of their late-summer supply and their buffer against drought, at the same time as the snowpack shrinks and reservoirs become less reliable. And because the losses vary so much from one range to the next, the effects on streams and ecosystems will be uneven too. Korea has no glaciers, but the lesson is familiar. Any natural storage, whether snow, glaciers, wetlands or groundwater, helps to smooth out the water supply between wet and dry seasons. When it disappears, the pressure on man-made storage grows. Questions to think about Why does a glacier provide more water in a hot, dry summer than in a cool one? Why is that useful? The smallest glaciers lost the largest share of their area. Why might small glaciers be more vulnerable? What natural forms of water storage exist in your region, and how are they changing? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). Fountain 등(2026)은 미국 본토의 모든 빙하를 20세기 중반 지형도와 2015년 무렵 항공·위성 자료로 처음 전수 비교해, 1,453개 빙하 중 398개(약 4분의 1)가 사라지고 면적은 약 35%(10년에 약 8%), 얼음 부피는 약 3분의 1(19.7 km³에서 13.2 km³로) 줄었음을 보였다. 감소 속도는 오스트리아 알프스, 노르웨이, 동부 히말라야보다 빨랐고, 작은 빙하일수록, 그리고 습윤한 워싱턴주보다 건조한 내륙(시에라네바다, 로키산맥)에서 손실이 훨씬 컸다. 대부분 1 km²보다 작은 이 빙하들은 고도보다 바람에 날린 눈, 눈사태, 절벽 그늘 같은 국지 지형에 기대어 겨우 유지되고 있다. 빙하는 가장 덥고 건조한 늦여름에 물을 공급하고 해마다의 유량 변동을 완충하는 ‘얼어 있는 저수지’이므로, 빙하의 축소는 산지 하천이 가뭄과 수온 상승에 더 취약해진다는 뜻이다. Reference Fountain, A. G., Glenn, B., McNeil, C., & Menounos, B. (2026). Extensive glacier loss in the coterminous United States. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(43), e2600941123. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2600941123 The figure is original. The Python script that produces it is available on GitHub.

title: When floods team up: what 378 studies tell us about compound flooding
description: A systematic review by Mohseni and colleagues looks at compound floods, where heavy rain, high rivers and storm surge strike together. Such events are much more likely than we assume if we treat each driver separately, and research is still thin where it matters most.
tags: compound flooding flood risk storm surge non stationarity climate change
text: We usually think of floods one at a time: a river overflows, a downpour overwhelms city drains, or a storm pushes the sea onto the coast. In reality, the worst floods often come when several of these happen at once. When Hurricane Harvey struck Texas in 2017, extreme rainfall, high rivers and storm surge combined. Scientists call such events compound floods. A new systematic review in Environmental Impact Assessment Review by Usman Mohseni, R. Vinnarasi, Abdou Khouakhi and Amir AghaKouchak, published online in July 2026, brings together 378 studies of compound flooding from 1961 to 2025 (Mohseni et al. 2027). It asks three questions: what drives compound floods, how we model them, and where research should go next. This post is the second this week involving AghaKouchak’s group; the first looked at how one drought can set off a chain of other hazards. 1. Three main drivers, and many helpers The review finds that most compound floods involve three main drivers: Heavy rain (pluvial flooding), which overwhelms drains and fills streets, especially in cities with sealed surfaces. High river flow (fluvial flooding), from long or intense rain, snowmelt or dam releases. Storm surge (coastal flooding), the rise of the sea pushed by strong winds and low pressure in storms. The danger lies in how they interact. A high sea can block a river from draining into it, so the river backs up and floods inland. A high tide can stop city drains from emptying, so even moderate rain floods the streets. Soils that are already wet from earlier rain cannot absorb more, so the next downpour runs straight off. Many secondary factors make things worse: high tides, waves, sea-level rise, sinking land in deltas and coastal cities, rising groundwater, snowmelt, ice jams, and human structures such as levees and drains that work well for one hazard but can shift the risk elsewhere. 2. Why “together” changes the odds The key point is that the combined flood can be much worse, and much more likely, than each driver alone would suggest. Figure 1 shows a simple example. Suppose heavy rain and storm surge each reach their 10-year level. If the two were completely independent, both would happen together only once in about 100 years. But they are often not independent, because the same storm brings both the rain and the surge. With a modest link between them, the combined event becomes a once-in-about-46-years event, and with a stronger link, once in about 26 years. Figure 1. How often two 10-year events happen together depends on how strongly they are linked. With no link (independence), the joint event happens once in about 100 years; with a correlation of 0.6, once in about 26 years. Figure by Daeha Kim, a simple illustration using a standard statistical model (a Gaussian copula), not taken from the review. This is why the review stresses that ignoring the dependence between drivers leads to underestimating flood risk. A design that assumes independence may protect a coastal city far less well than its engineers think. 3. How we model compound floods The review groups the 378 studies by their main method: Statistical models (53% of studies) estimate how often drivers occur together, often with copulas, a family of tools that describe how two or more variables move together. They are fast and need little data, but they say nothing about where the water goes. Numerical models (42%) simulate the physics of water flowing over land, in rivers and along coasts. They show which streets flood and how deep, but they are slow and need detailed data. Hybrid models (5%) combine the two, for example by using statistics to choose realistic storm scenarios and a physical model to simulate them, or by training machine learning to mimic a slow physical model. They are still rare but growing quickly since about 2019. The review also highlights a growing problem: non-stationarity. Traditional flood statistics assume that the past is a good guide to the future. With rising seas, sinking land, more intense rain and expanding cities, that assumption no longer holds, and even the link between drivers may change over time. Only a small share of studies so far take this into account. 4. What the research is about, and where it comes from Research on compound flooding has exploded. Fewer than 20 studies appeared between 1961 and 2000, but more than 230, over 60% of the total, were published in just 2021–2025. Yet the focus is uneven (Figure 2). Figure 2. (a) Main research focus of the 378 reviewed studies and (b) the five countries with the most studies. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on numbers reported by Mohseni et al. (2027). Most studies develop methods or analyze the hazard itself. Far fewer assess the actual impacts on people and property (5%) or try to forecast compound floods in real time (4%). Geographically, the USA alone accounts for nearly a third of the studies, followed by China and the UK. Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, where many people live in exposed coastal deltas and cities, remain largely unstudied. 5. Where research should go next The authors propose several directions: Use more and better data, from satellites, weather reanalyses, sensors and even crowdsourcing and social media, to describe floods where gauges are scarce. Build models that allow change over time, linking the behavior of flood drivers to factors such as sea-level rise, land use and climate patterns like El Niño. Create libraries of flood maps for compound events. Such libraries exist for river floods, so that forecasters can quickly look up the expected flooding, but not yet for compound floods. Explore many scenarios, not just one, to deal with the deep uncertainty about future climate and cities. Connect the physics with people, including exposure, vulnerability and how human decisions shape flood risk. Close the regional gaps, especially in the most vulnerable parts of the world. 6. Why this matters for Korea Korea has a long coastline, large tidal ranges on the west coast, and typhoons that bring heavy rain and storm surge at the same time. Many cities, such as Busan, Incheon and Changwon, sit where rivers meet the sea. The review lists Korea among the countries with a moderate number of compound flood studies, so there is a base to build on. As sea levels rise and summer rainfall intensifies, flood planning that treats rain, rivers and the sea separately may increasingly underestimate the risk. Questions to think about Why might the same storm make both heavy rain and storm surge more likely? What does that do to the chance of a compound flood? Think of a coastal city you know. Where do its rivers and drains meet the sea, and what happens to them at high tide? A levee may protect against river floods but trap rainwater behind it. How should engineers design for more than one driver at once? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). Mohseni 등(2027)은 1961–2025년에 발표된 378편의 연구를 체계적으로 검토해, 집중호우, 하천 범람, 폭풍해일이 함께 일어나는 ‘복합홍수’의 원인과 모형, 앞으로의 과제를 정리했다. 같은 태풍이 비와 해일을 함께 몰고 오는 것처럼 원인들이 서로 연관되어 있으면, 각각 10년 빈도인 두 사건이 함께 일어날 확률은 독립을 가정할 때(100년에 한 번)보다 훨씬 커지므로 이를 따로 다루면 위험을 과소평가하게 된다. 연구는 2021–2025년에만 230편 이상이 나올 만큼 급증했지만, 통계 모형과 수치 모형을 결합한 하이브리드 모형, 기후변화에 따른 비정상성, 실제 피해 평가와 실시간 예측은 아직 적고, 연구의 약 3분의 1이 미국에 집중되어 있다. 해안 도시가 많고 태풍이 비와 해일을 함께 가져오는 한국에서도 비, 하천, 바다를 따로 보지 않는 복합홍수 관점의 홍수 계획이 점점 더 중요해지고 있다. Reference Mohseni, U., Vinnarasi, R., Khouakhi, A., & AghaKouchak, A. (2027). A systematic review of compound flooding: drivers, models, and future directions. Environmental Impact Assessment Review, 122, 108620. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eiar.2026.108620 The figures are original. The Python scripts that produce them are available on GitHub: Figure 1 and Figure 2.

title: Beyond the drought map: monitoring what drought actually does
description: A Perspective by AghaKouchak and colleagues argues that drought monitoring should move from measuring how dry it is to forecasting what the drought will do, including the heatwaves, wildfires, debris flows and floods that often follow it.
tags: drought cascading hazards drought monitoring remote sensing water security
text: Drought monitoring has come a long way. A century ago, it meant counting the days without rain at a few weather stations. Today, satellites measure rainfall, soil moisture, vegetation, snow and even the total water stored underground, and drought maps are updated every week. Yet a Perspective in Nature Reviews Earth & Environment by Amir AghaKouchak and 21 colleagues argues that these maps still answer the wrong question (AghaKouchak et al. 2023). They tell us how dry it is. What farmers, water managers and emergency planners need to know is what the drought will do. 1. Seventy indicators, one blind spot The authors count more than 70 drought indicators. Some use a single variable, such as the Standardized Precipitation Index for rainfall or soil moisture percentiles. Others combine several variables into one composite index. Operational systems, such as the US Drought Monitor, blend many of these with the judgment of hundreds of local experts. This variety exists for a good reason: drought is not one thing. A shortage of rain (meteorological drought) can lead to dry soils (agricultural drought), which can lead to low rivers, reservoirs and groundwater (hydrological drought), each on its own timescale. Snow adds another layer. In many mountain regions, the snowpack is the largest natural reservoir, and a “snow drought” can occur even after a normal winter if warm weather melts the snow too early. But all of these indicators share one feature: they describe the hazard, not its consequences. They are “top-down”. A map can show that soil moisture is two standard deviations below normal, but not whether this means a 10% or a 50% loss of wheat yield, a water shortage in a city, or a fire season ahead. 2. Droughts rarely come alone The second problem is that droughts are monitored in isolation, while in reality they set off chains of other hazards (Figure, panel a). The authors call these cascading hazards: Heatwaves. When soils dry out, less of the sun’s energy goes into evaporating water and more goes into heating the air. Drought and heat then feed each other. The 2003 European drought and heatwave is estimated to have killed more than 70,000 people. Wildfires. Drought dries out vegetation and turns it into fuel. Several years of drought preceded the extreme fire seasons in Australia and the western USA in 2020. Debris flows. Drought weakens soils and opens deep cracks, and fire removes the vegetation that holds slopes together. When intense rain then falls on burned slopes, mud and boulders can rush downhill. In Montecito, California, a drought from 2012 to 2016 was followed by a large fire in December 2017 and, a month later, by intense rain that triggered the deadliest debris flow in the state’s history. Floods. Droughts and floods are two ends of the same water cycle, and droughts can make floods worse. Cracked soils can weaken levees: during the dry summer of 2003, a dyke failed at Wilnis in the Netherlands, flooding about 600 homes. California’s 2012–16 drought ended with extreme rain that badly damaged the spillway of the Oroville Dam, and Australia’s Millennium Drought ended in 2011 with widespread flooding. Water quality. Low river flows mean less dilution and warmer water, which encourage algal blooms. The authors link drought to the dead zone in Lake Erie in 2012, and toxins from algae closed the water supply of Toledo, Ohio, in 2014. Figure. (a) A drought can set off a chain of further hazards, illustrated with the Montecito, California example described by AghaKouchak et al. (2023); the timeline is not to scale. (b) The shift the authors propose, from monitoring how dry it is to forecasting what the drought will do. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic based on AghaKouchak et al. (2023). None of the existing indicators captures these links. A drought index does not tell you that a wildfire is likely, and nothing tells you that the cracked soil on a burned hillside has become dangerous when the rain returns. 3. From “how dry?” to “what will it do?” The authors’ main proposal is impact-based drought monitoring (Figure, panel b). Instead of starting from rainfall and soil moisture, it starts from the things people care about: crop yields, food prices, drinking water, hydropower, jobs, health and the risk of fire or flood. Drought information is then linked to models that translate the hazard into these impacts, ideally months in advance. One example in the paper is snow. In many basins, irrigated wheat, rice and maize depend heavily on snowmelt. Linking a snow drought map to these farms would turn “less snow than normal” into “this much less irrigation water for these crops this summer”. 4. Why it is hard If this is such a good idea, why is it not done already? The authors list several obstacles: Few consistent impact records. Damage from drought is slow, spread out and often unrecorded. Systems such as the US Drought Impact Reporter, which lets citizens and local officials report impacts, are a start, but such data remain patchy. Missing water-use data. The impact of a drought depends on how much water people take and where it comes from. Even in the USA, water use by sector is published only at the county level every five years. Los Angeles, for example, cannot judge its drought risk from local rainfall alone, because much of its water comes from northern California and the Colorado River. Unknown local storage. Groundwater and the water stored in lakes and reservoirs are poorly measured in much of the world, and satellite measurements of total water storage are too coarse for a single basin. Disconnected tools. Drought monitors, crop models, fire systems and flood forecasts are run by different agencies and rarely talk to each other. 5. New data and AI as part of the solution The authors see two developments that could help. New satellites, such as SWOT (Surface Water and Ocean Topography), launched in December 2022, measure both the area and the water level of lakes and reservoirs, giving a new picture of how much water is actually stored. And with data volumes growing far beyond what people can inspect by hand, artificial intelligence, especially models that combine physical knowledge with machine learning, can help learn the complicated links between drought and its impacts. 6. What this means for us For water researchers, the message is that a good drought index is only the first step. The next step is to connect it to what happens on the ground, and to monitor droughts together with the heatwaves, fires and floods they bring, instead of in separate silos. This also matters for Korea. Our droughts are often short and sharp, such as flash droughts during hot summers, and they increasingly overlap with heatwaves, wildfires in spring and heavy monsoon rain. Knowing what a dry spell will do to reservoirs, farms and burned mountain slopes may be more useful than knowing that it is dry. Questions to think about Think of the last drought in your region. What did the drought map say, and what actually happened to farms, water supplies or forests? Why might a drought end in a flood? Which processes make the transition dangerous? If you could collect one new kind of data to forecast drought impacts better, what would it be? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). AghaKouchak 등(2023)은 70개가 넘는 가뭄 지수와 위성 자료로 가뭄 감시가 크게 발전했지만, 여전히 ‘얼마나 건조한가’라는 위험(hazard)만 보여줄 뿐 ‘그 가뭄이 무엇을 일으킬 것인가’라는 영향은 알려주지 못한다고 지적한다. 실제로 가뭄은 폭염, 산불, 산불 뒤 집중호우에 의한 토석류, 홍수, 수질 악화로 이어지는 연쇄 재해를 일으키는데(예: 2012–16년 가뭄, 2017년 12월 산불, 2018년 1월 토석류로 이어진 미국 캘리포니아주 몬테시토), 현재의 감시 체계는 이들을 따로따로 다룬다. 저자들은 작물 수확량, 식수, 수력발전, 일자리 같은 영향에서 출발하는 ‘영향 기반 가뭄 감시’로 전환하자고 제안하며, 이를 위해 일관된 영향 기록과 지역별 물 사용·저류량 자료, SWOT 같은 새 위성 자료, 그리고 물리 지식과 결합한 AI가 필요하다고 본다. 짧고 강한 돌발가뭄이 폭염, 봄철 산불, 장마철 호우와 겹치는 한국에서도 가뭄을 다른 재해와 함께, 그리고 그 영향 중심으로 감시할 필요가 크다. Reference AghaKouchak, A., Huning, L. S., Sadegh, M., Qin, Y., Markonis, Y., Vahedifard, F., et al. (2023). Toward impact-based monitoring of drought and its cascading hazards. Nature Reviews Earth & Environment, 4, 582–595. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43017-023-00457-2 The figure is original. The Python script that produces it is available on GitHub.

title: Ten years after Paris: what the 2026 Lancet Countdown says about climate and health
description: The tenth Lancet Countdown report tracks 54 indicators of how climate change affects our health. Its message is that the harms have not only grown since the Paris Agreement, but grown faster, from deadly heat to droughts and extreme rainfall.
tags: climate change health heat drought extreme precipitation adaptation
text: Every year since 2016, the year the Paris Agreement entered into force, a large international team has published a check-up on how climate change is affecting human health. The tenth report of the Lancet Countdown, written by 146 researchers and published in The Lancet in October 2026, looks back over that whole decade (Romanello et al. 2026). Its title sums up the conclusion: “a decade of escalating health harms and a decisive moment for all.” The report is long, with 54 indicators covering heat, extreme weather, infectious disease, food, air pollution, money and politics. Here I pick out the main messages, with a focus on the water-related ones that matter most to hydrologists. 1. Not only worse, but getting worse faster The most striking finding is about speed. Comparing the ten years after Paris (2016–25) with the ten years before (2006–15), the report finds that many health threats have not just increased, but increased at an accelerating rate (Figure). Figure. Four headline indicators, before and after the Paris Agreement entered into force: (a) average heat-related deaths per year (the latest period is 2016–23), (b) heatwave days per person aged 65 and over, (c) share of global land with at least one month of extreme drought in a year, and (d) share of global land with at least one very extreme daily rainfall (rarer than once in ten years) in a year. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on numbers reported by Romanello et al. (2026). Heat. Heat was linked to about 540,800 deaths per year in 2016–23, up from about 398,400 per year in the previous decade. In 2023, the number reached a record of about 710,000, and the authors attribute 71.5% of those deaths to human-caused climate change. In 2025, the average person on Earth experienced 13.5 heatwave days, and 11.3 of them would not have been expected without climate change. People over 65, who are the most vulnerable, faced 11.5 heatwave days a year on average, up from 7.2. Work and money. Heat cost 573 billion potential working hours in 2025, equivalent to about 1.07 trillion US dollars in lost income. The burden is strikingly unequal: in countries with the lowest human development the losses equal 5.0% of GDP, ten times the 0.5% in the most developed countries. 2. Water extremes: drier and wetter at the same time For hydrologists, the drought and rainfall indicators are the most interesting part of the report. Drought. In 2016–25, on average 41.7% of the world’s land experienced at least one month of extreme drought each year, up from 28.4% in 2006–15. In 2025, the figure was 51.8%, the second highest on record after 2023 (54.9%). The report measures drought in two ways: from climate data, using a standard drought index that combines rainfall and evaporation, and from GRACE satellites, which weigh changes in the water stored on and under the land. Water storage. The satellite data show that between 2003 and 2025, water storage fell in about 43% of global land and rose in about 37%. Drying and wetting are happening side by side, often in neighboring regions. Extreme rainfall. In 2016–25, 17.2% of global land saw at least one very extreme daily rainfall (rarer than a 1-in-10-year event) each year, up from 14.8%. The growth itself has sped up: the increase was 57% larger than in the decade before. Droughts are the single most destructive climate hazard for agriculture, and floods bring injuries, drowning, contaminated water and waterborne disease. The report also warns that these hazards increasingly come together or one after another, so the real risk can be larger than any single indicator suggests. 3. Adaptation is lagging Protection is not keeping pace. By 2025, about three in four WHO member states had not reported completing a health vulnerability and adaptation assessment since 2020, and about seven in ten had no health adaptation plan. International climate finance has covered less than a third of even the limited adaptation needs that developing countries have reported, and development aid is falling sharply. The report notes that aid from the 17 largest donors is projected to drop by roughly a quarter within three years, with South Korea among the countries making the largest proportional cuts. There are bright spots. Early warning systems for climate-related health hazards now exist in 75 countries, and 56 countries have a health adaptation plan, up from 14 in 2015. 4. The fossil fuel problem, and the opportunity Fossil fuels still supply about 81% of the world’s energy. They also harm health directly: air pollution from burning them caused about 2.78 million deaths a year on average since 2016. Meanwhile, countries spent a cumulative 6.2 trillion US dollars on net fossil fuel subsidies between 2016 and 2024, and in 2024 ten countries spent more on these subsidies than on their health systems. But the report also documents real progress. Renewables are now cheaper than fossil power in many places, clean energy investment in 2025 exceeded fossil fuel investment by 82%, and in more than half of the 140 countries assessed, deaths from fossil fuel air pollution have fallen, saving an estimated 323,000 lives a year. Expected warming by 2100 has come down from 3.0–3.5 °C to 2.6–3.4 °C since the Paris Agreement. That is still far too high, but it shows that action works. 5. A decisive moment The authors are frank about the politics. The USA withdrew from the Paris Agreement and WHO, climate disinformation is growing, and the 2026 war involving Iran has disrupted oil markets, pushing some countries towards renewables and others back towards fossil fuels. Against this, the report calls for six priorities, including formally recognizing climate change as a global health emergency, putting the reduction of deaths and illness at the center of all climate policy, and building a global data commons on climate and health as a public good. That last point deserves attention from our field. Almost every indicator in this report rests on long, open records of temperature, rainfall, drought and water storage. Keeping those observations running, and openly available, is part of protecting health. Questions to think about The report measures drought both with a climate index and with satellite water storage. Why might the two give different pictures of the same drought? Heat costs the least developed countries ten times more of their GDP than the most developed ones. What makes the same heat so much more costly in some places? Which water-related health risks in your own country are tracked well, and which have no long-term record at all? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 파리협정 발효 10년을 맞아 146명의 연구진이 54개 지표로 기후변화가 건강에 미친 영향을 점검한 Romanello 등(2026)의 Lancet Countdown 10번째 보고서는, 지난 10년 동안 피해가 커졌을 뿐 아니라 그 증가 속도도 빨라졌다고 결론짓는다. 폭염 관련 사망은 연평균 약 39만 8천 명(2006–15년)에서 약 54만 1천 명(2016–23년)으로 늘었고, 극한 가뭄을 한 달 이상 겪은 육지 면적은 28.4%에서 41.7%로, 10년 빈도를 넘는 극한 강우를 겪은 면적은 14.8%에서 17.2%로 늘어 마르는 곳과 젖는 곳이 동시에 확대되고 있다. 반면 건강 적응 계획을 갖춘 나라는 여전히 소수이고 국제 원조는 줄어들고 있지만, 재생에너지 투자 확대로 대기오염 사망이 줄어든 나라도 절반을 넘는 등 행동의 효과도 분명히 나타나고 있다. 보고서는 기후변화를 세계 보건 비상사태로 인정하고 기후·건강 자료를 공공재로 구축할 것을 촉구하며, 이는 장기 수문·기상 관측을 지키는 일이 곧 건강을 지키는 일임을 보여준다. Reference Romanello, M., Walawender, M., Israelsson, J., Hasan, M. M., Battaglia, F., Dutta, A., et al. (2026). The 2026 report of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change: a decade of escalating health harms and a decisive moment for all. The Lancet, 408, 1979–2032. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(26)01779-4 The figure is original. The Python script that produces it is available on GitHub.

title: Push until it breaks: why good research tells you where it fails
description: A Nature Communications editorial asks engineers to test their methods and models until they fail and to report where and why. Hydrologists have argued the same for forty years, and a changing climate makes the point more urgent than ever.
tags: research practice hydrological modelling model evaluation climate change
text: Most research papers are success stories. A new method works, a model fits the data, a device performs as designed. What we rarely read is where the method stops working. A short editorial in Nature Communications argues that this silence is a missed opportunity, and asks authors to do something unusual: push their work until it breaks, and tell readers where and why (Nature Communications 2026). 1. What the editorial asks for The message is simple. Don’t only show that your system works under expected conditions; test its boundaries. Push your assumptions, methods, models or devices until they falter, and report the point where they fail and the reason. The editors acknowledge that testing to failure costs time and money. But they argue that the breaking points are not weaknesses to hide. They are some of the most useful information a paper can contain, because they tell others how the work can be used responsibly, and where the next advance has to come from. A paper that shows where it fails helps define the frontier of a field, instead of only adding to it. The editorial also offers practical advice: Be selective. Report the failures that matter for the main claims, and put side analyses in the supplementary material. Learn from past reviews. Since November 2022, the journal has published the peer-review files of its research articles. Reading what reviewers asked for in similar work shows which limitations the community cares about. Don’t fear rejection. Disclosed limitations, on their own, are not held against a paper by the editors, and reviewers are asked to take the same view. 2. Hydrologists have been saying this for forty years This idea will be familiar to hydrologists. In 1986, Vít Klemeš proposed a hierarchy of tests for hydrological models (Klemeš 1986). The simplest, the split-sample test, calibrates a model on one part of a record and checks it on another. But if both parts come from similar climate, the test says little about how the model behaves when conditions change. Klemeš therefore proposed a tougher differential split-sample test: calibrate the model in wet years and test it in dry years, or the other way around. A model meant for a changing world should pass that test. Two decades later, Andréassian and colleagues called for “crash tests” of hydrological models, borrowing the idea from the car industry: you learn the most about a car’s safety by deliberately driving it into a wall (Andréassian et al. 2009). When such tests were run on 216 Australian catchments, model errors grew as the climate of the test period moved further from that of the calibration period (Coron et al. 2012). 3. A toy crash test The figure below shows a simple example. Suppose the “real” relationship between annual precipitation and runoff in a catchment follows a Budyko curve, a well-established description of how precipitation is split between evaporation and runoff. Now fit a simple straight line to years with 1,100 to 1,500 mm of precipitation. Figure. A toy crash test. (a) “Real” annual runoff from a Budyko curve and a straight-line model fitted only to the years in the blue band. (b) The model’s error. Inside the calibration range the error is about 1%; below about 830 mm of precipitation it exceeds 20%, and in very dry years the model predicts negative runoff. Figure by Daeha Kim, an illustrative example that does not describe any real catchment. Inside the calibration range, the model is almost perfect, with errors around 1%. A paper that tested it only there would report an excellent model. But in drier years, the error grows quickly: at 800 mm the model underestimates runoff by more than a quarter, and below about 620 mm it predicts negative runoff, which is physically impossible. The useful finding is not that the model works, but where it stops working: somewhere around 830 mm of annual precipitation. This is exactly what the editorial asks for. Reporting that breaking point does not make the model worse. It tells users when they can trust it. 4. Why this matters more in a changing climate For water and climate research, the stakes are high. Almost every study of climate change impacts asks a model to work under conditions it has never seen: warmer temperatures, longer droughts, more intense rainfall. In a sense, every climate projection is a differential split-sample test that we cannot run, because the future data do not exist yet. The least we can do is test our models across the widest range of past conditions available and say clearly where they began to fail. The same applies beyond hydrology. Machine-learning models are notorious for performing brilliantly on data similar to their training set and failing on anything different. Engineering designs, statistical methods and AI tools all have edges, and users deserve to know where they are. 5. What this means in practice For students and young researchers, the editorial suggests a few habits worth adopting: State the range of conditions you tested, for example the climates, catchment types or data periods, and avoid claims beyond it. Deliberately test the hard cases, such as the driest years, the largest floods or the most unusual catchments, even if the results look bad. Report where and why your method fails, not just that it fails. The “why” is what helps others improve it. Treat limitations as results, not as an apologetic paragraph at the end of the discussion. It takes some courage to show where your own work breaks. But in research, as in engineering, knowing where things fail is as valuable as knowing that they work. Questions to think about In your last model study, what was the driest or most extreme condition you tested? Would you trust the model beyond it? Why do you think papers so rarely report failures? What could reviewers and journals do to change that? If you were asked to design a “crash test” for a model in your field, what wall would you drive it into? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). Nature Communications 사설(2026)은 공학 연구가 잘 되는 결과만 보여주지 말고, 방법과 모형을 한계까지 밀어붙여 어디서 왜 실패하는지를 보고하라고 요청하며, 밝힌 한계 자체는 심사에서 불리하게 보지 않겠다고 밝혔다. 수문학에서는 이미 1986년 Klemeš가 습윤한 해에 보정하고 건조한 해에 검증하는 ‘차등 분할표본 검정’을 제안했고, 2009년에는 모형을 일부러 극한 조건에 부딪쳐 보는 ‘충돌 시험’이 제안되었다. 간단한 예시에서 좁은 범위에 맞춘 모형은 그 안에서는 오차가 1% 정도로 완벽해 보이지만, 연 강수량이 약 830 mm 아래로 내려가면 오차가 20%를 넘고 매우 건조한 해에는 음의 유출을 예측한다. 기후변화 영향 연구는 모형이 겪어보지 않은 조건에서 쓰이는 만큼, 어디까지 시험했고 어디서 실패하는지를 분명히 밝히는 것이 결과만큼 중요하다. References Andréassian, V., Perrin, C., Berthet, L., Le Moine, N., Lerat, J., Loumagne, C., Oudin, L., Mathevet, T., Ramos, M.-H., & Valéry, A. (2009). HESS Opinions “Crash tests for a standardized evaluation of hydrological models”. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences, 13, 1757–1764. https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-13-1757-2009 Coron, L., Andréassian, V., Perrin, C., Lerat, J., Vaze, J., Bourqui, M., & Hendrickx, F. (2012). Crash testing hydrological models in contrasted climate conditions: an experiment on 216 Australian catchments. Water Resources Research, 48(5). https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR011721 Klemeš, V. (1986). Operational testing of hydrological simulation models. Hydrological Sciences Journal, 31, 13–24. https://doi.org/10.1080/02626668609491024 Nature Communications (2026). Push until it breaks: engineering is stronger when we know its limits. Nature Communications, 17, 8005. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76456-w The figure is original. The Python script that produces it is available on GitHub.

title: Ageing pipes, ageing people: the double ageing of water infrastructure
description: A reading of a Nature Water comment by Vahedifard and colleagues: much of the world's water infrastructure was built for young, growing societies after the Second World War, and both the pipes and the people they serve have now grown old, a mismatch that matters more as climate extremes intensify.
tags: water infrastructure climate risk population ageing water security adaptation
text: Most of the pipes, dams, levees and treatment plants that serve us today were built in a burst after the Second World War, mostly between the 1950s and 1970s. They are now reaching the end of their design lives at about the same time. That alone is a big engineering problem. A new comment in Nature Water by Vahedifard and colleagues argues that it is only half of the problem: the people these systems serve have aged too, and planning rarely takes that into account (Vahedifard et al. 2026). 1. The first ageing: the infrastructure The numbers the authors collect are striking: In the USA, nearly a fifth of drinking-water mains, more than 724,000 km of pipe, have already passed their design life of 75–100 years. In England and Wales, water mains were 57 years old on average in 2021, and 13% were more than 100 years old. US levees protecting property worth over 2 trillion US dollars are 62 years old on average. Large dams in the UK and Japan are, on average, more than a century old. Worldwide, more than half of large dams with a known completion date are already 50 years or older. On top of this, infrastructure built for the climate of the twentieth century is now being asked to cope with the floods, droughts and heatwaves of the twenty-first. 2. The second ageing: the people The postwar systems were built for young, growing societies with an expanding workforce and tax base. That is no longer the world they serve. The number of people aged 65 and over is projected to reach 1.6 billion by 2050, nearly double the 2021 level. Japan and more than twenty European countries already have a fifth to a third of their populations over 65. South Korea is the most dramatic case (Figure 1). In 1970, when much of its modern water infrastructure was being built, only about 3% of Koreans were 65 or older. In December 2024 the share passed 20%, making Korea a “super-aged” society, and in the most rural provinces, such as Jeollanam-do, it is above 27%. Figure 1. Share of the population aged 65 and over, 1960–2025, in five countries. The shaded band marks the post-war decades in which much of today’s water infrastructure was built. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on World Bank data (World Development Indicators, from the UN World Population Prospects). 3. When two kinds of ageing meet The authors call the growing mismatch between a water system and the society it serves the infrastructure–society ageing gap. A water network built in the 1960s for a young, growing town may, sixty years later, serve a smaller and older population with less money, more health vulnerabilities and different needs. The pipes and the people have aged by the same number of years, but they no longer fit each other. The gap shows up in four ways: Workforce. Experienced operators and engineers are retiring faster than they can be replaced, taking system-specific know-how with them. Health. Older people are more vulnerable when the water stops or becomes unsafe. They may find it harder to fetch bottled water, follow a boil-water notice or leave home during a flood. Money. Many utilities depend on water bills. A shrinking customer base means less money for maintenance, while pensions and healthcare compete for public budgets. Place. Older populations, the oldest pipes and the weakest utility finances tend to sit in the same places: rural, post-industrial and economically struggling regions. 4. A spiral that is hard to escape The real danger, the authors argue, is that these four effects feed each other (Figure 2). Old pipes break more often. Unreliable service pushes younger residents to move away. The town becomes smaller and older, uses less water and pays less in water bills. The utility postpones repairs to stay solvent, and the pipes deteriorate faster. Less water use even causes its own problems: water sits longer in oversized pipes, and quality can suffer. Figure 2. How ageing water infrastructure and an ageing, shrinking community can reinforce each other. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic of the decline spiral described by Vahedifard et al. (2026). There is no natural way out of this loop. Without outside investment, new policies or new plans, each round makes the next one worse, and the longer it runs, the more expensive it becomes to fix. 5. Why this is a climate-risk problem For me, the most important example in the comment is about floods. Imagine a levee that has been perfectly maintained and is structurally as good as the day it was built. When it was designed, it was assumed that residents would receive a warning and move themselves to safety within a few hours. If many of those residents are now in their eighties, some living alone and some in care homes, the protection the levee actually provides has fallen, even though the levee itself has not changed. In other words, protection is not only a property of the structure, but also of the people’s ability to benefit from it. The same is true for droughts and heatwaves: a water outage during a heatwave is far more dangerous for older people than for younger ones. As climate extremes become more frequent, the cost of ignoring who lives behind the levee or at the end of the pipe will rise. 6. Planning for the people, not only the pipes Major works on water infrastructure happen rarely. A water main may be replaced once every 75–100 years, and a levee raised once in a generation. Population change, by contrast, never stops. Each major intervention therefore sets the design assumptions for decades. The authors contrast two approaches. An intervention that ignores the gap simply restores the system to its original design, as if the population were still the same. An intervention that accounts for the gap asks a different question: not just “how old is this asset?” but “who will this system serve over its lifetime?” The physical work may be similar, but the design, emergency plans, communication and financing are updated for the people who actually live there now. In ageing communities, that might mean better protection and communication for vulnerable residents during outages, more affordable pricing, and financing that does not rely solely on a shrinking customer base. In young, growing places, it means flexibility and extra capacity. The authors call for standard indicators of this gap, an open global observatory linking population projections with infrastructure inventories and condition data, and international cooperation, raising the issue at the 2026 UN Water Conference. For Korea, where the population is ageing faster than in almost any other major economy and ageing is most advanced in rural areas, this seems especially relevant. Flood warnings, drought responses and pipe-renewal plans all quietly assume something about who will receive them, act on them and pay for them. It may be time to make those assumptions explicit. Questions to think about Think of a levee or dam near where you live. When it was built, who was it designed to protect, and has that population changed? If a rural water utility loses a third of its customers over the next 20 years, who should pay to keep its pipes working? How should flood warning and evacuation plans change in a town where a quarter of residents are over 65? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). Vahedifard 등(2026)은 2차 세계대전 이후 젊고 성장하는 사회를 위해 지어진 상수도, 댐, 제방 같은 물 인프라가 설계수명에 이르는 동시에 그 인프라가 서비스하는 사람들도 늙어 가는 ‘이중 고령화’를 지적하고, 이 둘의 어긋남을 ‘인프라–사회 고령화 격차’라고 불렀다. 숙련 인력의 은퇴, 고령자의 건강 취약성, 줄어드는 요금 수입, 그리고 노후 시설과 고령 인구가 같은 지역에 몰리는 현상이 서로를 강화해, 노후 관로 고장이 젊은 층의 유출과 수입 감소, 보수 지연으로 이어지는 악순환을 만들 수 있다. 특히 구조적으로 완벽한 제방이라도 주민 다수가 스스로 대피하기 어려운 고령자라면 실제 보호 수준은 떨어진 것이므로, 기후 극한이 잦아지는 시대의 기후위험 관리에서는 시설의 나이뿐 아니라 ‘이 시설이 앞으로 누구를 위해 쓰일 것인가’를 물어야 한다. 2024년 말 초고령사회에 들어선 한국, 특히 고령화가 빠른 농촌 지역의 물 관리 계획에 시사하는 바가 크다. References Vahedifard, F., Azhar, M., Li, J., AghaKouchak, A., Brown, D. C., Marfeo, E., Null, S. E., Spearing, L. A., & Tajik, N. (2026). title: Global fossil CO2 emissions set to fall in 2026, the first drop since Covid
description: The Hormuz crisis has pushed global oil demand into its first decline since 2020, and new estimates suggest fossil CO2 emissions will fall by about 0.5% this year. Why it is happening, how it compares with past declines, why coal is rising at the same time, and whether the drop can last.
tags: climate change carbon emissions energy fossil fuels
text: Global CO2 emissions from fossil fuels have fallen in only a handful of years since 1960, and almost every time something had gone badly wrong with the world economy. The last time was 2020, when Covid lockdowns emptied roads and skies. According to a new estimate from Carbon Brief, 2026 may join the list: global fossil-fuel CO2 emissions are set to fall by around 0.5% this year (Evans 2026). Half a percent sounds small, and it is. But emissions have risen in almost every year for decades, and the Global Carbon Project’s latest assessment projected a new record for 2025, about 1% higher than 2024 (Friedlingstein et al. 2026). A fall, if confirmed, would be the first since Covid and one of the few in more than 60 years. 1. What is happening The trigger is the war between the US and Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz since early 2026. Before the crisis, more than 20 million barrels of oil a day passed through the strait. The disruption sent oil and gas prices soaring. In October, Brent crude futures traded around 107 US dollars a barrel and diesel benchmarks reached all-time highs in Europe and the US (IEA 2026b). High prices and scarce fuel have cut demand. The International Energy Agency (IEA), whose monthly oil reports are the standard reference, started the year expecting global oil demand to grow by 930,000 barrels a day in 2026. Month by month, as the crisis began and then dragged on, it revised that forecast down. By October it expected demand to fall by 2.6 million barrels a day, about 2.5%, the first annual decline since 2020 (Figure 1). Even with a partial recovery, it expects 2027 demand to remain slightly below the 2025 level (IEA 2026b). Figure 1. The IEA’s forecast of the change in global oil demand in 2026, as published in its monthly Oil Market Reports during the year (the February value is not shown). Figure by Daeha Kim, based on IEA Oil Market Reports (2026) and Carbon Brief (Evans 2026). 2. Oil and gas down, coal up Carbon Brief’s estimate combines the IEA’s latest forecasts for each fossil fuel (Evans 2026): Oil: down about 2.4% from 2025, the main reason emissions are falling. Gas: down about 0.6% already in the IEA’s July forecast, with pressure from high prices growing since. Coal: up about 1.2%, instead of the small decline the IEA had expected at the start of the year. The rise in coal has prompted headlines about a “return to coal”, and part of it is indeed a response to expensive gas. But few countries can switch from gas to coal at scale, and much of the increase has nothing to do with Hormuz. One cause will be familiar to hydrologists: a strong El Niño has raised demand for cooling and reduced hydropower output in key markets, so coal plants have filled the gap left by dry reservoirs. Another is the large amount of wind and solar power that China’s grid could not absorb earlier in the year. Overall, the extra emissions from coal are more than offset by the declines in oil and gas. 3. China leads the fall China, the world’s largest emitter, shows the change most clearly. Its CO2 emissions fell by 3.1% year on year in the third quarter of 2026, the largest quarterly drop since the 2022 Covid lockdowns, and are now down about 0.5% for the year to date (Myllyvirta 2026). Coal use fell by 3% and oil use by 4%, with transport fuel down 9%. What makes China different is that clean alternatives were ready. In the third quarter, generation from solar, wind and nuclear rose by 110 terawatt-hours, more than twice the growth in electricity demand. Electric vehicles reached a record 67% of passenger car sales and half of heavy-truck sales in September. China’s emissions have now been flat or falling since March 2024. Elsewhere, too, high fuel prices have pushed electric car sales to record shares, from Australia to Europe, Indonesia and Thailand, and EV sales in markets outside China, Europe and North America nearly doubled year on year in July (Evans 2026). 4. How this compares with past declines Figure 2 shows every annual change in global fossil CO2 since 1960. Declines are rare, and nearly all of them line up with crises: the second oil shock after the Iranian revolution (1980–82), the collapse of the Soviet Union (1992), the global financial crisis (2009) and Covid-19 (2020). Each time, emissions rebounded once the economy recovered. In 2021, they jumped by almost 5%. Figure 2. Annual change in global CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and industry. Blue bars mark declines. The hatched bar is the Global Carbon Project’s projection for 2025 and the orange bar Carbon Brief’s estimate for 2026. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on Global Carbon Budget 2025 data (Friedlingstein et al. 2026, via Our World in Data) and Evans (2026). There is a striking historical echo here. The biggest decline before 1992 also followed an oil shock linked to Iran. In 1979–80, the Iranian revolution and the Iran–Iraq war sent oil prices soaring, and global emissions fell for three years in a row. That crisis had lasting effects: it pushed countries toward nuclear power, efficiency standards and, in some places, coal, and oil never regained its earlier share of the energy mix. 5. Will it last? That is the real question, and the honest answer is that nobody knows yet. Arguments on both sides: Why it may be temporary. The decline is driven by a supply shock, not by climate policy. If shipping through Hormuz recovers and prices fall, oil demand is likely to bounce back, as it did after 2009 and 2020. Analysts expect Chinese oil use to rebound once prices ease (Myllyvirta 2026). Coal could also rise again if gas stays expensive into 2027. Why it may not be. Unlike 1980 or 2020, cheap alternatives are now available at scale. A household that buys an electric car because petrol is expensive does not switch back when prices fall, and solar panels installed this year will generate for decades. “For every month the conflict lasts, the probability of permanent demand destruction increases,” as one analyst at the consultancy DNV put it (quoted in Evans 2026). The IEA, which had expected oil demand to keep growing until about 2030, now expects it to be roughly flat for two years. Governments that had planned to rely on imported liquefied gas are signaling a shift toward domestic clean energy, though some also toward keeping coal plants open longer. Why it is not enough either way. Even a lasting decline of half a percent a year falls far short of what the Paris goals require. The UN Environment Programme estimates that global greenhouse gas emissions would need to fall by about 42% by 2030 from 2019 levels to keep 1.5°C within reach (UNEP 2024). The Global Carbon Project estimates that the remaining carbon budget for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5°C was about 170 billion tonnes of CO2 at the start of 2026, roughly four years of current emissions (Friedlingstein et al. 2026). A peak is necessary, but it is only the first step. 6. What to watch The Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment, usually published in November around the UN climate summit, will give the first independent full-year estimate, and final figures will only come with energy statistics next year. Until then, a few things are worth watching: whether Hormuz traffic recovers, whether the strong El Niño now developing keeps pushing up coal use and cutting hydropower, and whether the EV surge in emerging markets continues once prices fall. Either way, 2026 is a reminder of something easy to forget: energy systems can change faster than expected when people are forced to choose. The open question is whether the world will remember the lesson when prices come down. Questions to think about The 1970s oil shocks reshaped energy policy for decades. What policies today would turn a temporary price shock into a lasting fall in emissions? Drought and El Niño reduced hydropower and raised coal use this year. How should water resource planning account for the link between droughts and carbon emissions? If emissions fall in 2026 mainly because fuel became scarce and expensive, should it be counted as climate progress? Why or why not? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 미국–이란 전쟁으로 호르무즈 해협 수송이 막히면서 유가와 가스 가격이 급등했고, Evans(2026)의 분석에 따르면 2026년 세계 화석연료 CO2 배출량은 약 0.5% 줄어 코로나 이후 처음으로 감소할 전망이다. 석유 수요가 약 2.4% 줄고 가스도 줄었지만, 석탄은 비싼 가스와 엘니뇨로 인한 수력발전 감소 등으로 오히려 1.2% 늘었고, 중국은 재생에너지와 전기차 덕분에 3분기 배출량이 3.1% 줄어 감소를 이끌었다. 1960년 이후 배출량이 줄어든 해는 대부분 오일쇼크, 소련 붕괴, 금융위기, 코로나 같은 위기 때였고 이후 곧 반등했지만, 이번에는 태양광과 전기차라는 값싼 대안이 이미 대규모로 존재한다는 점이 다르다. 다만 연 0.5% 감소는 1.5°C 목표에 필요한 감축(2030년까지 2019년 대비 약 42%)에 크게 못 미치므로, 정점은 시작일 뿐이다.
