title: The AI expectations gap: what the public and AI insiders expect by 2030
description: A reading of a new survey comparing about 11,000 US adults with staff at a frontier AI lab: both agree on what AI can do today, but they disagree sharply about 2030, about their own jobs and about the economy, and the gap seems to come from experience rather than from different theories.
tags: artificial intelligence large language models labor market survey forecasting
text: Ask people who build AI and people who do not what AI will be able to do in a few years, and you will get very different answers. That is not surprising. What is more interesting is why the answers differ: do the two groups hold different theories about how AI will affect work, or do they simply see different things every day? A report published in October 2026 by Sacher, Cotter, Jones, Korinek and McCrory at the Anthropic Institute tries to answer this with two surveys run in August 2026 (Sacher et al. 2026). One reached 10,980 US adults through the polling firm Morning Consult, weighted to be nationally representative. The other was an internal poll of 1,334 Anthropic staff, people who build frontier AI and use it all day. Both groups were asked the same questions about AI’s capabilities, how widely it will be used, how much time it saves, how independently it will work, and what happens to workers it displaces. One caution before the results: the report comes from an AI company and compares the public with that company’s own employees. I come back to what that means at the end. 1. Same view of today, different views of 2030 The two groups largely agree about the present. Asked when AI will be able to do each of eight tasks as well as a skilled professional, from writing routine emails to making a Nobel-level discovery, both ranked the tasks in nearly the same order of difficulty, and about a quarter of each group said AI can already design, conduct and publish a scientific study. They part ways about the future (Figure 1a). By 2027, about 9 in 10 staff expect AI to be able to run and publish scientific studies, against 38% of the public. By 2030, 91% of staff expect AI to be capable of a Nobel-level discovery, against 39% of US adults (44% when the survey was repeated in September). Perhaps the starkest difference: depending on the task, 19 to 40% of US adults said AI will never be able to do it, compared with at most 2% of staff. Figure 1. (a) Expectations of the US public (grey) and Anthropic staff (orange). The time-saving row compares US adults who use AI at work with staff; the last row compares employed US adults with staff and shows averages rather than shares. (b) Share expecting AI to do at least seven of eight named tasks by 2030, by experience with AI. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on data reported by Sacher et al. (2026). The gap is not only about the frontier. Staff expect AI to be used for 65% of the work tasks it could do by 2030; the public expects 42%. Staff expect AI to work largely on its own, with people checking the result; four in ten US adults expect people to keep doing most of the work with some AI help. Asked how long a task suited to AI takes with it, including time spent checking and fixing, 59% of staff said a quarter of the time or less, compared with 26% of US adults who use AI at work. Among those workers, 29% said the task takes just as long or longer with AI, against 5% of staff. 2. Experience explains much of the gap The most useful result, I think, is Figure 1b. Among US adults who have never used an AI tool, 28% expect AI to do at least seven of the eight tasks by 2030. Among all US adults the share is 41%, among those who use AI at work regularly (about one in five) it is 56%, and among staff it is 96%. Expectations rise with hands-on experience. But experience does not close the gap. Even US workers in computer, engineering and science occupations who use AI regularly expect it to do only 40% of their work by 2030, closer to the average US worker (28%) than to the average staff member (75%). A frontier lab is not a typical workplace. More than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase is now written by its own AI, according to the report, and staff estimate that AI already does about half of the work of building a frontier model. People in that environment may be extrapolating from the most automatable job in the economy. 3. Same reasoning, different inputs The two groups disagree sharply about their own jobs. On average, staff expect AI to be able to do 75% of their current work hours by 2030, and over half expect at least 80%. US workers put the share at 28%, and only 1 in 20 expect 80% or more. Yet when it comes to what this means for the labor market, the two groups reason in the same way. Respondents were told that US unemployment is about 4.2% and asked to forecast it for 2030. Among US workers, those who expect AI to do less than half of their work forecast 7 to 8%; those who expect it to do 80% or more forecast 12.2%, higher than the peak of the 2008 financial crisis. Every ten percentage points of work exposed adds about 0.4 points to the forecast, and staff at the same level of exposure give nearly the same answers. The groups do not hold different theories; they feed different inputs into the same theory. To a hydrologist this is familiar. Two modelers can run the same rainfall–runoff model and predict very different floods simply because they use different rainfall forecasts. Arguing about the model is pointless when the disagreement lies in the forcing. Two details complicate the picture. Staff expect AI to do most of their own work, yet 95% of them expect Anthropic’s headcount to grow over the next year, so automating tasks and shedding jobs are different predictions, at least inside a fast-growing lab. And staff are slightly more pessimistic than the public about how long a displaced worker would need to find a job in a new occupation: a median of 12 months, against 7 to 12 months for US adults. 4. What the expectations imply for the economy The authors ran each respondent’s answers through an economic model they had published earlier, which translates beliefs about capabilities, adoption, autonomy, time savings and re-employment into GDP growth (Figure 2). The median US adult’s answers imply growth of 5.4% in 2030, already more than twice the usual US rate. The median staff member’s answers imply 17.1%, at which the economy would double in size in about four and a half years. Visitors to an online version of the quiz, self-selected and interested in AI, fell in between at 12.5%. The spread within each group is wide, and the distributions overlap. Figure 2. Median model-implied US GDP growth in 2030 for each group, with the doubling time of GDP at that rate. Dashed lines mark the model’s Modest (2.4%), Substantial (5.4%) and Extreme (15.4%) scenarios. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on data reported by Sacher et al. (2026). These are not forecasts by the respondents. Nobody was asked to predict GDP; the numbers are what a particular model makes of their answers. Still, the exercise shows how quickly small-sounding differences in beliefs, such as how much time a task saves, compound into very different economies. 5. Who is right? The report does not say, and neither can I. But a few points are worth keeping in mind. Insiders see more, but they are not neutral. Lab staff see unreleased systems and use AI more intensively than anyone, so their expectations deserve weight. They also chose to work at an AI company, which is likely to attract people who believe in the technology, and the report was produced by the same company. The authors are careful to say that staff answers are personal views, not company forecasts, but readers should still treat them as the views of an unusual group. Other surveys find gaps in other directions. In a 2024 Pew survey, 56% of AI experts but only 17% of US adults expected AI to have a positive impact on the United States over the next 20 years. Yet 64% of the public expected AI to mean fewer jobs, against 39% of the experts (Pew Research Center 2025). Whether “insiders” look more optimistic or more alarming depends on who counts as an insider and what is asked. Adoption is not capability. Even if AI can do a task, people have to choose to use it. US adults named customers preferring to deal with a person, data privacy and security, unreliable AI, and laws and liability as the biggest obstacles. Technology often spreads more slowly than its builders expect, a point I discussed in an earlier post. Not every new technology raises output much, either: one that merely replaces workers at about the same cost, a “so-so” technology in the words of Acemoglu and Restrepo (2019), displaces work without adding much to GDP. The gap may close from either side. Public expectations rise with use, so they may move toward the insiders’ as AI spreads. Or the work of a frontier lab may turn out to be unusually well suited to AI, and insiders’ expectations may come down as AI meets messier jobs. As the authors put it, how far public expectations shift will depend on whether AI comes to do as much of the work elsewhere as it does at a frontier lab. For those of us who teach, the most practical lesson may be closer to home. The same gap exists in every classroom and research group, between people who use AI daily and people who have barely tried it. Their expectations of what students and researchers will need to know in five years differ for the same reason as in this survey: they see different things every day. Questions to think about In your own work, what share of your hours could today’s AI do, and what share do you expect by 2030? How did using AI yourself change that estimate? The two groups reason the same way but use different inputs. In your field, is the main uncertainty about AI’s impact in the “model” or in the “forcing”? If insiders tend to overestimate and outsiders to underestimate, how would you combine their views into a single forecast? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). Sacher 등(2026)은 2026년 8월 미국 성인 약 1만 1천 명과 AI 기업 Anthropic 직원 1,334명에게 같은 질문을 던져, 두 집단이 현재 AI가 할 수 있는 일에는 대체로 동의하지만 2030년에 대해서는 크게 갈린다는 것을 보였다. 예를 들어 2030년까지 AI가 노벨상급 발견을 할 수 있다고 본 비율은 일반인 39%, 직원 91%였고, 자기 업무 중 AI가 할 수 있는 비율도 일반인 근로자는 평균 28%, 직원은 75%로 예상했으며, 이 답을 경제모형에 넣으면 2030년 GDP 성장률이 각각 5.4%와 17.1%로 나온다. 흥미롭게도 자기 일이 더 많이 자동화된다고 보는 사람일수록 실업률을 높게 예측하는 관계는 두 집단에서 거의 같아서, 차이는 이론이 아니라 입력값, 즉 매일 AI를 얼마나 쓰고 무엇을 보는지에서 나오는 것으로 보인다. 다만 이 조사는 AI 기업이 자사 직원을 대상으로 한 것이고, 다른 조사에서는 일자리에 대해 오히려 일반인이 더 비관적이기도 하므로, AI 사용이 확산되면서 이 간극이 어느 쪽에서 좁혀질지는 지켜볼 일이다. title: How the brain invented learning, part VI: the future of intelligence
description: A closing note on Max Bennett's A Brief History of Intelligence: how short the age of language is on the geologic time scale, what AI has achieved since the book appeared, whether transformer-based language models can lead to a sixth breakthrough, and how uncertain the forecasts really are.
tags: artificial intelligence neuroscience large language models book notes
text: Over five posts, this series followed the five breakthroughs of Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023): steering (part I), reinforcing (part II), simulating (part III), mentalizing (part IV) and speaking (part V). The book ends with a short conclusion titled “The Sixth Breakthrough”, and the obvious candidate for that breakthrough is the one being built in data centers today. This last post steps back. It places the five breakthroughs on the geologic time scale, looks at what AI has done in the three years since the book was written, and asks whether today’s language models are on the road to a sixth breakthrough. The first half follows the book; the second half is my own reading of developments since 2024, and it is an opinion, not a forecast. 1. Five breakthroughs on the geologic time scale Earth scientists are used to deep time, but even for us Figure 1a is striking. The first brains appeared in the Ediacaran, about 600 million years ago. Vertebrates and their dopamine-based trial-and-error learning followed in the Cambrian, mammals and their simulating neocortex in the Jurassic, and primates near the start of the Paleogene, shortly after the asteroid impact that ended the age of dinosaurs. Speaking, which began with early humans about 2.5 million years ago, does not even get its own visible slice of the axis. It sits in the Quaternary, the thin pale band at the right end. Figure 1. (a) The five breakthroughs on the geologic time scale (Ed Ediacaran, Cm Cambrian, O Ordovician, D Devonian, C Carboniferous, P Permian, Tr Triassic, J Jurassic, K Cretaceous, Pg Paleogene; the Silurian, Neogene and Quaternary are unlabeled). (b) The same events on a logarithmic scale of years before present, with later milestones of human culture and computing. Dates are approximate. Figure by Daeha Kim, using period boundaries from the International Chronostratigraphic Chart and the breakthroughs of Bennett (2023). Bennett uses a calendar to make the same point, and it is worth extending. If the 600 million years since the first brains were compressed into one year, each real year would last about a twentieth of a second. Event Years ago On a one-year calendar First brains (steering) 600 million 1 January Early vertebrates (reinforcing) 500 million 2 March Early mammals (simulating) 150 million 1 October Early primates (mentalizing) 65 million 22 November Genus Homo (speaking begins) 2.5 million 30 December, before noon Homo sapiens 300,000 31 December, about 7:40 pm Writing 5,200 4.5 minutes before midnight First electronic computers 80 4 seconds before midnight ChatGPT 4 0.2 seconds before midnight Figure 1b shows the same events on a logarithmic axis, which is the natural way to see a process that keeps speeding up. Each breakthrough took less time than the one before, and once language let knowledge accumulate outside individual brains, the intervals collapsed: from writing to printing to computers to language models. Whatever the sixth breakthrough turns out to be, it is happening in the last fraction of a second of Bennett’s year. 2. What Bennett means by a sixth breakthrough In his conclusion, Bennett suggests that the next breakthrough may be intelligence that is no longer bound to biology: minds built from silicon rather than neurons, possibly far more capable than our own. His emphasis is less on when this happens than on what it inherits. Each earlier breakthrough was built from the parts of the ones before, and an artificial superintelligence would be built, at least at first, from the accumulated record of human language and the goals we choose to give it. The question he leaves the reader with is therefore partly technical and partly moral: what do we want such minds to value? 3. What has happened since the book Bennett wrote the book when ChatGPT was new. Much has happened since, and a striking pattern is that AI seems to be acquiring rough counterparts of the five breakthroughs in a different order from evolution (Figure 2). Figure 2. Evolution acquired the five breakthroughs in order over about 600 million years. AI systems have acquired rough counterparts of them in a different order, starting with language, within about a decade. The pairing on the right is my own interpretation, not a claim of the book. Figure by Daeha Kim. Evolution built language last, on top of a body, a value system, a world model and a model of minds. AI started with language. Large language models were trained first to predict text (speaking). They were then tuned with human ratings of good and bad answers, a crude sense of valence (steering). By 2023 they could pass many theory-of-mind tests (mentalizing, part IV). The developments since 2024 fill in the rest. Reinforcing returned. The biggest change since the book is the arrival of “reasoning” models, beginning with OpenAI’s o1 in September 2024. These models are trained by reinforcement learning to produce long chains of reasoning, rewarded when the final answer can be checked as correct. DeepSeek showed that this kind of training alone can make reasoning behaviors such as self-checking emerge (Guo et al. 2025). In Bennett’s terms, trial-and-error learning from part II, the oldest learning algorithm in vertebrates, was bolted onto a language model. Results that can be checked. In July 2025, an advanced version of Google DeepMind’s Gemini solved five of the six problems at the International Mathematical Olympiad, a gold-medal score certified by the competition’s coordinators and achieved in natural language within the time limit (Google DeepMind 2025a). DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve, a coding agent built on language models, found a way to multiply 4×4 complex matrices with 48 scalar multiplications, improving on an algorithm that had stood since 1969 (Google DeepMind 2025b). The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went in part to the developers of AlphaFold. Longer and longer tasks. METR measures the length of software tasks, timed by how long they take skilled humans, that AI agents can complete with 50% reliability. That length doubled roughly every seven months from 2019 to early 2025 (Kwa et al. 2025), and faster since. By 2026 METR noted that its measurements above 16 hours were unreliable with its current task suite, and in September 2026 it stopped updating its public chart. Puzzles designed to resist memorization. The ARC-AGI benchmarks consist of visual puzzles that are easy for people but were built to be hard for pattern-matching systems. When the interactive ARC-AGI-3 launched in March 2026, frontier models scored under 1%. By November 2026 the best entry on the public leaderboard scored 62.7% on ARC-AGI-3 and 95.0% on ARC-AGI-2, at a cost of tens of thousands of dollars per evaluation run (ARC Prize 2026). Simulating, at last. Google DeepMind’s Genie 3 (August 2025) generates interactive environments that a user or an agent can move through in real time, keeping them consistent for a few minutes (Google DeepMind 2025c). DeepMind describes such world models as a key step toward general intelligence. This is the closest AI has come to the rat at the fork in the maze of part III. 4. Are transformers enough? The progress is real. Whether it leads to superintelligence is a different question, and the people building these systems disagree. One camp argues that the current recipe, large transformer models plus reinforcement learning plus more compute, will keep working. Dario Amodei of Anthropic wrote in January 2026 that AI systems as capable as “a country of geniuses in a datacenter” could be as little as one to two years away, while adding that they could also be considerably further out (Amodei 2026). I discussed the limits of the scaling side of this argument in an earlier post. The other camp argues that something important is missing, and the missing pieces line up remarkably well with Bennett’s breakthroughs. No learning from ongoing experience. Richard Sutton and David Silver argue that AI is reaching the limits of what can be learned from human data and must enter an “era of experience”, in which agents learn continually from their own interaction with the world (Silver and Sutton 2025). Andrej Karpathy has said that today’s models lack continual learning and that working agents will take about a decade. A brain never stops learning; a deployed language model mostly does. This is the plasticity of part I and the trial-and-error learning of part II, applied for a lifetime rather than during a training run. No world model built from the world. Yann LeCun has long argued that predicting the next word is a dead end for human-level intelligence and that machines need world models learned from sensory data. He left Meta in late 2025 to build such systems. This is the simulating breakthrough of part III. Running out of words. Villalobos et al. (2024) estimated the stock of public human text at about 300 trillion tokens and projected that, at current trends, models would use it up between 2026 and 2032. A child learns language from a tiny fraction of that (part V), because it learns from a body, a world and other people, not from text alone. Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind sits between the camps: he has suggested that one or two more breakthroughs, in areas such as continual learning, planning and memory, may still be needed. 5. When? Nobody knows, and the honest answer is that forecasts move. In a survey of 2,778 AI researchers conducted in 2023, the median respondent gave a 50% chance that machines would outperform humans at every task by 2047, thirteen years earlier than the same question had produced only a year before, and a 10% chance by 2027 (Grace et al. 2025). The authors of the widely read “AI 2027” scenario pushed their own estimates later in late 2025 and then earlier again in 2026; by August 2026, two of its authors, writing on the project’s blog, placed superintelligence in 2029 and 2033 respectively (Kokotajlo et al. 2025). Lab leaders tend to give the shortest timelines, and some prominent researchers, such as Karpathy, give longer ones. As a hydrologist, I read these numbers the way I read long-range streamflow forecasts: the spread between them says more than any single value. Three observations seem robust to me. Progress is fastest where answers can be checked. Mathematics, programming and puzzles have clear right answers, so reinforcement learning works well there. Many important problems, from flood forecasting under a changing climate to policy, can only be checked slowly, partially or not at all. Expect AI to reach superhuman levels unevenly, first in verifiable domains. The missing pieces are old ones. Continual learning, grounded world models and learning from interaction are what evolution built first. Language models skipped them. Whether they can be added on top, or must be rebuilt from below, is perhaps the central question for the next decade. Values are not a detail. Bennett’s closing question, what we want these minds to want, becomes more pressing, not less, the faster the technical progress. 6. Closing Steering took the first brains, reinforcing took a backbone, simulating took a neocortex, mentalizing took a primate brain, and speaking took a human community. Each breakthrough was slower to arrive and faster to spread than anything before it, and each was built from the parts of the last. On Bennett’s calendar, the whole story of artificial intelligence so far fits in less than a second before midnight. I do not know whether the sixth breakthrough will come from transformers, from something that replaces them, or not for a long time. But this series has convinced me of one thing: the most useful guide to what machines are still missing is the long history of how brains got here. Questions to think about Which of Bennett’s five breakthroughs do you think current AI systems lack most, and how would you test for it? In hydrology, which problems have answers that can be checked quickly enough for AI to learn by trial and error, and which do not? If you could choose one value or goal to pass on to a future superintelligence, what would it be, and how would you make sure it was understood as you meant it? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 지질 시간 위에 놓으면 다섯 번의 돌파 과정 중 언어(speaking)는 6억 년의 마지막 0.4%에 불과하며, 6억 년을 1년으로 줄이면 ChatGPT는 자정 0.2초 전에 등장한다. 책이 쓰인 뒤 AI는 언어에서 출발해 사람의 피드백, 마음 이론 테스트, 강화학습 기반 추론 모델, 세계 모형으로 진화와 거의 반대 순서로 돌파 과정의 대응물을 갖추어 왔고, 수학 올림피아드 금메달 수준과 수십 년 된 알고리즘의 개선 같은 성과를 냈다. 그러나 경험에서 계속 배우는 능력, 세계에서 직접 배운 세계 모형, 고갈되어 가는 인간의 텍스트 같은 한계는 진화가 먼저 만든 바로 그 부분이어서, 트랜스포머만으로 초지능에 이를지는 여전히 논쟁 중이다. 전망 시점은 계속 앞뒤로 움직이므로 단일 값보다 그 폭을 읽어야 하며, 검증이 쉬운 분야부터 고르지 않게 발전할 가능성이 크고, Bennett가 남긴 질문처럼 그런 지능이 무엇을 원하도록 할지가 기술만큼 중요하다. title: How the brain invented learning, part V: speaking in A Brief History of Intelligence
description: Notes on the last of Max Bennett's five breakthroughs: how a perfect storm of savannah life, tool making, gossip and cooking gave early humans language, why language let ideas accumulate across generations, and what large language models, which learned language without a body, can and cannot tell us.
tags: artificial intelligence neuroscience large language models book notes
text: This is the last part of a series on Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023). Bilaterian worms learned to steer (part I), early vertebrates learned by trial and error (part II), early mammals learned to simulate the world in imagination (part III), and early primates learned to model minds, including their own (part IV). Figure 1 puts the five together. Figure 1. The five breakthroughs in Bennett’s account, the animals in which each first appeared, and the AI counterparts discussed in this series. Each breakthrough builds on the ones before it. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic summarizing Bennett (2023). The fifth breakthrough is speaking. It is the one that most obviously connects to today’s AI, because the most capable AI systems we have are, at their core, models of language. As before, the summary is my own paraphrase of the book’s argument, and some connections, notably to the data that children and language models learn from, come from the broader literature. 1. Breakthrough 5, Speaking: sharing what is in our heads Many animals communicate. Vervet monkeys have different alarm calls for eagles, leopards and snakes, and apes can be taught hundreds of signs. What sets human language apart, in Bennett’s account, is what it carries. Thanks to the earlier breakthroughs, a human brain holds a rich inner simulation of the world and of other minds. Language lets one brain put part of that simulation into another: what happened at the river yesterday, how to shape a stone tool, who cannot be trusted. That changes how learning works. Until now, every animal had to learn mostly from its own experience, plus whatever it could copy by watching. With language, a person can learn from the experience of people they have never met, including people who died long ago. Knowledge no longer has to be rediscovered in each generation; it can accumulate. 2. A perfect storm Why did this happen in our lineage and not in other apes? Bennett describes an unlikely combination of pressures, each of which made the next more likely. Out of the forest, into tools and meat As African forests shrank and gave way to savannah, early humans moved into a new way of life: making stone tools and eating meat. Tool making is hard to learn and easy to lose. If a skill is passed on poorly, each generation does a little worse, and the technology never improves. Bennett argues that early proto-languages helped tool-making skills survive accurately from one generation to the next. An experiment supports this idea. Researchers taught 184 modern volunteers to make simple stone flakes of the kind found at the oldest tool sites, passing the skill along chains of learners under five conditions, from examining finished flakes and watching an expert, to being taught by demonstration, with gestures or with speech (Morgan et al. 2015). Skill transmitted best when learners were taught, and best of all with spoken instruction; simply watching did little. The authors suggested that the very slow change of the oldest stone-tool tradition, which stayed much the same for roughly 700,000 years, may reflect how poorly skills spread without teaching and language. A learning program, not a new brain part Bennett argues that the brain did not need a new structure for language. Areas of the neocortex involved in language have counterparts in other primates. What changed, in his view, was a set of instincts that turns a child into a language learner: babies take part in back-and-forth “proto-conversations” with their caregivers long before they can speak, and they share attention with others, looking where someone points and pointing to show things themselves. Human infants begin to point to share interest at around their first birthday, a behavior that is rare or absent in other apes (Tomasello et al. 2007). Together, joint attention and turn-taking work like a curriculum. When a parent and child look at the same thing and the parent names it, the child can tie the word to a part of its inner simulation of the world. Trained this way, older neocortical areas were repurposed for language. Gossip, altruism and punishment Once humans could talk, they began to talk with people who were not close kin, and much of what they talked about was other people. Robin Dunbar has argued that gossip is one of the main functions of language: it lets people keep track of who is reliable in groups too large to monitor directly (Dunbar 2004). Bennett describes a feedback loop. Language made it possible to reward people who helped others and to punish cheaters by spreading the word about them, which made cooperation with strangers safer, which made larger groups possible, which in turn favored people with better language skills. Cooking and bigger brains As groups grew and ideas began to hop from brain to brain, there was more to learn and remember, and bigger brains became worth their cost. The human brain is about three times the size of a chimpanzee’s, and brain tissue is expensive to run. Bennett points to cooking, a hypothesis developed by Richard Wrangham, as one way our ancestors paid for it: cooked food yields far more energy for less chewing and digestion (Wrangham 2009). Whether cooking drove brain growth or was made possible by it, it offered the surplus that a growing brain needed. 3. A mind tethered to other minds From this perfect storm came the fifth and final breakthrough. Bennett’s closing point is that, with language, the human mind is no longer a single mind. Each of us is connected to others through a long history of accumulated ideas: tools, words, stories, mathematics and science, none of which any one of us could have invented alone. He also notes that language brought out both the best and the worst of us, from altruism toward strangers to coordinated cruelty. For a scientist this is a familiar idea. No hydrologist derives the water balance, Darcy’s law or the Penman equation from scratch; we inherit them through textbooks and papers and add a little to the pile. Science is an unusually disciplined form of the accumulation that language made possible. 4. The AI connection: language without a body Large language models are trained on exactly this accumulation: a large share of the text that humans have written down. In one sense they are the most direct AI counterpart of any breakthrough in the book. In another, they reverse the order in which evolution built intelligence. Evolution built the inner simulation first and added language on top, so that words are labels for parts of a world model. Language models start from the words. Bennett discusses how early large language models produced fluent text while failing simple questions that require picturing a physical situation, and how newer models have closed many of these gaps. Whether they did so by building something like a world model from text, or by learning ever better statistical patterns in text about the world, is still debated. Some researchers argue that a system trained only on linguistic form cannot, in principle, learn meaning (Bender and Koller 2020). The difference in how the two learn is easy to quantify (Figure 2). A child hears somewhere between a few million and a few tens of millions of words by age five, depending on how much language surrounds them. Even a 20-year-old who reads a great deal has met perhaps a few hundred million words. The training set of GPT-3 held about 500 billion tokens, and Llama 3 was trained on about 15 trillion (Frank 2023; Grattafiori et al. 2024). Frank (2023) suggests three possible reasons why children need so much less: a brain shaped by evolution before any data arrives, language grounded in sight, touch and action, and input that comes through social interaction in which the child takes part. These are, almost point for point, the earlier breakthroughs and the learning program described above. Figure 2. Language heard or read by people compared with the training data of three language models, on a logarithmic scale. For people, the dark part of each bar shows the estimate for children growing up with little language around them and the light part extends to the estimate for language-rich environments (and, at age 20, heavy reading). Figure by Daeha Kim, based on estimates from Frank (2023) and training-set sizes reported by Frank (2023) and Grattafiori et al. (2024). 5. The correspondence at a glance The table below pairs each biological mechanism with its AI counterpart. The last column is my own judgment of how close the match is. Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close Language as a way to share inner simulations Language models trained on human text Shared medium, reversed order Accumulated knowledge across generations Pretraining on the written record Close match Joint attention, naming what both can see Multimodal models linking words and images Partial match Proto-conversations, learning by interaction Instruction tuning, learning from human feedback Partial match Teaching skills with words Learning a task from instructions in a prompt Functional match Small data, rich prior structure Huge data, weak prior structure Contrast 6. Closing: five breakthroughs and a sixth Looking back over the series, each breakthrough solved a problem by building on the previous one. Steering needed a sense of good and bad; reinforcing used that sense to learn from experience; simulating let animals learn from experience they never had; mentalizing turned the simulator toward minds; and speaking let minds share their simulations, so that learning could continue beyond a single lifetime. Again and again, AI researchers have arrived at similar solutions, often without knowing that evolution had found them first. The book ends by asking what a sixth breakthrough might be, and the obvious candidate is the one being built now: minds that are not made of neurons at all. If Bennett’s history teaches anything, it is that each new kind of intelligence was built from the parts of the old ones. It will be interesting to see which of the five our machines are still missing. I take up that question in part VI, the last post of this series. Questions to think about Much of what a hydrologist knows was learned from papers and textbooks rather than from personal fieldwork. Which parts of your own expertise could not have been passed on in words? Morgan et al. found that stone-tool skills spread poorly by watching alone. Which skills in your field are still learned mainly by watching, and how could they be taught better? A child needs far less language than a language model. Which of Frank’s three explanations do you find most convincing, and how might it change how we train models? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 『A Brief History of Intelligence』의 다섯 번째이자 마지막 돌파 과정은 초기 인류가 얻은 언어(speaking)로, 머릿속 시뮬레이션을 다른 사람의 머리로 옮겨 경험을 세대를 넘어 쌓을 수 있게 했다. 숲이 줄어든 사바나에서 도구 제작과 육식이 시작되자 기술을 정확히 전수할 필요가 생겼고, 함께 바라보기와 주고받는 대화를 통해 아이가 단어를 세계 모형에 연결하는 학습 프로그램이 생기면서 기존 신피질이 언어에 쓰이게 되었으며, 험담, 이타성, 처벌의 되먹임과 요리로 얻은 에너지가 더 큰 뇌를 뒷받침했다. 그 결과 인간의 마음은 더 이상 혼자가 아니라 오랜 세월 쌓인 생각을 통해 서로 연결되었다. 대규모 언어모형은 이 축적된 기록에서 출발하지만 아이보다 수천~수십만 배 많은 언어 자료가 필요하며, 몸과 세계 모형 없이 배운 언어가 진짜 이해인지는 아직 논쟁 중이다. title: Green, amber, red: how geoscientists should use AI in research and publishing
description: A reading of a Nature Geoscience editorial on the responsible use of AI: the new Springer Nature traffic-light framework for authors, reviewers and editors, why disclosure and human accountability matter, and what the rules might mean for everyday work in hydrology.
tags: artificial intelligence large language models research integrity scientific publishing
text: Machine learning has been part of the geosciences for a long time. Hydrologists have trained neural networks on rainfall and runoff for decades, and deep learning models such as LSTMs now rival or beat traditional rainfall–runoff models in many catchments (Kratzert et al. 2018). A review in 2019 argued that the future of Earth system science lies in combining such data-driven models with physical understanding (Reichstein et al. 2019). What is new is that AI has moved from the analysis to the writing. Large language models now help draft, edit, translate and review manuscripts. In its November 2026 editorial, Nature Geoscience argues that the geoscience community needs shared, transparent rules for this, and announces that its policies now follow a new risk-assessment framework from its publisher, Springer Nature (Nature Geoscience 2026). The editorial is short, but the framework behind it will affect how many of us write papers and review them. 1. How much are scientists already using LLMs? More than many realize. One large study looked for statistical traces of LLM writing, such as a sudden rise in words that LLMs favor, in more than 1.1 million papers and preprints from arXiv, bioRxiv and Nature portfolio journals published between January 2020 and September 2024 (Liang et al. 2025). After ChatGPT appeared, the estimated share of LLM-modified text rose steadily, reaching up to 22% in computer science and up to 9% in mathematics and in Nature portfolio journals. An earlier version of the study found the highest rates in shorter papers, in crowded research areas and among authors who post preprints often. Using an LLM to improve a paper is not, by itself, a problem. The editorial lists the benefits plainly: clearer, more readable manuscripts and better communication. The risks are just as plain: plagiarism, inaccurate or invented content, and the spread of misinformation, all of which erode trust in research. LLMs also make it cheaper for paper mills to produce fake papers at scale (Kendall and Teixeira da Silva 2024). 2. The traffic-light framework The framework classifies AI use by its risk, not by the tool used, and applies the same three levels to authors, peer reviewers and editors (Figure 1). Figure 1. The three risk levels of the Springer Nature framework for AI use in research and publishing, with examples paraphrased and shortened from the policy. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on the Springer Nature journal policies on artificial intelligence (2026). Green (permitted) covers assistive uses that help with expression or efficiency without adding new intellectual content: polishing language, suggesting how to structure a section, translating or clarifying reviewer comments, cleaning data. The common feature is that the result can be checked and reversed, and the scientific judgment stays with the human. Disclosure is encouraged. Amber (use with care) covers uses in which AI contributes to reasoning or interpretation: suggesting methods or statistical tests, drafting explanatory summaries, comparing results with the literature, finding patterns in exploratory data, explaining model output in plain language. These are allowed, but only with human verification, human control and disclosure. Red (not permitted) covers uses in which AI replaces human judgment, produces outputs that cannot be verified, or breaks confidentiality: presenting AI-generated hypotheses or conclusions as one’s own, fabricating data, citations or results, listing an AI system as an author, handing peer review to an LLM, and creating photorealistic fake images. 3. Four principles behind the colors The policy rests on four principles, and the editorial repeats them in its own words. Accountability stays human. Authors remain fully responsible for what they publish, whatever tools they used. An AI system cannot be an author because it cannot be held accountable. AI may support judgment but not replace it. This applies to editors and reviewers as much as to authors. AI can help with editorial and review work, but decisions about a manuscript rest on the expertise and judgment of people. Transparency builds trust. Authors should say how AI was used, so that readers and editors do not have to guess. The editorial adds that the use of machine learning and other AI tools for data analysis must also be disclosed. Confidentiality is not negotiable. Manuscripts under review and other non-public material must not be pasted into open or unsecured AI systems. For reviewers, this is probably the rule most easily broken without thinking. 4. What it might mean for everyday work in hydrology The policy’s examples are general, so it is worth asking how they apply to typical tasks in our field. The table below is my own reading, not an official classification. Task Likely level Why Polishing the English of a manuscript Green Language only; you check every change Writing code to remove duplicate gauge records Green Data cleaning that can be verified Asking an LLM which trend test to use for streamflow Amber It recommends a method; you must judge it Letting an LLM compare your results with earlier studies Amber Check every cited paper exists and says that Using an LSTM to fill gaps in a discharge record Disclose Machine learning in analysis must be stated Pasting a manuscript you are reviewing into a public chatbot Red Breaks confidentiality Letting an LLM write your review report Red Peer review cannot be delegated Publishing an LLM-written discussion as your own reasoning Red Undisclosed AI reasoning The amber rows deserve the most attention. LLMs are very good at producing fluent comparisons with the literature, and very good at citing papers that do not exist or do not say what is claimed. The amber label is a reminder that the time saved in drafting has to be spent again in checking. 5. Why this matters Rules like these will keep changing, as the editorial admits. Detection tools are imperfect and disclosure depends on honesty, so the framework cannot be enforced perfectly. Its main value is that it gives authors, reviewers and editors a shared vocabulary for a question that used to be answered privately and inconsistently: not whether AI was used, but how, and who checked the result. For students, I think the most useful lesson is the simplest one. An LLM can make a paper easier to read, but it cannot take responsibility for whether the paper is right. That part of the work, and the credit or blame that comes with it, still belongs to us. Questions to think about In your last paper or thesis chapter, which uses of AI would fall under green, which under amber, and did you disclose them? Where exactly is the line between “polishing language” (green) and “extensive writing support” (amber)? How would you decide for your own text? If you receive a review report that you suspect was written by an LLM, what should you do as an author, and what should an editor do? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 최근 한 지구과학 학술지의 사설(2026)은 AI가 데이터 분석을 넘어 논문 작성과 심사에까지 쓰이면서, 저자, 심사자, 편집자 모두가 투명한 원칙을 따라야 한다고 강조한다. 출판사 Springer Nature의 새 신호등 체계는 AI 사용을 위험도에 따라 초록(문장 다듬기, 데이터 정리처럼 검증 가능한 보조), 주황(분석 방법 제안, 문헌 비교처럼 해석에 영향을 주므로 사람의 검증과 공개가 필요한 사용), 빨강(AI 결론을 자기 것으로 제시, 데이터나 인용 조작, AI를 저자로 표기, 심사를 LLM에 맡기기)으로 나눈다. 핵심 원칙은 책임은 끝까지 사람에게 있고, AI는 판단을 돕되 대신할 수 없으며, 사용 방식을 공개하고, 심사 중인 원고를 공개된 AI 도구에 넣지 않는 것이다. AI는 논문을 읽기 쉽게 만들 수는 있지만 그 내용이 맞는지에 대한 책임까지 대신 지지는 않는다. References Kendall, G., & Teixeira da Silva, J. A. (2024). title: How the brain invented learning, part IV: mentalizing in A Brief History of Intelligence
description: Notes on the fourth of Max Bennett's five breakthroughs: how early primates built a model of their own mind, why theory of mind, imitation learning and planning for future needs may be three uses of that one model, and what language models passing false-belief tests do and do not show.
tags: artificial intelligence neuroscience large language models book notes
text: In part I, bilaterian worms learned to steer. In part II, early vertebrates learned by trial and error. In part III, early mammals learned to simulate: a model of the world and a model of the self let them try things out in imagination before trying them in the world. This post covers the fourth breakthrough in Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023): mentalizing. In Bennett’s account it arrived with the early primates, and it added one more model on top of the others, a model of one’s own mind. As before, the summary is my own paraphrase of the book’s argument, and the AI connections, notably to inverse reinforcement learning and to language models taking theory-of-mind tests, come from the broader literature. 1. Breakthrough 4, Mentalizing: a model of one’s own mind A rat that pauses at a fork in the maze is simulating the world and its own movements in it. What it does not seem to do is think about its own thinking: what it knows, what it wants, what it believes and why. Bennett argues that early primates gained this ability, and that it came with a new region of the frontal cortex, the granular prefrontal cortex, which first evolved in primates. The idea follows naturally from part III. The sensory neocortex is a generative model of the world. The agranular prefrontal cortex is a generative model of the animal’s own body and intent. The granular prefrontal cortex, in Bennett’s account, models the activity of those older models themselves: a model of a model, or a second-order generative model. Its subject is the animal’s own mind. Figure 1 sums up this stacking of models and the three abilities that, Bennett argues, follow from the newest one. Figure 1. Models within models. Early mammals gained a model of the world and a model of their own body and intent (part III); early primates added a model of their own mind, which can be projected into another individual or into one’s own future. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic summarizing the argument of Bennett (2023). Three abilities that arrived together Bennett points to three abilities that appeared in primates: Theory of mind: inferring what another individual intends and knows. Imitation learning: acquiring a new skill by watching someone else perform it. Anticipating future needs: acting now for a want one does not yet feel. These look like separate talents, but Bennett suggests they may be three uses of the same thing. If you can model your own mind, you can run that model with someone else’s situation as input and ask what you would want and know in their place. You can run it with someone else’s movements and ask what they are trying to do. And you can run it with your own future situation and ask what you will want then. Why one model, not three Bennett gives several lines of evidence that the three abilities share a common basis. They depend on overlapping brain regions, centered on the granular prefrontal cortex. Children acquire them at roughly similar ages; for example, children usually begin to pass false-belief tests, which ask where someone will look for an object that was moved while they were away, at around four years old (Wimmer and Perner 1983). Damage to these regions tends to impair them together. The same regions are also used when we reason about our own minds, and damage to them can disrupt the sense of self in striking ways. Bennett mentions conditions such as mirror-sign syndrome, in which a patient no longer recognizes their own reflection, and alien hand syndrome, in which one hand seems to act with a will of its own. In development, a child’s ability to reason about her own mind tends to appear before her ability to reason about others’. Finally, the new primate regions are not built from new parts. The neocortex is made of the same basic circuit repeated across its surface, an observation going back to Vernon Mountcastle. If that circuit learns generative models, as the line of thought from Helmholtz to Hinton, Hawkins and Friston suggests, then a new region can be a new application of the same machinery, this time modeling the rest of the brain. 2. Three abilities, one model Theory of mind The term comes from a 1978 paper that asked whether chimpanzees attribute mental states to others (Premack and Woodruff 1978). The hardest version of the question is whether an animal understands that another individual can hold a false belief. In 2016, an eye-tracking study showed great apes videos in which a person saw an object being hidden, left, and missed it being moved. The apes looked in anticipation at the place where the person wrongly believed the object to be, not where it actually was (Krupenye et al. 2016). In this limited sense at least, our closest relatives seem to track what others believe. Imitation learning Watching others is a cheap way to learn. A young primate does not have to discover how to crack a nut or fish for termites by trial and error; it can watch an expert. But copying movements alone is not enough. The learner has to understand what the demonstrator is trying to do, so that it can fill in what it cannot see and ignore what does not matter. In Bennett’s account, this is where the model of one’s own mind helps: the learner infers the demonstrator’s intent, then simulates the movements needed to achieve the same goal. The AI connection. Robotics distinguishes two ways of learning from demonstration. Behavior cloning copies the expert’s actions directly. Inverse reinforcement learning first infers what reward the expert must be pursuing and then learns its own way to pursue it (Ng and Russell 2000). The second is closer to what Bennett describes: imitation as inference about another’s goals. Large language models can also be seen as imitation learners on an enormous scale, since their pretraining consists of predicting the next word that a human writer would produce. Anticipating future needs Many animals can learn to act for a reward they currently want. Acting now for a need one does not feel yet is harder: a well-fed animal has little reason to save food. In a classic test of this ability, bonobos and orangutans chose a tool that would be useful in another room later, carried it out of the test room and brought it back for use one hour later, and in a further experiment fourteen hours later (Mulcahy and Call 2006). Because both species did it, the authors suggested that the precursors of planning for the future were present in great apes before about 14 million years ago. 3. Why primates? Why did this breakthrough happen in primates? One well-known answer is the social brain hypothesis: primates live in large, complex groups, and keeping track of allies, rivals and debts requires a large neocortex. Across primates, the relative size of the neocortex rises with typical group size (Dunbar 1998). A competing answer is ecological. In a larger sample of more than 140 primate species, diet predicted brain size better than group size did, with fruit-eaters having larger brains than leaf-eaters (DeCasien et al. 2017). Bennett argues that the two hypotheses may be two sides of the same coin. Ripe fruit is scattered in space and time, so a fruit eater benefits from planning ahead for where and when food will be ready, and from learning foraging tricks from others. The same model of minds that helps with foraging also helps with politics: predicting who will side with whom and keeping track of who knows what. Mentalizing was useful for both. 4. The AI connection: machines that model minds Do language models have a theory of mind? Michal Kosinski gave 11 language models 40 false-belief tasks, each counted as solved only if every one of its eight related scenarios was answered correctly (Kosinski 2024). Older models solved none. GPT-3 davinci-003 and ChatGPT-3.5-turbo each solved 20%. ChatGPT-4 solved 75%, comparable to six-year-old children in earlier studies (Figure 2). Figure 2. Share of 40 false-belief tasks solved by language models released between 2022 and 2023. A task counted as solved only if all eight of its scenarios were answered correctly. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on the results reported by Kosinski (2024). A larger study compared GPT-4, GPT-3.5 and LLaMA2 with 1,907 human participants on a battery of theory-of-mind tests (Strachan et al. 2024). GPT-4 performed at or above human levels on indirect requests, false beliefs and misdirection, but struggled to detect faux pas. Further experiments suggested this was not a failure to infer the speaker’s mental state but an overly cautious reluctance to commit to an answer. LLaMA2’s apparent advantage on faux pas turned out to be an artifact of a bias toward one kind of answer. What these results mean is debated. One view is that a model trained to predict human writing must, to some extent, learn to model the people who wrote it, because much of human writing is about what people know, want and believe. Another is that the tests themselves appear in many forms in the training data, and that small changes to a task can still trip the models up. In Bennett’s terms, the question is whether the model has a model of minds or has learned the surface patterns of text about minds. A useful practical point is that the same kinds of tests used for children and apes can now be used to probe machines, and the results change quickly from one model generation to the next. 5. The correspondence at a glance The table below pairs each biological mechanism with its AI counterpart. The last column is my own judgment of how close the match is. Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close Granular prefrontal cortex as a model of one’s own mind Models that represent their own uncertainty and reasoning Loose Theory of mind, false-belief understanding Language models on false-belief tests Similar test scores, debated mechanism Imitation by inferring the demonstrator’s intent Inverse reinforcement learning Same idea Copying movements directly Behavior cloning Functional match Learning from others at scale Pretraining on human-written text Partial match Anticipating future needs Planning with predicted future rewards Partial match Same cortical circuit reused for new models One architecture (transformer) reused for many tasks Analogy only 6. Closing: a mind that can step outside itself Mentalizing let primates step outside their own point of view, into another individual’s head, another’s body, or their own future self. With it came reading the intentions of others, learning skills by watching, and preparing today for tomorrow’s hunger, which together made primates better foragers and better politicians. Bennett places this breakthrough in a long timeline. If the 600 million years since the first brains were compressed into one calendar year, our last common ancestor with chimpanzees, who lived about 7 million years ago, would appear only in the last week of December. Everything that separates us from other apes, from foraging for fruit to launching rockets, happened in those final days. Bennett’s fifth and last breakthrough, speaking, is where that story begins, and it is the subject of part V. Questions to think about When you explain a hydrological model to a policymaker, you have to guess what they already know and what they want from it. Which parts of that task are theory of mind, and which are knowledge of hydrology? A student who copies a senior’s code line by line and a student who first understands what the code is for are learning in different ways. Which is closer to behavior cloning and which to inverse reinforcement learning? If a language model passes a false-belief test, what further evidence would you want before saying it understands what others believe? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 『A Brief History of Intelligence』의 네 번째 돌파 과정은 초기 영장류가 과립 전전두피질을 통해 얻은 마음 읽기(mentalizing), 곧 자기 마음에 대한 모형이다. 이 모형을 남에게 투사하면 상대의 의도와 앎을 짐작하는 마음 이론이, 남의 몸에 투사하면 보고 따라 배우는 모방 학습이, 미래의 자신에게 투사하면 아직 느끼지 않는 필요를 미리 준비하는 능력이 생긴다. 과일을 찾아다니는 생태적 요구와 복잡한 무리 생활이라는 사회적 요구가 모두 이 능력을 키운 것으로 보인다. AI에서는 시연자의 목표를 추론하는 역강화학습이 이와 닮았고, Kosinski(2024)에 따르면 GPT-4는 틀린 믿음 과제의 75%를 풀어 여섯 살 아이 수준에 이르렀지만, 이것이 진짜 마음 모형인지는 아직 논쟁 중이다. References Bennett, M. (2023). title: How fast will AI spread, and how many chips will it need? A rough estimate
description: A back-of-the-envelope look at when demand for AI might peak, built from how slowly earlier office technologies changed work, how fast generative AI is spreading in 2026, and a simple model of why chip purchases peak long before AI use does. An estimate with stated assumptions, not a forecast or investment advice.
tags: artificial intelligence technology adoption semiconductors economics
text: By November 2026, AI tools can write code from a description, draft a paper and run multistep tasks on their own; I have written about vibe coding and about using LLMs for writing and coding. Yet capability is not the same as adoption. When spreadsheets arrived, companies did not dissolve their bookkeeping departments overnight. When Python made it possible to do most of what ArcGIS does, only some analysts made the switch, mostly those who could imagine doing so. New programming languages keep appearing, and most people never use any of them. So how long will it take for AI tools to be absorbed into ordinary work, and when will demand for them peak? And what does that mean for the semiconductors behind them? Nobody can answer these questions precisely. But the history of earlier technologies, the adoption data of the last three years and a simple model can at least frame the answer. Everything below is an estimate with stated assumptions; it is not a forecast and not investment advice. How long earlier tools took Office technologies have usually taken one to three decades to reach half of their potential users. Computers at work. The share of US workers using a computer on the job rose from 24.6% in 1984 to 49.4% in 1997 and about 56% in 2003 (NCES 2004). From the IBM PC in 1981 to half the workforce took 16 to 20 years. The internet at home. US households with internet access went from 18% in 1997 to 50% in 2001, roughly eight years after the web browser appeared (US Census Bureau 2010). Cloud computing. Seventeen years after Amazon Web Services launched, only 45% of EU firms bought cloud services in 2023 (Eurostat 2023). Electricity. Electric motors drove less than 5% of US factory machinery in 1899 and about half around 1920, and the productivity gains came only in the 1920s, once factories were redesigned around the new power source (David 1990). The spreadsheet story is especially telling. Spreadsheets made bookkeeping tasks cheap and “what if” analysis easy, and the number of accountants grew while the number of bookkeeping clerks declined. Yet bookkeeping, accounting and auditing clerks were still a 1.6-million-job occupation in the United States in 2024, forty-five years after the first spreadsheet program (US Bureau of Labor Statistics 2025). Work changes far more slowly than tools do. Economists call the lag the productivity J-curve: firms must first invest in new processes, skills and organization, intangible investments that take years to pay off (Brynjolfsson et al. 2021). AI has spread fast, but only on the surface Generative AI broke every record for how fast people try something new. Among US adults aged 18 to 64, 44.6% used it in August 2024 and 54.6% in August 2025, less than three years after ChatGPT. At the same age, household adoption of the PC was 19.7% and of the internet 30.1% (Bick et al., via St. Louis Fed 2025). In February 2026, 49% of all US adults had used an AI chatbot and 24% used one daily (Pew Research Center 2026). Firms are slower. In May 2026, 19.8% of US businesses used AI to produce goods or services, rising to 37% among firms with 250 or more employees (US Census Bureau 2026). In the EU, the share of enterprises using AI rose from 8% in 2023 to 20% in 2025 (Eurostat 2025). And the depth of use is still small. AI assisted 6.3% of all US work hours in the second quarter of 2026, up from 4.1% in late 2024, and saved about 2% of them (FRED Blog 2026). Figure 1 puts these numbers next to earlier technologies. Breadth came at record speed because AI rode on the phones, laptops and broadband people already had. Depth, the reorganization of actual work, is moving at something closer to the old pace. This is the ArcGIS-and-Python gap: almost everyone has tried the tool, but only some people have imagined how to rebuild their work around it. Figure 1. Adoption by years since launch: US workers using a computer at work, US households with internet access, EU firms buying cloud services, US adults aged 18–64 using generative AI, EU firms using AI, and the share of US work hours assisted by AI. The measures differ and are not strictly comparable; the figure shows speed, not exact levels. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from NCES, US Census Bureau, Eurostat, St. Louis Fed and FRED data. Three kinds of “peak” “When will AI demand peak?” has different answers depending on what is counted. Users. In the United States, simple adoption curves fitted to the survey data reach 90% of their likely ceiling between 2027 and 2030. Worldwide, where about one in five working-age people used AI by mid-2026 according to Microsoft’s telemetry, the fastest growth is still ahead, roughly 2028–2030, with saturation in the mid-2030s. These are rough curve fits with assumed ceilings. Usage. For computing, the number of users matters less than how much each one uses. Google processed 9.7 trillion tokens a month in May 2024, about 480 trillion in May 2025 and 3.2 quadrillion in May 2026 (Google 2026). Most of that growth came from heavier use per person, especially agents and reasoning models that consume many more tokens per task, not from new users. With AI assisting only 6% of work hours, there is a long way to go: usage will very likely keep growing well into the 2030s. Its growth rate, however, has already peaked: from fiftyfold in a year to sevenfold. Chips. This is where the answer surprises. Why chip demand peaks first Chips are bought to add capacity and to replace old ones. So annual chip purchases depend on how fast the need for computing is growing, not on how large it is. Meanwhile, every year the industry squeezes more tokens out of each dollar of hardware, through better chips, better software and smaller models. Comparing the sevenfold growth in Google’s tokens with the roughly twofold growth in AI hardware spending in 2026 suggests a gain of about three to four times more tokens per hardware dollar each year (my estimate). The consequence is a simple rule: spending on AI chips keeps rising only while usage grows faster than about 3.5 times a year. Figure 2 shows a simple model built on this rule. If token growth slows quickly, chip spending peaks as early as 2027 even though usage keeps rising. On a path consistent with mainstream forecasts, such as McKinsey’s estimate of 5.2 trillion US dollars of AI data-center investment by 2030 (McKinsey 2025), spending peaks around 2029 at roughly twice the 2026 level. Only an “agent boom”, with usage growing five to six times a year until the end of the decade, pushes the peak into the 2030s, and that path would cost more than the largest buyers’ entire cash flow, so power and finance would ration it. Hyperscaler capital spending was already growing about 70% a year in 2026 against about 23% for their operating cash flow (Epoch AI 2026). Figure 2. (a) Three assumed paths for annual growth in AI usage (tokens), starting from Google’s sevenfold growth in 2025–26, and the break-even growth rate above which chip spending rises. (b) The annual chip spending each path implies in a simple stock-flow model: required capacity grows with token use divided by efficiency gains, chips last five years, and the cost of capacity falls 1.4 times a year. 2026 is set to 1, roughly 400 billion US dollars of AI chips (my estimate from NVIDIA, Broadcom and AMD data-center revenue). Figure by Daeha Kim, an illustrative model, not a forecast. The model ignores order backlogs, long-term contracts and supply shortages, which would smooth the curves. Its message is about shape, not exact numbers: the hardware cycle turns when usage growth slows, years before usage itself stops growing. Lessons from railways and fiber History offers sobering analogs. In 1847, the peak year of Britain’s railway mania, investment in railways was, relative to the size of the economy, the equivalent of more than one trillion US dollars today, and many of the lines authorized during the mania were never built (Odlyzko 2010). Around 2000, telecom companies built networks for internet traffic that was widely said to double every three or four months, more than tenfold a year, when actual growth was about 100% a year (Odlyzko 2000). Much of the new fiber sat unused for years, and equipment makers such as Lucent and Nortel lost almost all of their value, even though the internet kept growing. The lesson is not that the technology failed. Railways and the internet were transformative. Investors lost because they paid for capacity on the assumption of growth that arrived later than expected. AI has one important difference. Fiber lasts decades, so the unused strands were eventually lit and became the cheap backbone of the 2000s internet. AI chips become obsolete in about five years. A chip bought for demand that arrives three years late has lost most of its value by then. The durable parts of the AI build-out, such as sites, buildings and power connections, are more like railway track; the chips are more like the telecom switching gear. The big picture Putting this together gives a long-run optimistic and a medium-run cautious view. Usage keeps growing into the 2030s. As with electricity and computers, the real gains come when work is reorganized, and that takes a decade or more. Usage per worker, not the number of users, is the driver. Chip demand is cyclical. Annual spending depends on whether usage growth stays above the pace of efficiency gains. On current trends, the turning point could come anywhere from 2027 to the end of the decade. The most exposed parts of the chain are memory and manufacturing equipment, which respond to changes in the growth rate of spending, and new chip factories ordered at a boom tend to come online just as the boom fades. Five numbers would tell which path we are on: year-on-year growth in AI tokens relative to about 3.5 times; the ratio of AI capital spending to operating cash flow; memory prices and inventories; the share of work hours assisted by AI (6.3% in 2026); and the share of firms running AI agents at scale (about one in five large companies). None of this is investment advice. It is a way to see which assumptions current spending plans already contain. Bottom line AI reached half of American adults faster than any office technology before it, but it has changed only about 6% of working hours. If history is a guide, the deeper reorganization of work will take another decade or more, and AI usage will keep growing through it. Chip demand behaves differently: because efficiency improves several-fold each year, annual chip purchases rise only while usage grows faster than about 3.5 times a year. On current trends that condition may fail sometime between 2027 and 2030, so the semiconductor cycle is likely to turn long before AI demand peaks. Questions to think about In your own organization, which work could already be done with AI tools but is still done the old way, and what is holding it back: skills, rules, trust or imagination? Spreadsheets reduced bookkeeping clerks but increased accountants. Which jobs in your field might AI expand rather than replace? If you had to pick one of the five indicators above to watch, which would you choose, and why? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 스프레드시트, PC, 인터넷, 클라우드 같은 도구는 사람들의 절반에 퍼지기까지 대개 10~20년이 걸렸고, 일하는 방식이 바뀌는 데는 그보다 더 오래 걸렸다. 생성형 AI는 3년 만에 미국 성인의 절반 이상이 써 볼 만큼 역대 가장 빠르게 퍼졌지만, 실제로 AI의 도움을 받는 근무 시간은 아직 약 6%에 불과해 일의 재편은 예전 기술과 비슷한 속도로 진행되고 있다. 따라서 AI 사용량은 2030년대까지 계속 늘어날 가능성이 크지만, 반도체 수요는 다르다. 칩은 늘어나는 사용량만큼 새로 사는 것이고 효율이 해마다 몇 배씩 좋아지므로, 사용량이 연 3.5배 이상 늘어날 때만 칩 구매가 계속 늘어나고, 현재 추세라면 2027~2030년 사이에 반도체 사이클이 먼저 꺾일 수 있다. 이는 투자 조언이 아니라 가정을 드러낸 대략적인 추정이다. title: An AI that reasons like a physician? The Science study, and how far models have come since
description: A summary of Brodeur et al. (2026) in Science, which tested OpenAI's o1 against hundreds of physicians on clinical reasoning and in a real emergency department, with the models and dates involved and my view of how today's models would compare.
tags: artificial intelligence large language models medicine evaluation research practice
text: In 1959, Robert Ledley and Lee Lusted argued in Science that computers could help with medical diagnosis, and that the right test was to give them difficult clinical cases (Ledley and Lusted 1959). For more than sixty years, every generation of diagnostic software, from Bayesian calculators to rule-based expert systems, was measured against that standard. In April 2026, Science published what may become a landmark answer: a study in which a large language model outperformed physicians on most tasks of clinical reasoning, including second opinions on real patients in an emergency department (Brodeur et al. 2026). What makes this study different Earlier studies of language models in medicine mostly used multiple-choice exam questions or narrow tasks, often without any human comparison. This study, led by researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Harvard Medical School and Stanford, did three things differently. It compared the model with baselines from hundreds of physicians. It had physicians score the model’s answers with validated rating scales, often without knowing whether a human or the AI had written them. And it went beyond published cases to real, unstructured patient records from an emergency department in Boston. The six experiments Difficult published cases. On 143 clinicopathological case conferences from the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), the long-standing test bed for diagnostic software, the model listed the correct diagnosis among its possibilities in 78% of cases and named it first in 52%. Counting very close or helpful answers, it was useful in 98%. Performance did not differ significantly between cases published before and after the model’s training data cutoff, which suggests it was not simply recalling answers. On 70 cases previously given to GPT-4, the exact or a very close diagnosis appeared in 89% of the new model’s answers versus 73% of GPT-4’s. Asked which test to order next, it chose the right one in 88% of cases. Showing its reasoning. On 20 virtual patient cases used to teach clinical reasoning, the model’s written reasoning earned a perfect score on 78 of 80 attempts, against 47 of 80 for GPT-4, 28 of 80 for attending physicians and 16 of 72 for residents. It was not, however, significantly better at listing the “cannot-miss” diagnoses that must be ruled out early. Management decisions. On five cases asking what to do next, scored against a consensus of 25 expert physicians, the model’s median score was 89%, compared with 42% for GPT-4, 41% for physicians using GPT-4 and 34% for physicians using conventional resources. Unpublished diagnostic cases. On six cases deliberately never released, to rule out memorization, the model scored a median of 97%, but this was not significantly higher than GPT-4 (92%) or physicians (74–76%). Probabilistic reasoning. Asked to estimate the probability of disease before and after a test, a task given to 553 clinicians in an earlier study, the model performed similarly to GPT-4 and was far less variable than the clinicians. Real emergency department patients. Finally, the team took 76 randomly selected patients from the emergency department and asked the model and two experienced attending physicians for a differential diagnosis at three points: triage, the first physician evaluation, and admission. Two other attending physicians scored the answers without knowing their source, and mostly could not tell which were written by AI. The model’s top five diagnoses contained the exact or a very close diagnosis in 67% of cases at triage, against 55% and 50% for the two physicians, and it stayed ahead at the later points (72% and 82%), although the gap narrowed as more information became available (Figure 1). Figure 1. Selected results: (a) the exact or a very close diagnosis among the model’s possibilities on 70 NEJM cases; (b) share of perfect scores for documented clinical reasoning; (c) median score on management cases; (d) the exact or a very close diagnosis in the top five at emergency department triage for 76 real patients. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Brodeur et al. (2026). Which model, and when This matters for interpreting the results. Five of the six experiments used o1-preview, the first of OpenAI’s “reasoning” models, released on 12 September 2024. The emergency department study used the full o1 model and, for comparison, GPT-4o. The work first appeared as a preprint on 14 December 2024, then covering only the o1-preview experiments, under the title “Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician”. The emergency department study was added in 2025, the paper was submitted to Science on 2 June 2025, accepted on 23 February 2026 and published on 30 April 2026. The word “superhuman” was dropped from the published title. In other words, the paper published in 2026 describes models from late 2024. By the authors’ own account, o1-preview had already been superseded by newer models such as o3, and they expected performance to be sustained or improved. What the authors caution The study covers text only. Real clinical work also relies on what a physician sees and hears, from imaging to a patient’s level of distress. The cases came mostly from internal and emergency medicine, and many were curated for teaching, which may overstate performance on messy real-world records. The emergency department task, a second opinion at fixed points, is a proof of concept. Emergency care is mostly about triage, disposition and immediate treatment, not diagnostic accuracy alone. The model was not always clearly better, notably on cannot-miss diagnoses and on the unreleased cases. What is needed now is prospective trials that test whether such tools improve patient outcomes. How would today’s models do? This section is my own view, not the paper’s. On these tasks, almost certainly better, but the benchmarks are running out of room. Medical results published since the study point in one direction. On HealthBench, a set of 5,000 realistic health conversations scored with rubrics written by physicians, OpenAI reported that its scores rose from 32% for GPT-4o to 60% for o3 within about a year (Arora et al. 2025). Microsoft’s diagnostic orchestrator, running on o3 and working through 304 hard NEJM cases step by step, reached 80–86% accuracy, against an average of 20% for generalist physicians on the same cases (Nori et al. 2025; Figure 2). The same group that wrote the Science paper later built an AI system that produced the first AI-generated diagnosis published in the century-long history of the NEJM case conferences (Buckley et al. 2025). Today’s frontier models, two generations further on, also hallucinate considerably less on hard factual questions than the models of 2024, as discussed in an earlier post. But when a 2024 model already writes perfect clinical reasoning 97% of the time, there is little room left to show improvement. The authors’ warning about “benchmark saturation” applies even more today. Figure 2. Two later results: (a) HealthBench scores reported by OpenAI for three successive models; (b) accuracy on 304 NEJM cases solved step by step, for generalist physicians and for Microsoft’s MAI-DxO orchestrator running on o3. The two benchmarks measure different things and cannot be compared with Figure 1 directly. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Arora et al. (2025) and Nori et al. (2025). The bottleneck has moved from the model to everything around it. The most telling number in the paper may be this one: physicians who had GPT-4 available scored no better than GPT-4 alone (41% versus 42%) on management cases. A more capable model does not automatically make a more capable doctor. Whether physicians and AI together do better than either alone, how to handle incomplete and noisy records, how to combine text with images and examinations, and who is responsible for a wrong suggestion are questions that better models do not answer. Those require the prospective trials the authors call for. What scientists in other fields can take from it The study is also a model of how to evaluate AI fairly, useful well beyond medicine. It compared the model with real experts rather than only with older models; it had blinded experts score open-ended answers; it held back unreleased cases to rule out memorization; and it checked performance before and after the training cutoff. The same design would serve any field, hydrology included, that asks whether an AI can do expert work. Bottom line Brodeur and colleagues showed, with hundreds of physicians as a baseline and real emergency patients, that OpenAI’s o1 models matched or exceeded physicians on most text-based tasks of diagnostic and management reasoning, and clearly exceeded GPT-4. The models tested date from late 2024; today’s models are very likely better still, but many of these benchmarks are close to their ceiling. The open question is no longer whether a language model can reason through a clinical case on paper, but whether doctors working with one will make better decisions for real patients. Questions to think about Physicians with access to GPT-4 did no better than GPT-4 alone. What would have to change for a human and an AI together to outperform either one? If a benchmark is saturated, how would you design a harder, fairer test of clinical reasoning? Which expert task in your own field could be evaluated with the same design: expert baselines, blinded scoring and unreleased cases? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). GPT-4를 쓴 의사도 GPT-4 단독보다 낫지 않았다는 결과가 보여주듯, 이제 핵심 질문은 의사와 AI가 함께 실제 환자를 더 잘 돌볼 수 있느냐이며, 이는 전향적 임상시험으로만 답할 수 있다. References Brodeur, P. G., Buckley, T. A., Kanjee, Z., Goh, E., Ling, E.
