title: How the brain invented learning, part III: simulating in A Brief History of Intelligence
description: Notes on the third of Max Bennett's five breakthroughs: how early mammals built models of the world and of themselves, what simulation let them do, from planning and counterfactual learning to episodic memory and planned movement, and how the same idea became model-based reinforcement learning.
tags: artificial intelligence neuroscience reinforcement learning book notes
text: In part I, bilaterian worms learned to steer toward the good and away from the bad. In part II, early vertebrates learned by trial and error, with dopamine signaling whether things turned out better than expected. Both kinds of learning share a limitation: the animal has to actually do something to learn from it. This post covers the third breakthrough in Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023): simulating. In Bennett’s account it arrived with the first mammals and their new brain structure, the neocortex, which let an animal try things out in imagination before trying them in the world. In AI, the same idea is called model-based reinforcement learning. As before, the summary is my own paraphrase of the book’s argument, and some connections, notably to Dyna, AlphaGo and MuZero, come from the broader literature. 1. Breakthrough 3, Simulating: trying things out in the head A fish that learns by trial and error stores, for each situation, how good each action has turned out to be. This works, but it has a cost: every lesson requires a real attempt, and some attempts are fatal. It is also inflexible. If the world changes, for example if food moves to a new place, the fish must relearn by trial and error, because it has no idea why its old habits worked. An animal with a model of its world can do better. It can ask “what would happen if I went left?” and answer the question without moving. In Bennett’s account, this is what set early mammals apart. Fish and lizards, then as now, can move quickly, remember patterns and learn by trial and error, but they do not plan their movements. The ancestors of mammals were small animals living under the constant threat of dinosaur predators, and the ability to simulate gave them a way to outthink rather than outrun their enemies. Rats that think before they turn In 1948, Edward Tolman reported that rats allowed to explore a maze without any reward later learned to run it much faster than rats that had never seen it, and that they could take shortcuts they had never been trained on (Tolman 1948). He concluded that rats build a “cognitive map” of their surroundings, not just a list of rewarded turns. Tolman and his contemporaries also noticed that rats at a choice point often pause and look back and forth between the options, a behavior called vicarious trial and error. Almost sixty years later, recordings from the rat hippocampus showed what happens during those pauses. Place cells, which fire when a rat is at a particular location, fired in sequences that swept ahead of the animal, first down one path and then down the other, as if the rat were mentally walking each route before choosing (Johnson and Redish 2007). 2. Two simulators: a model of the world and a model of the self The sensory neocortex: a model of the world The neocortex is the structure that most distinguishes the mammalian brain. Bennett’s central claim about its sensory regions is that they work as a generative model: they learn how the world is structured well enough to produce plausible sensory experience on their own. This idea is older than modern AI. In the nineteenth century, Hermann von Helmholtz argued that perception is a kind of unconscious inference: we do not simply receive images, we infer the most likely world that would have produced them. That is why we fill in the blind spot and see shapes in ambiguous pictures. If the brain can generate what it expects to see, the same machinery can be run without input, and that is imagination. The AI connection. Neural network researchers arrived at similar ideas. The “wake-sleep” algorithm of the 1990s trained a network to recognize inputs while a second, generative pathway learned to produce them, alternating between a waking phase driven by data and a “sleeping” phase driven by the network’s own fantasies (Hinton et al. 1995). Predictive coding models of the visual cortex proposed that higher brain areas send predictions downward and only the errors travel upward (Rao and Ballard 1999). Today’s generative AI, which produces text, images and video from learned models, is the most visible descendant of this line of thought. The first frontal cortex: a model of the self A model of the world is not enough to plan; an animal also needs a model of itself. Bennett argues that the first region of the frontal neocortex, the agranular prefrontal cortex, plays this role. It models the animal’s own movements and internal states, such as hunger, and builds something like intent: an account of what the animal is trying to do that explains its own behavior. Working together, the self model and the world model let an animal pause and run through situations it is not actually in: “if I, being hungry, go down this path, what will I find?” This combination is what AI researchers call model-based reinforcement learning. The search problem Simulation raises a new difficulty. There are far too many possible futures to imagine them all, and imagining takes time an animal in danger may not have. Bennett credits the frontal cortex with solving this search problem, at least well enough: it chooses which paths are worth simulating and decides when it is worth stopping to simulate at all. The AI connection. The same problem limits game-playing programs. Go has vastly more possible continuations than any computer can explore. AlphaGo dealt with this by letting a neural network propose a few promising moves and spending its simulations on those (Silver et al. 2016), much as a rat considers two or three routes rather than every possible path. 3. What simulation buys Planning A model lets an animal compare futures before committing to one, as the hippocampal sweeps suggest rats do. This is planning, and it is most useful when mistakes are costly and the situation is new. Learning from imagined experience A model also lets an animal learn from experiences it never had. During sleep and rest, the rat hippocampus replays sequences of place-cell activity from the day’s runs (Wilson and McNaughton 1994), a candidate mechanism for consolidating and extending what was learned. The AI connection. In 1990, Richard Sutton proposed Dyna, an architecture in which an agent learns a model of its environment from real experience and then also learns from simulated experience generated by that model (Sutton 1990). The effect is dramatic even in a tiny maze. Figure 1 shows a simulation I ran of the maze used in Sutton and Barto’s textbook: an agent that learns only from real steps needs about 28 trips to find a near-shortest path, while one that adds 50 imagined steps for each real step needs about 3. Replaying stored experience later became a key ingredient of deep reinforcement learning, including DQN, which learned to play 49 Atari games directly from the screen pixels (Mnih et al. 2015). Figure 1. Steps needed to reach the goal in a small maze, for an agent that learns only from real experience and for agents that also learn from 5 or 50 imagined steps per real step, generated from a model learned along the way (Dyna-Q). Averages over 30 runs; the first episode is omitted. Figure by Daeha Kim, a simulation of the Dyna maze described in Sutton and Barto (2018). Learning from what did not happen A model makes it possible to ask “what if I had chosen otherwise?” Rats seem to do this too. In a task where they chose between restaurants offering food after different delays, rats that skipped a good deal and then met a worse one looked back toward the option they had passed, and neurons in their orbitofrontal cortex represented the missed option, a pattern the authors interpreted as regret (Steiner and Redish 2014). Learning from counterfactuals extracts more from each experience than learning from outcomes alone. It also offers a better answer to the credit assignment problem from part I. An animal that only links outcomes to whatever came just before them is easily misled; an animal that can compare what happened with what would have happened otherwise can give credit to the actual cause, including its own choice. Remembering specific episodes Simulation also made possible episodic memory: recalling a specific past event, including what the animal itself did, and using it to adjust behavior. Memory and imagination appear to share the same machinery. Patients with damage to the hippocampus not only struggle to remember the past; they also struggle to imagine new experiences, producing fragmented scenes when asked to picture, for example, lying on a beach (Hassabis et al. 2007). Planning the body In later mammals, Bennett notes, the motor cortex evolved, which let them plan and simulate specific body movements: a cat looking at the branches ahead and deciding where to put each paw before it jumps. This is a skill we rarely think of as intelligence, yet it is one of the hardest for machines. Robots still struggle with dexterous movement that animals perform effortlessly, a contrast known as Moravec’s paradox (Moravec 1988). Habits and plans side by side Mammals did not replace the old system with the new one. They kept both. Fast, cached habits handle familiar situations; slow, model-based planning handles new or changing ones. An influential computational account proposes that the brain arbitrates between the two according to which is more reliable at the moment, with planning favored early in learning and habits once a task is well practiced (Daw et al. 2005). 4. The AI connection: planning with a model The most famous AI systems of the last decade are, at their core, simulators. AlphaGo combined neural networks, which learned to evaluate positions and suggest moves, with tree search, which simulated possible continuations of the game before each move. It played Go using a perfect model of the rules. MuZero went a step further: it learned its own model of the environment and planned inside that learned model, reaching superhuman play in Go, chess and shogi and strong play in Atari games without being told the rules (Schrittwieser et al. 2020). DreamerV3 learns a world model and trains its behavior largely in imagined trajectories, and with one fixed configuration it learned to collect diamonds in Minecraft from scratch (Hafner et al. 2025). These are the engineering versions of a rat pausing at a fork in the maze. 5. The correspondence at a glance The table below pairs each biological mechanism with its AI counterpart. The last column is my own judgment of how close the match is. Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close Cognitive map (Tolman) Learned model of the environment Same idea Sensory neocortex as a generative model of the world Generative models (wake-sleep, modern generative AI) Same principle, very different mechanisms Agranular prefrontal cortex as a model of the self and its intent Agents that model their own actions and goals Loose Choosing which paths to simulate (search problem) Policy networks guiding tree search (AlphaGo) Functional match Perception as inference, predictive coding Predictive coding networks Influential hypothesis on both sides Vicarious trial and error, hippocampal sweeps Planning by simulation (tree search) Functional match Replay during sleep and rest Dyna, experience replay Functional match Regret, counterfactual learning Counterfactual updates in planning Partial match Episodic memory Stored episodes for replay and retrieval Partial match Motor cortex: planning body movements Motion planning in robotics Still far apart (Moravec’s paradox) Arbitration between habits and planning Hybrid model-free and model-based agents Active research on both sides 6. Closing: imagination has a price Simulation made mammals flexible learners. With a model of the world and a model of themselves, small mammals could outplan predators far larger than themselves, learn from experiences they never had, credit the real causes of good and bad outcomes, remember specific episodes and plan their own movements. But simulation is slow and costly, which is why habits remain, and a simulation is only as good as the model behind it. A wrong model produces confident plans that fail, a problem that model-based AI shares. Bennett’s next breakthrough, mentalizing, turns the simulator inward and toward others: primates began to model not just the world but minds, including their own. That is the subject of part IV. Questions to think about A model-free learner needs many real trials; a model-based learner needs a good model. In which of your own problems is it easier to collect experience, and in which is it easier to build a model? Hydrologists run rainfall–runoff models to compare flood-control options before choosing one. In what ways is that like a rat pausing at a fork in the maze, and in what ways is it different? If imagination and memory share the same machinery, what might that mean for how reliable our memories are? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 『A Brief History of Intelligence』의 세 번째 돌파 과정은 초기 포유류가 신피질을 통해 얻은 시뮬레이션(simulating) 능력이다. 감각 신피질은 바깥 세계의 모형을, 처음 생긴 전두엽 영역인 무과립 전전두피질은 자기 몸과 상태의 모형을 만들었고, 둘이 함께 지금 겪고 있지 않은 상황을 머릿속에서 시뮬레이션하게 했다. 이 덕분에 포유류는 갈림길에서 멈춰 가능한 길을 미리 시도해 보고, 하지 않은 선택의 결과와 비교해 진짜 원인을 가려내고, 지난 일을 떠올려 행동을 고칠 수 있게 되었으며, 이후 운동피질이 생기면서 몸의 움직임까지 계획하게 되었다. 공룡의 위협 속에서 살아남은 작은 포유류의 이 능력은 AI에서 모형 기반 강화학습으로 다시 나타나, Dyna에서 AlphaGo와 MuZero로 이어졌다. title: Why climate science and economics talk past each other
description: A reading of a Nature Climate Change comment by Sherwood and colleagues: why the gap between physical climate science and economics distorts the climate costs that reach policy and finance, and four ways to close it.
tags: climate change climate economics social cost of carbon uncertainty science communication
text: “Each degree of warming will cost X% of world GDP.” Numbers like this drive carbon prices, bank stress tests and public debate. But behind each one is a long chain of translation: from emissions to warming, from warming to floods and heatwaves, from hazards to damaged houses and lost working hours, and from there to money. Physical climate scientists build the first half of that chain, economists the second. A comment in Nature Climate Change by Steven Sherwood and thirteen colleagues from climate science, economics and finance argues that the two communities do not communicate well, and that the damage from this gap reaches far beyond academia (Sherwood et al. 2026). This post summarizes their argument. The numbers are necessary The authors start by defending quantification. Since Nordhaus’s first integrated climate–economy model (Nordhaus 1992), cost estimates have shaped mitigation and adaptation policy, the social cost of carbon used in regulation, and the climate risk assessments of banks and insurers. Refusing to put numbers on climate damage does not remove numbers from these decisions. It replaces carefully examined estimates with implicit ones that nobody examines. The problem is how the numbers travel. Each estimate is valid only under the assumptions and models that produced it, but it is usually passed on as if it were a self-contained fact. Why the gap is serious Two narrow pipes. Most of the conversation between the disciplines, and between them and the public, runs through two numbers: global mean surface temperature and gross domestic product. Both are useful summaries, and both are asked to carry more meaning than they can. Nobody experiences a global average temperature; people experience floods, droughts, storms, humid heat and rising seas, which depend on regional patterns, natural variability and time lags. GDP, in turn, measures the flow of production, not the houses, roads, health and ecosystems on which future well-being depends. After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, the recorded losses of GDP were small compared with the destruction of housing, infrastructure and lives. If only temperature leaves climate science and only GDP leaves economics, most of what each field knows is filtered out before the conversation starts. False precision. Published estimates of global losses differ by an order of magnitude for the same amount of warming, and the spread has widened over two decades. The authors stress that this is not mainly error. It reflects legitimate differences in which hazards are counted, how adaptation is assumed, how losses are spread across regions and incomes, and how the future is discounted. Some of it is genuine scientific uncertainty, some of it reflects value judgments. When results are compressed into a headline number, these distinctions disappear, and users from journalists to central banks are left with a precision that does not exist. Risks that are poorly understood, such as tipping points and compound events, are included inconsistently or not at all (Rising et al. 2022). Lessons that did not cross over. Many recent damage estimates are empirical: they measure how economies have responded to year-to-year weather and extrapolate to a warmer future. Climate science learned the hard way that such relationships can mislead. A study of extreme rainfall in Australia found that the observed link between daily rainfall extremes and local temperature understates how much extremes will intensify under warming, partly because heavy rain itself cools the air on the days it falls (Bao et al. 2017). The same trap, the comment argues, may affect empirical damage functions. A culture clash. Physical climate scientists usually judge a model by whether it represents known processes and matches observations. Economists more often value models that clarify choices and mechanisms, even with deliberately stylized assumptions. Each side, judging the other by its own standards, finds the other’s models either dangerously unrealistic or opaque. Different users, different questions. Investors and regulators care about shocks over the next decade, when natural variability can outweigh the warming trend. Vulnerable communities care about the weather they will have to adapt to. No single number serves all of them. Four ways to close the gap 1. Make assumptions and uncertainty part of the headline. Long lists of caveats can make an estimate look useless, so the key is to report the conditions that materially change the result or its use. The authors suggest layers: a clear central message, followed by visible statements of the key assumptions, omitted risks, time horizon and uncertainty range. Figure 1 applies this idea to the estimate of heat-related labour losses discussed in an earlier post. Users also need to learn that a conditional estimate is usually more trustworthy, not less. Figure 1. An example of a layered presentation: the labour component of the social cost of carbon estimated by Moore et al. (2026), shown with the conditions that change how it should be used. Figure by Daeha Kim, applying the recommendation of Sherwood et al. (2026) to numbers reported in Moore et al. (2026). 2. Widen the pipes. Report damage to capital stocks and to different groups alongside GDP totals, and describe climate change in the hazards that matter for decisions rather than in global averages alone. For investors and regulators, that means loss estimates with explicit time horizons that separate sudden shocks from gradual change. 3. Link a suite of models transparently. A single model that does everything is neither realistic nor desirable. Instead, the links from physical hazard to exposure, adaptation, economic loss and financial risk should be visible, so users can see which assumption drives which conclusion (Figure 2). Figure 2. The chain that turns warming into an economic cost, and the choices made at each link. The upper links are the domain of physical climate science, the lower links of economics and finance; the middle links belong to both. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic based on the argument of Sherwood et al. (2026). 4. Let the IPCC set the standard. The Seventh Assessment Report will again separate physical science and economics into different working groups, which reduces the chance for translation. The authors ask that physical scientists, economists and finance experts work together closely in this cycle, and that no headline number reach the Summary for Policymakers without its conditions stated in plain language. What a hydrologist takes from it This is our problem too. Flood risk assessment has long been framed as hazard, exposure and vulnerability, which is exactly the chain in Figure 2. Hydrologists can help move the conversation from global temperature to the hazards people actually face: river floods, flash droughts, low flows and humid heat. Nonstationarity applies to economies as well. Hydrologists learned that statistics fitted to past records can mislead when the climate shifts. The rainfall example in the comment is the same lesson. Damage functions fitted to historical weather deserve the same caution as flood frequency curves fitted to a changing climate. Conditional is not weak. Engineering design already works this way: a design flood comes with a return period, a record length and a confidence interval. Climate costs could be communicated the same way. Bottom line Climate cost estimates are indispensable, but they pass through two narrow pipes, global temperature and GDP, that strip out most of what climate scientists and economists know. The result is a spread of numbers that look precise and contradictory at the same time. Sherwood and colleagues propose four remedies: put assumptions and uncertainty in the headline, report hazards and losses beyond the two averages, link models transparently, and use the next IPCC assessment to set the standard. A number with its conditions attached is not a weaker number; it is one that decision-makers can actually trust. Questions to think about Which climate hazard would be more useful than global mean temperature for a water manager in your region, and why? If two damage estimates differ by a factor of ten, how would you explain to a policymaker which parts of the difference are uncertainty and which are value judgments? What would a “layered” presentation look like for a flood risk estimate you have worked with? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). Sherwood 등(2026)은 물리 기후과학과 경제학 사이의 소통 단절이 학계 내부 문제를 넘어 정책, 금융, 대중 논의까지 왜곡한다고 지적한다. 두 분야는 주로 전지구 평균기온과 GDP라는 두 숫자로만 대화하는데, 평균기온은 사람들이 실제로 겪는 홍수·가뭄·폭염을 담지 못하고, GDP는 생산의 흐름만 잴 뿐 주택, 기반시설, 건강, 생태계 같은 자산의 손실은 놓친다. 같은 온난화에 대한 피해 추정치가 열 배나 차이 나는 것은 오류라기보다 어떤 위험을 포함하고 적응과 할인을 어떻게 가정했는지의 차이인데, 헤드라인 숫자로 압축되면 이 차이가 사라져 거짓 정밀성이 생긴다. 저자들은 가정과 불확실성을 헤드라인에 함께 제시하고, GDP와 평균기온 외의 손실과 위험을 함께 보고하며, 위험에서 손실까지 이어지는 모델들을 투명하게 연결하고, IPCC 7차 보고서에서 이를 기준으로 삼자고 제안한다. 과거 자료로 만든 관계가 기후가 바뀌면 틀릴 수 있다는 점은 수문학의 비정상성 문제와 같은 교훈이다. title: More compute, better AI: how much better?
description: What neural scaling laws actually predict when hardware and compute grow, where the extra compute comes from, how much thinking longer adds, and the limits of power, data and money, checked against the primary sources as of October 2026.
tags: artificial intelligence large language models scaling laws computing
text: “Scaling laws” are the reason AI companies are building gigawatt data centers. The idea is that a language model improves predictably as it gets more computing power, more parameters and more data. But how much better? If we had ten or a hundred times more computing power than today, what would we get? This post works through the answer using the original papers and the latest data, as of October 2026. The scaling law in one sentence In 2020, Kaplan and colleagues at OpenAI showed that a language model’s loss, a measure of how badly it predicts the next word, falls as a power law of training compute, over eight orders of magnitude (Kaplan et al. 2020). In 2022, DeepMind’s “Chinchilla” study refined the recipe: for a given compute budget, parameters and training data should grow together, roughly 20 tokens of text per parameter (Hoffmann et al. 2022). A later replication by Epoch AI corrected the fitted constants but confirmed the 20-to-1 rule (Besiroglu et al. 2024). The corrected fit makes the returns concrete. Loss has an irreducible floor, set by the inherent unpredictability of text, and only the gap above that floor can be closed. Each 10× increase in compute closes about a third of the remaining gap; 100× closes about half (Figure 1a, my calculation from the fit). In other words, every halving of what is left to gain costs about a hundredfold more compute. Figure 1. (a) Pretraining loss predicted by the Chinchilla scaling law (with Epoch AI’s corrected constants) when compute is allocated optimally between model size and data, with the approximate training compute of some well-known models and of the largest run Epoch AI judges feasible by 2030. (b) The number of training tokens the same law calls for, compared with the estimated stock of public human-written text. The fit describes one family of models; it shows the shape of the curve, not the exact loss of any frontier model. Figure by Daeha Kim, calculated from Besiroglu et al. (2024), with compute estimates from Brown et al. (2020) and Epoch AI, and the data stock from Villalobos et al. (2024). Does lower loss mean a smarter model? Loss falls smoothly, but people experience abilities, and abilities sometimes seem to appear suddenly with scale. A 2023 study showed that most of these apparent jumps are artifacts of all-or-nothing scoring: more than 92% of the claimed “emergent abilities” came from just two metrics that give credit only for a perfectly right answer (Schaeffer et al. 2023). Measured with continuous scores, the same abilities improve gradually. Real-world capability has nonetheless improved fast. METR measures the length of software tasks, in human working time, that AI agents can complete half the time. That “time horizon” doubled about every seven months between 2019 and 2025 (Kwa et al. 2025), and on METR’s updated task suite the doubling time shortened to about 130 days since 2023 and 89 days since 2024 (METR 2026). By mid-2026 the best models were near the ceiling of what the suite can measure. METR stopped updating its measurements in September, so there is no reliable figure for the months since. Faster chips are only part of the story The obvious way to get more compute is better hardware, but chips alone improve slowly. Epoch AI decomposed the growth of frontier training compute, about 4.2× per year since 2018 (Epoch AI 2025; Figure 2): more chips per training run: 1.7× per year; longer training runs: 1.5× per year; faster chips: 1.4× per year. In log terms, faster chips supply only about a quarter of the growth. At 1.4× per year, a tenfold improvement from chips alone takes about seven years. The frontier gets ten times more compute about every year and a half mainly by spending more: the cost of the largest training runs has grown about 2.4× per year (Cottier et al. 2024), and the largest single data centers now draw about a gigawatt. Better algorithms add a further multiplier. The compute needed to reach a given level of language-model performance has halved about every eight months, equivalent to about 2.8× more “effective” compute every year (Ho et al. 2024). Combining both, effective compute has grown roughly tenfold or more per year, my calculation. Figure 2. Median yearly growth of training compute for frontier models since 2018 and its three components, and the yearly gain from better algorithms expressed as equivalent compute. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported by Epoch AI (2025) and Ho et al. (2024). A second axis: thinking longer Since 2024, a second kind of scaling has mattered as much as the first. Reasoning models such as OpenAI’s o1 improve when they are allowed to spend more compute on each question. On the AIME 2024 math competition, o1 solved 74% of problems with one attempt, 83% with a majority vote over 64 attempts, and 93% when a learned scorer picked the best of 1,000 (OpenAI 2024). On the ARC-AGI puzzle benchmark, o3 rose from 75.7% to 87.5% when given about 172 times more compute per task (ARC Prize 2024). The pattern is the same as in pretraining: gains are roughly linear in the logarithm of compute, so each additional step costs ten to a hundred times more (Figure 3). Reinforcement learning, the training method behind these reasoning models, shows a similar shape but levels off at a ceiling set by the training recipe (Khatri et al. 2025). Figure 3. Accuracy of OpenAI’s o1 on AIME 2024 and of o3 (preview) on ARC-AGI-1 as more samples are used per problem. The o1 points use different ways of combining samples (a single attempt, a majority vote and re-ranking by a learned scorer). Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported by OpenAI (2024) and ARC Prize (2024). The limits ahead: power, data and money Epoch AI estimates that a training run of about 2×10²⁹ FLOP, roughly 400 times the largest known run of 2025, is likely feasible by 2030, but power is the first constraint to bind: such a run would need about 6 gigawatts, while today’s largest single sites draw about one (Sevilla et al. 2024). Data may bind even earlier. The stock of public human-written text is estimated at about 300 trillion tokens (Villalobos et al. 2024). A compute-optimal run of 10²⁸ FLOP would already need about 150 trillion tokens, half of it (Figure 1b). Repeating data helps for a while, since up to about four passes over the same text is nearly as good as new data (Muennighoff et al. 2023), and synthetic data and reinforcement learning on checkable tasks are partly a response to this limit. Have the returns diminished? In late 2024 and 2025, reports suggested that simply making pretraining bigger was paying off less than expected, and OpenAI’s GPT-4.5 was widely seen as a modest step. In November 2025, Ilya Sutskever described the period from 2020 to 2025 as an “age of scaling” now giving way to an “age of research.” Yet over the same period, measured capability accelerated: an Epoch AI analysis found that several capability indices, including METR’s time horizon, sped up around 2024, driven largely by reasoning models and concentrated in code and mathematics (Epoch AI 2026). Both observations fit the scaling law. Returns to pretraining compute were always diminishing in the sense shown in Figure 1, so a few times more compute buys a modest step. What changed is that labs found a second, cheaper axis, reinforcement learning and inference-time compute, and better algorithms on top. So how much does more hardware buy? On paper: each 10× in training compute closes about a third of the remaining gap in loss. Large, steady gains require exponential increases in compute. In practice: that 10× arrives about every 18 months, but mostly from more chips and more money; faster chips alone would take about seven years to deliver it. Beyond pretraining: letting models think longer adds similar log-linear gains per question, at a cost paid every time the model is used. Limits: power and data, not chip speed, are the constraints most likely to bind before 2030. Scaling laws do not promise that more hardware makes AI arbitrarily capable. They promise steady improvement for exponentially rising cost, and so far that bargain, combined with better algorithms, has been good enough to keep progress fast. Questions to think about If each halving of the remaining loss costs a hundredfold more compute, what would make it worth paying? Inference-time compute is paid every time a model is used. How does that change the economics compared with training compute, which is paid once? Many scientific models also improve with resolution and data following power laws. Where in your own field have you seen diminishing returns of this kind? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 스케일링 법칙에 따르면 언어 모델의 손실은 학습 연산량의 거듭제곱 법칙으로 줄어들지만, 줄일 수 있는 부분에는 바닥이 있어 연산량을 10배 늘릴 때마다 남은 격차의 약 3분의 1, 100배 늘리면 약 절반이 줄어든다. 최첨단 모델의 학습 연산량은 해마다 약 4배씩 늘었지만 칩 성능 향상(연 1.4배)의 기여는 4분의 1 정도이고, 나머지는 더 많은 칩, 더 긴 학습, 더 큰 투자에서 나왔으며, 알고리즘 개선이 해마다 약 2.8배의 연산 효과를 더했다. 2024년 이후에는 답하기 전에 더 오래 생각하게 하는 추론 연산이 두 번째 축이 되었지만, 이 역시 연산량의 로그에 비례해 좋아져 한 단계 나아갈 때마다 10–100배의 비용이 든다. 앞으로는 칩 속도보다 전력(2030년 규모의 학습에 약 6 GW)과 데이터(공개 텍스트 약 300조 토큰)가 먼저 한계가 될 가능성이 크다. title: Model distillation: how AI models learn from each other, and what they lose
description: What distillation is, why it lets new models catch up with the frontier so quickly, why it has become a dispute between AI labs, whether it can be prevented, and the limits of models built this way.
tags: artificial intelligence large language models distillation research practice
text: In July 2026, the White House science adviser accused the Chinese company Moonshot AI of building its Kimi K3 model by “distilling” Anthropic’s Claude Fable. China’s embassy in Washington called the allegation “entirely unfounded” (Business Today 2026), and several AI researchers doubted it, noting that K3 appeared only about two weeks after Fable became public and that distillation alone is unlikely to produce such a strong model so quickly (AI Weekly 2026). True or not, the episode shows how central one technique has become to the competition between AI labs. This post explains what distillation is, why it works, whether it can be stopped, and what models built this way tend to lack. What distillation is Distillation means training a smaller or newer model, the “student,” to imitate a stronger one, the “teacher.” The idea was popularized by Hinton and colleagues in 2015 (Hinton et al. 2015). Their key observation was that a teacher’s full output carries more information than its final answer. When a language model completes “The capital of Australia is …,” it assigns a high probability to Canberra, but also a noticeable probability to Sydney and almost none to Perth (Figure 1a). Those small numbers encode how the teacher sees the world, which mistakes are plausible and which are not. Hinton called it “dark knowledge.” A student trained to match the whole distribution learns faster and from fewer examples than one trained only on correct answers. Inside a lab, distillation is routine and legitimate. The fast, cheap versions of frontier models are typically distilled from larger ones, and DeepSeek released a family of small open models distilled from its R1 reasoning model (DeepSeek-AI 2025). The controversial version works from the outside. A competitor cannot see another lab’s probabilities, but it can send millions of questions through the public interface, collect the answers, and train its own model on them. The student then sees much less than in the classic setup: one sampled answer instead of a full distribution, and often no reasoning at all (Figure 1b). Figure 1. (a) An illustrative next-word distribution from a teacher model: besides the right answer, it shows which wrong answers are close. (b) What a student model can learn from, from a lab distilling its own model to a competitor working through a chat interface. The probabilities and bar lengths are illustrative. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic based on Hinton et al. (2015). Why it has become a dispute The attraction is obvious: answers from a frontier model are far cheaper to collect than the compute, data and expertise needed to develop the same abilities independently. In February 2026, Anthropic reported that three Chinese labs, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI and MiniMax, had generated more than 16 million exchanges with Claude through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts, targeting its strongest abilities: agentic reasoning, tool use and coding (Anthropic 2026; Figure 2). These are Anthropic’s attributions; the labs have not confirmed them. The July accusation about Kimi K3 went further, but its evidence has not been made public. Figure 2. Exchanges with Claude that Anthropic attributed to distillation campaigns by three AI labs, as reported in February 2026. According to Anthropic, the campaigns targeted agentic coding and tool use (MiniMax); agentic reasoning, tool use, coding, computer use and vision (Moonshot AI); and reasoning and the grading of answers for reinforcement learning (DeepSeek). Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Anthropic (2026). The dispute has an uncomfortable side for the accusers, too. Frontier models were themselves trained on vast amounts of text written by others, and the line between learning from public outputs and copying is contested. What makes the current cases different, in the labs’ view, is the use of fake accounts and the violation of terms of service to extract a competitor’s specific capabilities at scale. Can it be prevented? Not completely. Anything a model shows its users, it also shows a potential student. What labs can do is make distillation slower, costlier and less useful: Detection. Classifiers that recognize distillation patterns, such as huge numbers of similar prompts or systematic attempts to extract reasoning, and that link many accounts to one operator (Anthropic 2026). Access control. Stronger identity checks for the account types most often abused, and sharing of indicators between labs and cloud providers. Hiding the reasoning. Since 2024, several labs show only a summary of their models’ step-by-step reasoning. OpenAI cited competitive advantage, alongside safety monitoring, when it decided not to show the raw reasoning of its o1 models (OpenAI 2024). Poisoned outputs. Researchers have proposed “antidistillation sampling,” which subtly changes how a model picks its words so that the answers remain useful to people but are much less useful as training data for a student (Savani et al. 2025). Each defense has a cost for legitimate users, who also want to see the reasoning and use the model at scale. The realistic goal is to keep distillation from being a shortcut, not to make it impossible. What distilled models lack Distillation lets a model catch up quickly. But copying has limits. Style transfers more easily than substance. In a careful 2023 study, researchers fine-tuned open models on ChatGPT outputs. Human raters judged the imitations close to ChatGPT, because they had learned its confident, well-structured style, yet on targeted tests of factual knowledge, coding and problem solving they improved little or not at all (Gudibande et al. 2024). The authors concluded that closing the gap requires a stronger base model, not more imitation. A distilled model can therefore look better than it is, which also makes some benchmark scores and first impressions misleading. The student learns only what it is asked. A campaign aimed at coding and agents transfers coding and agents. Rare facts, niche fields, other languages and unusual situations are covered thinly, and the student sees only sampled answers without the teacher’s uncertainty. As discussed in an earlier post on hallucination, rare facts are exactly where models make things up. It inherits mistakes, and copies of copies degrade. A student copies its teacher’s errors and biases along with its strengths. When models are trained repeatedly on the output of other models, the rare parts of the original data, the tails of the distribution, gradually disappear, a process known as model collapse (Shumailov et al. 2024). It stays one step behind. A student rarely surpasses its teacher in what it copies, and it can only copy what already exists. Distillation is a way to follow the frontier, not to move it. Safety behavior may not come along. Anthropic argues that illicitly distilled models are unlikely to keep the safeguards built into the original, such as refusals to help with weapons or cyberattacks (Anthropic 2026). Provenance becomes a risk. For companies, universities and public agencies, a model built in violation of another provider’s terms carries legal and reputational risk, and possibly sanctions. That matters when choosing a model for sensitive work. Bottom line Distillation is an old and useful idea: a small model learns faster from a teacher’s full judgments than from right answers alone. Done from the outside, through millions of questions, it lets new models catch up with the frontier at a fraction of the cost, which is why it has become a source of accusations between labs and governments. It cannot be fully prevented, only made harder. And it has clear limits: distilled models copy style more easily than substance, cover what they were asked and little else, inherit their teachers’ errors and stay one step behind. For users, the lesson is to test such models on their own tasks, especially rare and specialized ones, before trusting their benchmark scores. Questions to think about If a model’s benchmark scores come partly from imitating a stronger model, how would you design a test that reveals the difference? Where should the line be drawn between learning from public outputs, which all models do, and illicit distillation? Would you use a model of uncertain provenance for research with sensitive data? What would you need to know first? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 증류(distillation)는 작거나 새로운 모델(학생)이 더 강한 모델(교사)의 출력을 따라 하며 배우는 방법으로, 교사가 정답뿐 아니라 어떤 오답이 그럴듯한지까지 담은 확률 분포를 학생에게 전해 준다. 연구소 안에서 작고 빠른 모델을 만드는 데는 흔히 쓰이지만, 경쟁사가 수백만 개의 질문을 보내 답만 모아 학습하는 외부 증류는 최근 큰 분쟁이 되었다. Anthropic은 2026년 2월 중국의 세 연구소가 약 2만 4천 개의 가짜 계정으로 Claude와 1,600만 회 이상 대화했다고 밝혔고, 7월에는 미국 정부가 Kimi K3가 Claude Fable을 증류해 만들어졌다고 주장했지만 근거는 공개되지 않았다. 증류는 탐지, 계정 확인, 추론 과정 숨기기 등으로 어렵게 만들 수는 있어도 완전히 막을 수는 없다. 이렇게 만든 모델은 빠르게 따라잡을 수 있다는 장점이 있지만, 내용보다 말투를 더 쉽게 배우고, 질문받은 분야 밖의 드문 지식에 약하며, 교사의 오류를 물려받고, 늘 한발 뒤처진다는 한계가 있다. title: How the brain invented learning, part II: reinforcing in A Brief History of Intelligence
description: Notes on the second of Max Bennett's five breakthroughs: how early vertebrates learned by trial and error, how reinforcement learning ran into the same problem, and why dopamine turned out to be the TD error.
tags: artificial intelligence neuroscience reinforcement learning book notes
text: In part I, we followed the first of the five breakthroughs in Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023): steering. Bilaterian worms learned to move toward the good and away from the bad, and to store experience in the strength of their synapses. Their dopamine meant only “something good is nearby.” This post covers the second breakthrough, reinforcing: how early vertebrates acquired trial-and-error learning, how AI researchers ran into the same problem, and how the same molecule, dopamine, was turned into a learning signal. As before, the summary is my own paraphrase of the book’s argument. 1. Breakthrough 2, Reinforcing: try it, then learn from the result The stage for the second breakthrough is the early vertebrates that emerged about 500 million years ago, after the Cambrian explosion. The brains of these fish-like ancestors already had the basic blueprint that persists all the way to the human brain: a precursor of the cortex (the pallium), the basal ganglia, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, and hindbrain. What this blueprint made possible was trial-and-error learning. The nematode’s associative learning was about learning that “good things follow this stimulus.” Vertebrates learn that “good things follow when I do this.” They learn the consequences not of stimuli but of their own actions. From Thorndike to Minsky In 1898, Edward Thorndike placed cats in puzzle boxes and watched. At first they poked at everything until they happened to release the latch, but with repetition their escape times fell. Actions followed by satisfying outcomes are repeated; actions followed by unpleasant ones fade. This is the law of effect, and fish learn the same way. The trouble surfaced when people tried to put this principle into machines. In the early 1950s Marvin Minsky built SNARC, a neural-network machine that learned by reinforcement, and he later named the critical obstacle: the temporal credit assignment problem. When you win a game of chess, which of the dozens of earlier moves contributed to the win? The later the reward arrives, the harder it is to know which action to reinforce. Sutton’s answer: learn from changes in prediction, not from the reward itself Temporal difference (TD) learning, formalized by Richard Sutton in the 1980s, sidesteps the problem elegantly. Instead of waiting for the final reward, the learner keeps a running prediction of how good things are going to be, and learns from the difference between successive predictions. If the position suddenly looks better, the action just taken was probably a good one. \[\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)\] Here \(V(s)\) is the predicted value of state \(s\), \(r\) is the immediate reward, and \(\gamma\) is the discount factor. \(\delta\), the TD error, measures how much better things turned out than expected. The architecture is often split in two: a critic that evaluates states, and an actor that adjusts its policy using the critic’s error. In 1992, Gerald Tesauro at IBM used this method to build TD-Gammon, a neural network that plays backgammon. Learning by playing against itself, it reached a level close to the best human players. It was the first striking evidence that reinforcement learning really works. 2. Dopamine is the TD error The most dramatic moment in the book is the discovery that an algorithm AI researchers had devised on paper was already running inside the brain. In the 1980s and 1990s, Wolfram Schultz recorded the activity of dopamine neurons in the monkey midbrain. The setup was simple: a light (the cue) comes on, and a few seconds later juice (the reward) arrives. But the dopamine neurons’ behavior could not be explained as a response to reward. Before learning: when juice arrives unexpectedly, dopamine neurons fire strongly. After learning: they fire when the light comes on, and do not respond when the juice itself arrives. When the light is not followed by juice: firing drops below baseline at the moment the juice should have come. In all three cases, dopamine tracks not the reward received but the difference between the reward received and the reward expected. These three patterns are exactly how the TD error \(\delta\) behaves. An unexpected reward is a positive error, a predicted reward is zero error, and the absence of an expected reward is a negative error. And the moment a prediction of “something good is coming” first appears, when the light comes on, is precisely when the outlook improves. When Schultz, Peter Dayan, and Read Montague published this correspondence in Science in 1997, the view took hold that dopamine is not a “pleasure chemical” but a reward prediction error signal. Dopamine changed its meaning Seen through Bennett’s evolutionary lens, the finding becomes even more interesting. In the nematode, dopamine was a state signal: “something good is nearby.” In vertebrates, the same molecule is repurposed as a learning signal: “things just got better than expected.” Evolution did not invent a new molecule. It changed the meaning of an existing broadcast channel. The structure that receives this signal and adjusts behavior is the basal ganglia. The basal ganglia select one action from the available options and reinforce choices followed by a positive dopamine signal, so that those choices become easier to repeat. In reinforcement-learning terms, the basal ganglia play the actor, and the dopamine signal is the critic’s error. Curiosity: surviving in a world of sparse rewards Bennett argues that vertebrates also became curious at this stage. Fish explore novel things, and dopamine neurons respond not only to reward but also to novel stimuli. Novelty itself works as a kind of reward. AI ran into the same problem. In environments where reward is very rare, such as the Atari game Montezuma’s Revenge, random exploration never reaches the first reward, so learning never gets started. Researchers’ fix was intrinsic motivation: a bonus for visiting states not seen before, in effect artificial curiosity. It is the same answer evolution reached 500 million years earlier. 3. The correspondence at a glance The table below pairs each biological mechanism with its AI counterpart. The last column is my own judgment of how close the match is. Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close Law of effect (trial and error) Policy reinforcement Direct Dopamine as reward prediction error TD error δ Quantitative match (Schultz et al., 1997) Action selection in the basal ganglia Actor (actor-critic) Rough match; details debated Dopamine response to novelty Intrinsic motivation, exploration bonus Functional match 4. Closing: similar, but not the same Following the two breakthroughs reveals a single thread. Neurons arose for fast response, the bilaterian brain for steering by good and bad, synaptic plasticity for storing experience, and dopamine’s reinterpretation for learning from delayed reward. Each step reuses the parts of the one before rather than discarding them. Still, it is too early to say that “the brain is a reinforcement learning algorithm.” A few differences are clear. Learning rule: synapses change using only local information. Whether the brain has anything like backpropagation, which sends the output error precisely back through the layers, remains an open question. Data efficiency: TD-Gammon needed hundreds of thousands of self-play games. A fish learns in a handful of trials. Forgetting: animals keep old memories in suppressed form while learning new ones. Artificial networks are still weak here. Dopamine’s other faces: dopamine does more than signal reward prediction error. It is involved in movement, motivation, and novelty, and how to interpret the signal is still an active research question. Even so, the correspondence is illuminating. AI researchers did not reach these answers by copying the brain; they reached them by trying to solve the same problems. That evolution and engineering converged independently on the same solutions suggests that those solutions may come from the structure of the problems themselves. Bennett’s next breakthrough, simulating, concerns the mammalian neocortex and its ability to simulate the future in the mind: trying things out in imagination rather than in reality. That is the story of model-based reinforcement learning, taken up in part III. Questions to think about Dopamine changed from a state signal in worms to a learning signal in vertebrates. What other cases do you know where evolution, or engineering, repurposed an existing channel for a new job? A fish learns in a handful of trials, while TD-Gammon needed hundreds of thousands of games. What might explain the difference? TD learning learns from changes in prediction rather than from the final outcome. Where in your own field could a model learn from forecast updates rather than from observed outcomes alone? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 약 5억 년 전 초기 척추동물은 자신의 행동 결과로부터 배우는 시행착오 학습(reinforcing)을 얻었다. Schultz 등(1997)은 원숭이의 도파민 뉴런이 보상 자체가 아니라 “예상보다 얼마나 좋았는가”에 반응한다는 것을 보였고, 이는 Sutton이 고안한 시간차(TD) 학습의 오차 신호와 같다. 진화는 새로운 물질을 만들지 않고, 선충 때부터 있던 도파민 신호의 뜻을 “근처에 좋은 것이 있다”에서 “예상보다 좋았다”로 바꾸었다. 뇌와 강화학습 사이에는 차이도 많지만, 둘이 서로 모른 채 같은 해법에 이르렀다는 것은 그 해법이 문제 자체의 성격에서 나온다는 것을 시사한다. title: Heat-stressed workers add about $41 to the social cost of carbon
description: A reading of Moore et al. (2026) in Nature Climate Change: lost labour productivity under heat stress costs about 41 US dollars per ton of CO₂, a revised agriculture estimate falls from 95 to 29 dollars, and the total social cost of carbon settles near 180 dollars with much less uncertainty.
tags: social cost of carbon heat stress climate economics agriculture humidity
text: How much damage does one more ton of CO₂ do? Economists answer with the social cost of carbon: the present value of all future harm caused by emitting one extra ton today. It is the number behind carbon prices, cost–benefit analyses of regulations and some infrastructure decisions, so what goes into it matters. Until now, one obvious harm was missing. When it is hot and humid, people work more slowly and take more breaks, and outdoor workers in particular lose hours. A study in Nature Climate Change led by Frances Moore puts a price on this lost productivity for the first time within a modern framework for the social cost of carbon, and at the same time revises the estimate for agriculture (Moore et al. 2026). The two changes nearly cancel, but they change what the number is made of. Heat stress is about humidity, not only temperature The authors measure heat stress with the wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT), the standard metric for workplace safety. WBGT combines air temperature and sunlight, which heat the body, with humidity and wind, which control how well sweat can cool it. A hot, dry day can be safer for a worker than a slightly cooler, humid one. They computed WBGT every three hours on a 0.25° grid from 15 bias-corrected climate models, then translated it into lost productivity using two response functions that act as upper and lower bounds. One is based on the international standard (ISO) for how much rest workers need at a given WBGT and work intensity. The other, used by the Lancet Countdown, is based on field observations of rice harvesters in India and miners in South Africa. Productivity loss was calculated separately for indoor and outdoor work at three levels of effort, with indoor exposure adjusted for how common air conditioning is in each country (from 0% in South Sudan to 90% in Japan). Although WBGT rises most at high latitudes, the losses concentrate where it is already close to physiological limits: South and Southeast Asia, West Africa and the Amazon. Construction, with its heavy outdoor work, is hit hardest. These productivity losses were then fed into a global economic model, which lets production, trade and consumption adjust, before entering the calculation of the social cost of carbon. The results Labour costs about US\$41 per ton of CO₂. For a ton emitted in 2025 (in 2020 dollars, with a 2% discount rate), the mean labour damage is US\$41, with a median of US\$32 and a 90% range from US\$1 to US\$108 (Figure 2a). The ISO function alone gives US\$52, the Lancet function US\$30. An independent working paper using a completely different method, based on observed weekly working hours, arrived at a similar US\$39. Labour is now the second-largest component of the social cost of carbon, after heat-related deaths (US\$98) and ahead of the other sectors. The burden falls on hot, humid, populous countries. India alone accounts for about US\$9 of the US\$41, followed by Nigeria (US\$6), China (US\$4) and Pakistan (US\$3) (Figure 2b). Per person, the damages are largest in Gulf states such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates and in sub-Saharan Africa. With the ISO function, at 3°C of warming above 1995–2015, South Asia loses more than 6% of its income through heat-related labour losses alone, while Europe’s losses are negligible. Agriculture costs less than thought. The previous estimate of agricultural damages relied on about 1,000 crop-yield projections from 56 studies compiled for the IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report. The update uses 8,703 projections from 202 studies compiled for the Sixth. With this much larger evidence base, projected yield losses at high warming are smaller and much less uncertain. Agricultural damages fall from US\$95 to US\$29 per ton, and the 95th percentile drops by US\$260. The total barely moves, but becomes more certain. Adding labour and revising agriculture lowers the mean social cost of carbon from US\$204 to US\$179 per ton (Figure 1). The long upper tail shrinks, and the probability that the true value is zero or negative falls from 0.6% to below 0.008%. Figure 1. Mean social cost of carbon for a ton of CO₂ emitted in 2025 (2020 US dollars, 2% near-term discount rate), by damage sector, in the previous version of the GIVE model and in the revised version. Energy and sea-level rise are unchanged and shown as the remainder. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Moore et al. (2026). Figure 2. (a) Labour component of the 2025 social cost of carbon: the preferred estimate (mean, median and 90% range), the estimates using each response function alone, and an independent estimate by Rode et al. using a different method. (b) The four countries with the largest contributions. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Moore et al. (2026). What the numbers do and do not include The authors are explicit about what could push the estimate up or down. Cold benefits are not counted. Warmer winters might help some outdoor workers, but evidence suggests this effect is small. Adaptation is partly included. The economic model shifts work to cooler hours of the day, moves production between sectors and regions, and substitutes machines for labour. It does not include the future spread of air conditioning, or changes such as shading construction sites, which would lower the cost, though not for free. Health costs are only partly covered. Heat deaths are counted elsewhere in the social cost of carbon, but heat-related illness and injury are not. Agriculture covers only four crops. Wheat, rice, maize and soybeans account for about half of cropped area; other crops, meat and dairy are not directly modeled. Why this matters The paper’s own conclusion is that a social cost of carbon near US\$200 per ton, the value adopted by the US Environmental Protection Agency in 2023, is well supported, and that a value of zero can be ruled out with high confidence. That is a pointed statement at a time when US federal guidance no longer monetizes climate damages in regulatory analysis. There is also a quieter lesson about how such numbers improve. The agricultural estimate fell not because the climate risk disappeared but because the evidence base grew roughly eightfold and narrowed the uncertainty. The labour estimate rose because a real, well-documented harm was finally counted. Both changes come from better science, and they pull in opposite directions. What a hydrologist takes from it Humidity is a hydrological variable. Because WBGT depends on humidity, land and water management can change heat stress directly. Irrigation, for example, cools the surface but adds moisture to the air, and in India it has been shown to intensify humid heat extremes (Mishra et al. 2020). Decisions about irrigation therefore have consequences for the people who work in irrigated fields. Wind matters for workers, too. In the previous post, wind sped up evaporation from ecosystems. In WBGT, wind does the same for the human body: it helps sweat evaporate. Calm, humid days are the most dangerous. The losses follow the seasons. Even in the hottest regions, the thresholds that trigger productivity losses are crossed only during part of the year, and in agriculture those weeks often coincide with planting and harvest. Seasonal forecasts of humid heat could help farmers and builders plan around them. Bottom line Heat stress already slows workers, and climate change will make it worse, especially in hot, humid and populous regions of South Asia and Africa. Moore and colleagues estimate this cost at about US\$41 per ton of CO₂, making labour one of the largest components of the social cost of carbon. A better-supported agricultural estimate falls from US\$95 to US\$29, so the total settles near US\$180 per ton with much less uncertainty. Both revisions show that the social cost of carbon is not a fixed number but a running summary of what we know. Questions to think about Two response functions, one physiological and one observational, give US\$52 and US\$30. Which would you trust more for Korean construction workers in July, and why? If expanding irrigation raises humid heat stress for farm workers, how would you weigh that against the yield benefits? Should a country’s own social cost of carbon count damages to workers in other countries? How would that change the number? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 탄소의 사회적 비용(SC-CO₂)은 오늘 CO₂ 1톤을 더 배출했을 때 미래에 발생하는 모든 피해의 현재 가치로, 탄소 가격과 정책의 비용·편익 분석에 쓰인다. Moore 등(2026)은 그동안 빠져 있던 폭염에 따른 노동 생산성 손실을 처음으로 포함했다. 기온뿐 아니라 습도, 일사, 바람을 함께 반영하는 습구흑구온도(WBGT)를 15개 기후모델로 3시간·0.25° 해상도로 계산하고, ISO 기준과 현장 관측 기반의 두 반응함수, 각국의 에어컨 보급률, 세계 경제모형을 결합했다. 그 결과 2025년 배출 CO₂ 1톤당 노동 피해는 평균 41달러(90% 범위 1–108달러)로, 열 관련 사망(98달러) 다음으로 큰 항목이 되었다. 피해는 인도(9달러), 나이지리아(6달러), 중국(4달러), 파키스탄(3달러)처럼 덥고 습하며 인구가 많은 나라에 집중되고, 3°C 온난화 시 남아시아는 소득의 6% 이상을 잃지만 유럽의 손실은 미미하다. 반면 IPCC 6차 보고서의 훨씬 많은 작물 수확량 연구(202편, 8,703개 추정치)를 반영하자 농업 피해는 95달러에서 29달러로 줄었다. 두 변화가 거의 상쇄되어 전체 SC-CO₂는 204달러에서 179달러로 조금 낮아졌지만 불확실성은 크게 줄었고, 그 값이 0 이하일 확률은 0.008% 미만이다. title: Wind makes ecosystems spend more water for the same carbon
description: A hydrologist's reading of Wang et al. (2026) in Nature Climate Change: across 146 flux towers, windier days lower ecosystem water use efficiency, mostly by speeding up evaporation, and the decline of global winds ('stilling') has been quietly raising it.
tags: water use efficiency evapotranspiration wind speed carbon cycle eddy covariance
text: Ecosystems trade water for carbon. To take up CO₂ through their stomata, leaves have to let water vapor out, and the ratio between the two, the carbon gained per kilogram of water evaporated, is called water use efficiency (WUE). It is one of the most useful single numbers in ecohydrology. Rising WUE has usually been credited to rising CO₂, which lets plants narrow their stomata (Keenan et al. 2013), and to changes in temperature, sunlight and air dryness. Wind has been mostly left out of that story. A new study in Nature Climate Change by Xiang Wang, Zheng Fu and colleagues brings it back (Wang et al. 2026). Using flux towers around the world and climate models, they show that on windier days, ecosystems use water less efficiently, and that the slow decline of winds over land in recent decades has been nudging WUE upward. What they found The authors used daily measurements of photosynthesis (gross primary productivity, GPP) and evapotranspiration (ET) from 146 eddy-covariance towers in the FLUXNET2015, AmeriFlux, ICOS and OzFlux networks. For each site they asked how WUE (GPP divided by ET) varied with wind speed during the growing season, after removing the effects of temperature, precipitation, sunlight, CO₂ and vapor-pressure deficit (VPD). The answer was remarkably consistent. WUE fell significantly with wind at 79.5% of sites and rose significantly at only 5.5% (Figure 1a). The pattern held for almost every vegetation type and for different definitions of the growing season. Among all the drivers they examined, wind speed had the largest median standardized effect on WUE, ahead of sunlight, VPD and temperature. On average, each additional meter per second of wind lowered WUE by about 0.26 grams of carbon per kilogram of water. The effect was strongest in evergreen needleleaf forests and in humid climates, and close to zero in arid climates (Figure 1b). Figure 1. (a) Partial correlation between daily WUE and wind speed at 146 eddy-covariance sites during the growing season, after controlling for temperature, precipitation, CO₂, solar radiation and VPD. (b) Change in WUE per 1 m/s increase in wind speed (median and interquartile range) for all sites, two vegetation types and two climate classes. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Wang et al. (2026). Why: wind mostly speeds up evaporation WUE can fall because carbon uptake drops or because water loss rises. Splitting the two, the authors found that wind acts mainly on the water side: its effect on ET was almost three times as large as its effect on GPP (standardized sensitivities of +0.11 and −0.04). The mechanism is familiar to anyone who has used the Penman–Monteith equation. Wind thins the layer of still air around leaves and increases the aerodynamic conductance, the ease with which water vapor is carried away from the canopy. In the paper, wind changed aerodynamic conductance strongly (standardized sensitivity 0.66) but barely changed canopy conductance, which reflects how far the stomata are open (0.03). In other words, the plants did not open up; the air simply carried more water away. Windier days were also drier: wind and VPD were positively correlated at 67% of sites, and higher VPD lowered WUE at 70% of them. Wind also coupled the canopy more tightly to the atmosphere, so that transpiration responded more to air dryness and less to sunlight. GPP declined a little as well, probably because drier air makes leaves partly close their stomata and because strong winds stress plants mechanically. Why conifer forests and humid places respond most The strong effect in needleleaf forests has a neat physical explanation, which the authors mention and which a simple calculation makes vivid. Tall conifer canopies are aerodynamically rough, and in humid regions they are often wet with intercepted rain. Evaporation from a wet canopy is not limited by stomata at all, so it responds directly to how fast the wind removes vapor. Figure 2 shows this with the Penman–Monteith equation under identical weather. For a dry canopy, going from 1 to 5 m/s of wind raises transpiration by about 20%, over both grass and forest. For a wet forest canopy, the same change more than triples evaporation. Wind therefore matters most where the canopy is rough and wet, which matches where the authors observed the largest effects. Figure 2. Increase in evaporation with wind speed, relative to 1 m/s, from the Penman–Monteith equation for a grass canopy and a 20 m conifer forest with the same canopy conductance (10 mm/s), and for the same forest when its canopy is wet with intercepted rain (no stomatal limit). Same weather in all cases: 150 W/m² of available energy, 20°C and a VPD of 1 kPa. Aerodynamic conductance from the logarithmic wind profile under neutral conditions. Figure by Daeha Kim, an illustrative calculation, not a result of Wang et al. (2026). Leaves versus ecosystems The result seems to contradict an earlier leaf-scale study, in which wind increased leaf WUE because it cooled sunlit leaves and so lowered their transpiration (Schymanski and Or 2016). The authors argue that the two are complementary. Leaf experiments last minutes under strong light, where convective cooling dominates. An ecosystem also loses water from soil and wet canopy surfaces, and over days these non-stomatal losses respond strongly to wind. What holds for a leaf does not automatically scale up to a forest. Wind trends and the future Near-surface winds over land weakened over several decades, a trend known as “stilling” (McVicar et al. 2012). For hydrologists, stilling is already familiar from the “pan evaporation paradox”: measured pan evaporation declined in many regions despite rising temperatures. Roderick and Farquhar (2002) traced the decline to dimming sunlight, and later work showed that weakening winds also contributed in many regions (McVicar et al. 2012). The new study adds a biological counterpart: weaker winds have let ecosystems fix carbon with less water. The authors then used CMIP6 climate models, which reproduce the negative effect of wind on WUE, to estimate how wind trends will affect WUE in the future (Figure 3). In the historical period (1995–2014), declining winds raised WUE. By the end of the century, this wind-driven gain shrinks by about 80% under the low-emission SSP1-2.6, where stilling stops, and disappears under SSP2-4.5, where winds still weaken but WUE is less sensitive to them. Under the high-emission SSP5-8.5, stilling intensifies and the wind-driven gain in WUE stays about as large as in the historical period. Figure 3. (a) Trends in near-surface wind speed over land in CMIP6 models for 1995–2014 and for 2081–2100 under three emission scenarios. (b) Trend in WUE caused by these wind changes, calculated as the sensitivity of WUE to wind multiplied by the wind trend. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Wang et al. (2026). There is a feedback, too. Global greening makes the land surface rougher, which slows near-surface wind, which in turn raises WUE. Ecosystems are not only affected by wind; they help shape it. Caveats Daily relationships, not long-term experiments. The analysis uses day-to-day variation. Persistent changes in wind can also alter canopy structure, phenology and mortality, and those slower effects are not captured. Wind trends are not smooth. Observations show that global terrestrial stilling reversed around 2010 (Zeng et al. 2019), which reminds us that wind trends can change direction within a decade. ET partitioning remains uncertain. Separating transpiration from soil and canopy evaporation at flux towers is difficult, which limits how precisely the mechanism can be pinned down. Models treat wind only indirectly. Earth system models represent wind through turbulence and the energy balance but have no explicit wind effects on stomata or photosynthesis. What a hydrologist takes from it WUE trends need wind in the attribution. If wind affects WUE as strongly as temperature or sunlight, part of the rise in WUE commonly attributed to CO₂ may reflect stilling. Studies that attribute long-term WUE trends should include wind speed as a driver. Aerodynamic terms deserve the same attention as stomata. In much of ecohydrology, the canopy conductance gets the attention and the aerodynamic conductance is treated as a technicality. This study shows that at the ecosystem scale, the air side of the Penman–Monteith equation can dominate. Interception is part of the carbon–water story. The strongest effects appeared where canopies are rough and often wet. Rainfall interception, a classic topic in forest hydrology, turns out to shape how efficiently ecosystems use water. Bottom line Across 146 flux towers, windier days lower ecosystem water use efficiency at four out of five sites, mainly because wind speeds up evaporation rather than because plants photosynthesize less. The effect is strongest in conifer forests and humid climates, where rough, often wet canopies lose water quickly to moving air. The long decline of winds over land has quietly raised WUE, and how much this continues depends on emissions. Wind belongs alongside CO₂, temperature and dryness as a driver of the carbon–water balance. Questions to think about If part of the observed rise in WUE comes from stilling rather than CO₂, how would you design an analysis to separate the two? Why might the effect of wind on WUE be close to zero in arid climates, where VPD is high? Rainfall interception is often ignored in large-scale WUE studies. In a Korean forest catchment, how large would you expect the wet-canopy contribution to growing-season ET to be? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 물 이용 효율(WUE)은 생태계가 물 1 kg을 증발시키며 얻는 탄소의 양으로, 그동안 CO₂, 기온, 일사, 대기 건조도의 영향은 많이 연구되었지만 바람의 역할은 거의 다뤄지지 않았다. Wang 등(2026)은 전 세계 146개 에디 공분산 관측소 자료를 분석해, 다른 기상 요인의 영향을 제거해도 바람이 강한 날 WUE가 낮아지는 지점이 79.5%에 이르고 반대인 지점은 5.5%뿐임을 보였다. 풍속 1 m/s 증가당 WUE는 평균 약 0.26 gC/kg 감소했고, 상록침엽수림과 습윤 기후에서 가장 컸으며 건조 기후에서는 거의 0이었다. 원인은 주로 증발산 증가다. 바람은 기공을 더 열게 하는 것이 아니라 공기역학적 전도도를 높여 수증기를 더 빨리 실어 나르고, 대기를 더 건조하게 만든다. Penman–Monteith 식으로 계산해 보면 건조한 canopy의 증산은 풍속이 1에서 5 m/s로 늘 때 약 20% 늘지만, 차단된 빗물로 젖은 침엽수림 canopy의 증발은 세 배 이상 늘어 거칠고 젖은 canopy에서 바람의 영향이 가장 크다는 것을 알 수 있다. 지난 수십 년 동안 육상 풍속이 줄어든 현상(stilling)은 WUE를 조용히 높여 왔으며, CMIP6 전망에서는 이 효과가 저배출 시나리오에서 크게 줄고 고배출 시나리오에서는 현재 수준으로 유지된다. 따라서 장기 WUE 변화를 CO₂ 효과만으로 해석해서는 안 되며, 바람을 주요 요인으로 함께 고려해야 한다.
