title: How the brain invented learning, part I: steering in A Brief History of Intelligence
description: Notes on the first of Max Bennett's five breakthroughs: how the first neurons and brains appeared, how bilaterian worms learned to steer by good and bad, and how even their simple learning already faced problems that AI still struggles with.
tags: artificial intelligence neuroscience neural networks book notes
text: The problems a worm solved 600 million years ago, and a fish solved 500 million years ago, look remarkably like the problems AI researchers ran into in the late twentieth century. Max Bennett’s A Brief History of Intelligence (2023) is built around that overlap. Bennett is not a neuroscientist; he is an AI entrepreneur. That gives the book an unusual angle. He asks: at the points where we get stuck trying to build intelligence into machines, how, and in what order, did evolution get past them? His answer is organized into five “breakthroughs”: steering, reinforcing, simulating, mentalizing, and speaking. This post covers the first, steering: the story of how bilaterian animals got the first brains. The second, reinforcing, the story of how early vertebrates acquired trial-and-error learning, follows in part II. The main characters in both are neurons, synapses, and dopamine, and each maps with surprising precision onto the weights of artificial neural networks and the reward signal of reinforcement learning. The summary below is my own paraphrase of the book’s argument. A few connections, notably the three-factor learning rule, come from the broader neuroscience literature rather than from the book itself. 1. The birth of the neuron: speed was the price of eating Neurons came before brains. And they evolved not for thinking, but because of how animals eat. Plants and fungi live by absorbing sunlight or the nutrients around them. They have no reason to hurry. Animals took a different path: they eat other living things. Food moves, and you might be food yourself. That strategy demands a body that can respond quickly and as a whole. Chemicals diffusing slowly from cell to cell were not enough. Neurons solve this. They carry electrical signals (action potentials) from one end of the body to the other almost instantly, then pass the signal to the next cell across a synapse using chemical messengers (neurotransmitters). The contrast is telling: sponges, which feed by filtering water, have no neurons, while cnidarians such as jellyfish have a diffuse nerve net spread across the body. But a jellyfish’s nerve net mostly runs reflexes. A stimulus arrives, and a fixed response goes out. A central processor that pools many signals into a single decision, a brain, comes only in the next step. The AI connection. The artificial neuron that McCulloch and Pitts proposed in 1943 is a radical simplification of the biological one: multiply the inputs by weights, sum them, and fire if the sum crosses a threshold. Synaptic strength became the weight, and whether a neuron fires became the activation function. Every layer of modern deep learning still rests on this abstraction. 2. Breakthrough 1, Steering: toward the good, away from the bad The first brains appeared about 600 million years ago in bilaterians, animals with a head and a tail, a left and a right. Once a body has a front end, sense organs and neurons cluster there, and the animal becomes something that must decide which way to go. The nematode C. elegans offers a living glimpse of what these early animals were like. With only 302 neurons, this tiny worm turns toward a strengthening food odor and away from a strengthening danger signal. It has no map and no representation of a goal. It moves on a single question: is this direction getting better or worse? Bennett calls this the first breakthrough, steering. Its core is the ability to sort the world into good and bad, what neuroscientists call valence. Food odor is good; toxins are bad. This simple binary is where intelligence begins. The original jobs of dopamine and serotonin Remarkably, dopamine, the molecule we know as the “reward chemical,” is already present in this worm, but in a different role. In nematodes, dopamine roughly signals “something good is nearby.” When the worm is near food, dopamine is released, and the worm slows down to search the area thoroughly. Serotonin, by contrast, signals “I have eaten; I am full,” and makes the worm stop searching and rest. At this stage, then, neuromodulators are less like messages carrying specific information and more like broadcasts that shift the state of the whole body. Bennett locates the origin of emotion here. Combinations of valence and arousal form primitive affective states, and these states make behavior persist. They are what keep the worm searching even when the food scent briefly fades. The AI connection: Roomba Bennett’s analogy is the Roomba robot vacuum. Rodney Brooks’s behavior-based robotics does not model the world in detail. Instead, it stacks simple reaction rules on top of sensor input to produce sensible-looking behavior. Bump into a wall, turn; find a dirty patch, scrub it longer. It is the same principle as the nematode’s steering. The lesson is clear: useful, intelligent-looking behavior is possible without a model of the world. But a Roomba cannot learn from experience. The nematode went one step further, and the difference lies in the synapse. 3. Synaptic plasticity: the first learning Bilaterians do more than run reflexes. Nematodes and the sea slug Aplysia both show associative learning. If food has always followed a particular odor, the odor alone becomes enough to draw them in. It is the same principle as Pavlov’s dog salivating at the sound of a bell. The physical basis of this learning is synaptic plasticity: when two neurons are active together, the synapse between them strengthens. Donald Hebb proposed this rule in 1949, and it is often summarized as “neurons that fire together, wire together.” Eric Kandel used the simple circuits of Aplysia to show that learning is indeed stored as changes in synaptic strength, work that earned him the 2000 Nobel Prize. Two problems that primitive learning already faced Bennett makes a striking point here. Even the simplest associative learning already confronted two problems that AI still struggles with today. First, the credit assignment problem. If several stimuli were present just before food was found, which one deserves the credit? Animals handle this with a handful of tricks: Eligibility traces: only synapses that were active within a short window before the outcome are candidates for change. Overshadowing: among several stimuli, the stronger or more salient one takes the association. Latent inhibition: a stimulus that has often been experienced with no consequence is slow to acquire a new association. Blocking: if one stimulus already predicts the outcome well, a newly added stimulus is not learned. Second, the continual learning problem. How do you learn something new without losing what you already know? Artificial neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting: training on new data overwrites old knowledge. In animals, an extinguished association is not erased but suppressed. The evidence is spontaneous recovery, where the old response returns on its own after some time, and the fact that relearning is much faster than the original learning. The AI connection: weights and the three-factor rule Synaptic strength as a weight, and plasticity as a weight update, is a natural mapping. Stepping slightly beyond the book, there is a more precise one. A pure Hebbian rule looks at only two factors: were the two neurons active together? In the real brain, a neuromodulator such as dopamine enters as a third factor. Co-activation leaves a trace at the synapse, and if dopamine is broadcast shortly afterward, that trace is consolidated into a lasting change. This structure, known in neuroscience as the three-factor learning rule, closely resembles how a single scalar in reinforcement learning (“that outcome was good”) modulates the direction of updates across the whole network. In the nematode, dopamine still meant “something good is nearby.” The heart of the second breakthrough is that this signal became a more refined learning signal: “that was better than expected.” 4. The correspondence so far The tables below pair each biological mechanism with its AI counterpart. The last column is my own judgment of how close the match is. Groundwork Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close Neuron (action potential, fire or not) Artificial neuron (McCulloch–Pitts, activation function) Extreme simplification Synaptic strength Weight Conceptually direct Steering Biological mechanism AI counterpart How close Approach and avoidance by valence Reactive robots (Roomba, behavior-based robotics) Same principle Global neuromodulator broadcast (dopamine, serotonin) Global scalar signal (reward, learning-rate modulation) Same principle Synaptic plasticity (Hebbian rule) Weight update Different rules (local in the brain, backpropagation in deep learning) Eligibility traces Eligibility traces (TD(λ)) Same term, same role Spontaneous recovery after extinction Catastrophic forgetting Contrast: the brain suppresses, networks overwrite 5. Closing: a sense of good and bad, and a memory Steering and synaptic plasticity gave the first brains two things: a way to sort the world into good and bad, and a way to store experience in the strength of synapses. Each maps neatly onto something in AI, from reactive robots to weight updates. But the nematode’s learning was about stimuli, not about its own actions, and its dopamine still meant only “something good is nearby.” How that signal became a learning signal, and why it turned out to match an algorithm AI researchers had already written down, is the subject of part II. Questions to think about A Roomba behaves sensibly without learning anything. Which tasks in your own field could be handled by simple steering rules, and which need learning? Animals suppress old associations rather than erase them. What would an artificial network need in order to do the same? Eligibility traces, overshadowing, latent inhibition and blocking are the animal’s tricks for credit assignment. Which of them have counterparts in how scientists attribute an observed change to one of several possible causes? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). AI 기업가 Max Bennett는 『A Brief History of Intelligence』에서 지능의 진화를 다섯 번의 돌파 과정(steering, reinforcing, simulating, mentalizing, speaking)으로 정리하며, AI 연구자들이 막혔던 문제를 진화가 어떤 순서로 풀었는지를 다룬다. 이 글은 첫 단계인 조향(steering)을 다룬다. 약 6억 년 전 좌우대칭동물은 좋고 나쁨(valence)에 따라 다가가거나 피하기 시작했고, 함께 활동한 신경세포 사이의 연결이 강해지는 방식으로 경험에서 배우게 되었다. 그런데 이 단순한 학습도 오늘날 AI가 겪는 두 가지 어려움을 이미 안고 있었다. 하나는 먹이를 찾기 직전에 냄새, 빛, 온도 같은 여러 자극이 함께 있었다면 그중 어느 것을 기억해야 하는지 가려내는 일(신용 할당)이고, 다른 하나는 새로운 것을 배울 때 예전에 배운 것이 지워지지 않게 하는 일(지속 학습)이다. Reference Bennett, M. (2023). A Brief History of Intelligence: Evolution, AI, and the Five Breakthroughs That Made Our Brains. Mariner Books.

title: Why LLMs make things up, and what you can do about it
description: A short guide to LLM hallucination (confabulation): what it is, why it happens, why reasoning-era models do it less, which models do it least as of October 2026, and practical habits that cut the errors you see.
tags: artificial intelligence large language models hallucination research practice
text: Anyone who uses large language models (LLMs) for research has met the problem: a confident answer, a plausible citation, and then the discovery that the paper does not exist. This is usually called hallucination. Here is what we know about why it happens, how much it has improved, and what users can do about it. Hallucination, or confabulation “Hallucination” is the popular term, but many researchers prefer confabulation, a word borrowed from neurology. A patient who confabulates fills gaps in memory with invented details and believes them, with no intent to deceive. That is close to what an LLM does: it produces fluent, specific and wrong content, with the same confidence as when it is right. Farquhar et al. (2024) use confabulation for a narrower case: answers that are both wrong and arbitrary, so that asking the same question again gives a different answer. That distinction turns out to be useful, as we will see below. Why it happens A 2025 analysis by Kalai and colleagues at OpenAI gives the clearest explanation so far (Kalai et al. 2025). It has two parts. Pretraining makes some errors unavoidable. A model learns by predicting text. For facts that appear many times in the training data, such as the boiling point of water, it learns the pattern. For facts that appear only once or rarely, such as a particular researcher’s birthday or the page numbers of a 2003 paper, there is no pattern to learn. The authors show that the error rate on such facts is tied to how many of them appear only once in training data. Bibliographic details, numbers, names and niche facts are exactly this kind of knowledge. Training and evaluation reward guessing. Most benchmarks score an answer as right or wrong. “I don’t know” scores zero, the same as a wrong answer, so a model that always guesses scores higher than one that admits uncertainty. The authors compare it to a multiple-choice exam with no penalty for wrong answers: the rational strategy is to never leave a blank. Models were, in effect, trained to be good test-takers. Why reasoning models do it less Hallucination has dropped markedly over the past year, but not simply because models now “think” before answering. When OpenAI released its first strong reasoning model, o3, in 2025, it hallucinated more than its predecessor on an internal test of facts about people: 33% versus 16% for o1, because it made more claims overall (OpenAI 2025a). Reasoning gives a model more chances to be right and more chances to be wrong. What changed is better explained by three things. Rewarding abstention. After the diagnosis above, labs began training models to decline when unsure. OpenAI reported that in its GPT-5 thinking model, the share of factual claims containing errors was 65% lower than in o3 (OpenAI 2025b). Using reasoning to check. Thinking time helps when a model uses it to test its own answer, not only to build a longer argument. Tools. Models that can search the web or read a supplied document answer from evidence instead of memory. Much of the improvement in everyday use comes from this. The result shows clearly on AA-Omniscience, a benchmark by Artificial Analysis that asks hard factual questions without web access and, unusually, does not penalize “I don’t know” (Figure 1). Figure 1. Out of 100 hard factual questions answered without web search, how many each model got right, got wrong, or declined (or answered only partly), for current models and two models released in November 2025. Wrong answers are computed as accuracy minus the AA-Omniscience Index. Gemini 4 Argon was not yet public when these results were recorded. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from AA-Omniscience results (Artificial Analysis) as compiled on 4 October 2026. Which model hallucinates least? As of October 2026, the answer depends on what you want. Fewest wrong answers among frontier models: Gemini 4 Argon. It gets about half the questions right, declines most of the rest, and gives a wrong answer to only 8 in 100. Best balance of knowing and admitting: Claude Opus 5.5 leads the AA-Omniscience Index (correct minus wrong), with GPT-6 Astra close behind. These models know more, so they answer more questions correctly, but they still guess on about 20 in 100. Large differences remain: some capable models still answer almost every question and get about half of them wrong. A year earlier, the leading models gave wrong answers to 33–40 questions in 100. The improvement is real. Two caveats apply. Rankings change every few months, and they differ between tasks: on summarizing a supplied document faithfully, a different leaderboard (Vectara’s) ranks models in another order. And no model is at zero. What you can do Even with the best model, the habits of the user matter more than the choice of model. These are the ones I find most effective, most of them also recommended by the model developers themselves (Anthropic 2026). Give it the source. Paste the paper, report or data, and ask it to answer only from that material. Asking for exact quotes first, and building the answer on them, works especially well for long documents. Give permission not to know. Say explicitly: “If you are not sure, say so.” This simple sentence counters the guessing habit described above. Turn on search for facts, and open the links. A cited source is only useful if it exists and says what the model claims. Check DOIs and page numbers yourself; this is where fabrication is most common. Ask twice. Ask the same factual question in a new conversation, or rephrase it. If the answers disagree, treat both as unverified. This is the practical version of Farquhar’s method, which detects confabulations from inconsistency across repeated answers. Ask for a separate check. After a draft, ask the model to list each factual claim and verify it, ideally in a fresh session. Splitting generation and verification reduces errors (Dhuliawala et al. 2023). Don’t lead the witness. “Isn’t it true that…?” invites agreement. Ask neutral questions, and be suspicious when the model simply confirms what you hoped. Know the danger zones. References, numbers, names, dates, recent events and very specialized facts are where models fail most. Reasoning, coding and explaining well-documented concepts are much safer. Bottom line Hallucination is not a mysterious bug. It follows from how models learn rare facts and from training that rewarded guessing. The newest models hallucinate much less, mainly because they have learned to say “I don’t know” and to check with tools, not just because they reason longer. The best defense is still on the user’s side: give the model the evidence, allow it to be uncertain, and verify anything that matters, especially citations and numbers. Questions to think about Would you prefer a model that answers 66 of 100 questions correctly and 20 wrongly, or one that answers 50 correctly and 8 wrongly? Does your answer depend on the task? Kalai and colleagues argue that benchmarks should penalize wrong answers more than abstentions. How would that change how we grade students? Which of the seven habits above could you build into your group’s standard workflow for literature reviews? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). LLM이 그럴듯하지만 틀린 내용을 자신 있게 만들어내는 현상을 흔히 환각(hallucination)이라고 부르지만, 기억의 빈틈을 지어낸 내용으로 메우는 신경학 용어를 빌려 작화(confabulation)라고도 한다. Kalai 등(2025)에 따르면 원인은 두 가지다. 학습 데이터에 드물게 등장하는 사실(서지 정보, 수치, 인명 등)은 패턴으로 학습할 수 없고, 대부분의 평가가 “모른다”를 오답과 똑같이 0점 처리해 추측을 보상해 왔다. 추론 모델이라고 저절로 나아진 것은 아니어서, 2025년 o3는 이전 모델보다 오히려 더 많이 틀렸다. 최근의 큰 개선은 모를 때 답을 거절하도록 한 학습, 추론을 자기 검증에 쓰는 것, 검색 같은 도구 사용 덕분이다. 2026년 10월 기준 웹 검색 없이 어려운 사실 질문 100개를 풀게 하면, 틀린 답이 가장 적은 최상위 모델은 Gemini 4 Argon(약 8개)이고, 정답과 오답의 차이가 가장 큰 모델은 Claude Opus 5.5와 GPT-6 Astra(정답 63–66개, 오답 약 20개)이다. 1년 전 주요 모델은 오답이 33–40개였다. 사용자가 할 수 있는 일로는 원문 자료를 주고 그 안에서만 답하게 하기, “모르면 모른다고 하라”고 명시하기, 검색을 켜고 인용 링크와 DOI를 직접 확인하기, 같은 질문을 새 대화에서 다시 해 보기, 별도의 검증 단계를 두기, 유도 질문 피하기, 그리고 참고문헌·수치·인명·최신 정보처럼 오류가 잦은 영역을 특히 조심하기가 있다. title: Farm lime turns out to be a carbon sink
description: Climate inventories count agricultural lime as a CO₂ source. A century of Mississippi River chemistry says the opposite: measured against the acids that farming and pollution add to soils, liming has removed CO₂ from the air.
tags: carbon cycle agriculture soil river chemistry carbon dioxide removal
text: Every year, American farmers spread tens of millions of tonnes of crushed limestone on their fields. The reason is simple: farming makes soils acidic, and acidic soils grow poorer crops. Climate accounting has long treated this practice as a small but certain source of carbon dioxide, since limestone is calcium carbonate and dissolving it can release CO₂. A study published in Nature in September turns this assumption around (Suhrhoff et al. 2026). Using a century of records from the Mississippi River Basin, Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, Noah Planavsky and colleagues show that liming has, on balance, taken CO₂ out of the atmosphere. In an accompanying commentary, Philip Robertson and Stephen Hamilton, who reported early evidence of the same effect in Michigan almost twenty years ago (Hamilton et al. 2007), call it an unexpected carbon sink (Robertson and Hamilton 2026). The argument is a lesson in choosing the right baseline, and the decisive evidence comes from river water. Why farmers lime Soils become more acidic under intensive farming for several reasons. Nitrogen fertilizer and manure are converted by soil microbes into nitric acid. Burning fossil fuels has added sulfuric and nitric acid through acid rain. Decomposing soil organic matter adds more. In the cornfields of the US Midwest, natural processes cannot keep up, so farmers add lime (ground limestone or dolomite) to bring the soil pH back to where crops do best. Two ways lime can dissolve What happens to the carbon in lime depends on which acid dissolves it (Figure 1). When lime meets a strong acid such as nitric or sulfuric acid, its carbon is released as CO₂. When it meets carbonic acid, which forms when CO₂ from roots and microbes dissolves in soil water, the reaction goes the other way: it takes up CO₂ and stores it as bicarbonate. Bicarbonate drains into groundwater and rivers, reaches the ocean, and stays there for thousands of years. Soils are patchy, so both reactions happen side by side, and the balance between them decides whether lime is a net source or a net sink. Figure 1. Lime that dissolves in strong acids releases CO₂; lime that dissolves in carbonic acid captures CO₂ as bicarbonate, which rivers carry to the sea. Strong acids release CO₂ even without lime, which is the baseline the new study uses. Figure by Daeha Kim, a schematic based on Suhrhoff et al. (2026) and Robertson and Hamilton (2026). The missing baseline The key step in the paper is a question about the counterfactual: what would happen if the acids were added but the lime were not? The strong acids do not disappear. They react with the bicarbonate already present in soils, groundwater and streams, and convert it to CO₂, which escapes to the air either on the spot or farther downstream. In other words, the CO₂ is released by the acid, not by the lime. Lime only determines where and how it happens. Current inventories ignore this. The default method of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) assumes that all the carbon in applied lime ends up as CO₂, and the US national inventory assumes about half does. The authors argue that this kind of accounting gives the right answer only when lime inputs exactly balance acid inputs for a long time, which has rarely been true. The fair comparison is between “acid with lime” and “acid without lime”. A century of acid and lime in the Mississippi Basin The Mississippi River Basin is a natural test case. It covers 41% of the contiguous United States and about 65% of its cropland, and it receives most of the country’s agricultural lime. The authors reconstructed, county by county and year by year, how much acid and how much lime entered the basin since 1900. Acid inputs roughly doubled to tripled over the century, from 450–800 moles per hectare per year in the early 1900s to 1,350–1,600 after 1970. Nitrification of fertilizer nitrogen now supplies about half of the total, a share that has grown as clean-air rules cut acid rain. Lime use rose sharply between 1935 and 1950, from about 1 million to about 20 million tonnes a year nationwide. Even so, lime has not kept pace with acid: by 2015 the basin had received about 20 trillion moles more acid than lime, roughly half of all the acid added. Lime is concentrated in the Corn Belt, where it offsets or exceeds the acid; much of the western basin receives acid but almost no lime. What the model says Feeding these inputs into a reactive transport model of soil chemistry, the authors compared CO₂ release with and without lime. In 1980, for example, the acids alone would have released about 20 million tonnes of CO₂ a year; with lime, the release fell to about 15 million tonnes (Figure 2a). The inventory methods, which count only lime, put the figure at about 7 million tonnes (IPCC) or 3.5 million tonnes (US inventory), and attribute all of it to the lime. Lime did cause a brief pulse of extra CO₂ when its use first surged in the late 1930s, because it first had to neutralize acidity already stored in the soil. After that, it lowered emissions. What the river says A model is only as good as its check against reality, and here the check comes from hydrology. The lower Mississippi has some of the longest water-chemistry records in the world, including alkalinity measurements kept by the New Orleans water utility and the US Geological Survey, which had already shown that the river’s bicarbonate export grew during the twentieth century (Raymond et al. 2008). When lime captures CO₂, the extra bicarbonate has to leave the basin through the river. Comparing river bicarbonate fluxes with a pre-1935 baseline, the authors estimate that about 0.40 billion tonnes of CO₂ (±0.09) left the basin as lime-related bicarbonate between 1900 and 2015. If every bit of lime added since 1900 had reacted with carbonic acid, the maximum possible removal would have been 0.44 billion tonnes. About 90% of the potential has therefore been realized (Figure 2b). The soil model gives a lower but overlapping 0.22–0.37 billion tonnes, and changes in the river’s ratio of calcium and magnesium to bicarbonate point the same way. Losses of bicarbonate to deep groundwater, about 11% in this basin, are not counted and would add to the sink. Figure 2. (a) CO₂ released by soil acid–base reactions in the Mississippi River Basin in 1980: modeled with anthropogenic acid inputs alone and with lime added, compared with the lime-only estimates of the IPCC default method and the US national inventory. (b) Cumulative CO₂ removed by lime, 1900–2015: the ideal maximum, the estimate from river bicarbonate records (with ±1 standard deviation) and the range of the soil model. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Suhrhoff et al. (2026). The river also reveals a delay. Carbon removal shows up in the river decades after lime is applied. Calcium released by lime first sticks to soil particles and pushes off stored acidity, and the water then takes time to travel through soils and aquifers; groundwater in the Mississippi system is about ten years old on average. Tile drains, which carry water quickly from fields to ditches, probably shorten this delay. What it means For greenhouse-gas inventories, the source should be booked against the acid inputs, mainly nitrogen fertilizer and acid rain, rather than against the lime that neutralizes them. Counting lime as a source misrepresents the size, and over large areas and long periods even the sign, of its climate effect. It may also discourage farmers from keeping soil pH at the level that is best for crops. For carbon markets, the picture is more nuanced. Robertson and Hamilton point out that liming at normal agronomic rates is ordinary practice, so it would not count as additional carbon removal deserving credit. The authors add a different warning: because ordinary liming is already a sink, projects that spread crushed rock to remove CO₂ (enhanced weathering) must not claim the removal that business-as-usual liming would have achieved anyway. In very acidic soils, lime may also release CO₂ first and remove it only years later, so short-term claims need care. For agriculture, the result removes an apparent trade-off. Liming raises yields, improves soil health and can reduce emissions of other greenhouse gases; now it appears to remove CO₂ as well, at least at the scale of a large basin over decades. The authors are careful about the limits. The estimate applies to the Mississippi Basin under its historical liming rates. Other regions, much heavier applications or very acidic soils may behave differently, and the modeled delay is uncertain by about 30 years across plausible hydrological settings. What a hydrologist takes from it Rivers are integrating sensors. A single sampling point near the mouth of the Mississippi summarizes the chemistry of 41% of a continent. Without that century-long record of alkalinity, this argument would rest on a model alone. Long records are irreplaceable. The baseline before 1935 exists only because a city water utility kept measuring the river. Monitoring programs often look expensive and unexciting until a question like this one arrives. Water travel times set carbon timescales. The delay between lime application and carbon export is partly a hydrological residence time. Questions about soil carbon removal are, in part, questions about how fast water moves through soils and aquifers. Bottom line Agricultural lime has been counted as a CO₂ source because dissolving limestone in acid releases CO₂. But the acid comes from fertilizer and pollution, and it would release CO₂ anyway by destroying bicarbonate in soils and rivers. Measured against that baseline, a century of liming in the Mississippi Basin has removed about 0.4 billion tonnes of CO₂, around 90% of its maximum potential, with a delay of decades. The finding calls for revising how inventories treat liming and shows how much a long river record can reveal about the carbon cycle. Questions to think about If the CO₂ source is the acid rather than the lime, how would you change the carbon footprint of nitrogen fertilizer? Why might the decades-long delay between liming and river carbon export be shorter in tile-drained fields than in naturally drained ones? Many Korean upland soils are acidic and receive lime. Which river and soil data would be needed to test whether liming acts as a carbon sink in a Korean catchment? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 농경지 산성화를 막기 위해 뿌리는 석회(탄산칼슘)는 녹을 때 CO₂를 내놓는다는 이유로 그동안 온실가스 배출원으로 계산되어 왔다. Suhrhoff 등(2026)은 미시시피강 유역의 100년간 산·석회 투입 기록과 하천 수질 기록을 분석해 이 통념을 뒤집었다. 석회는 질산·황산 같은 강산과 만나면 CO₂를 내놓지만, 토양 속 탄산과 만나면 오히려 CO₂를 흡수해 중탄산염 형태로 바다까지 운반한다. 더 중요한 점은 비료와 산성비에서 온 강산은 석회가 없어도 토양과 하천의 중탄산염을 CO₂로 바꿔 배출하므로, 배출의 원인은 석회가 아니라 산이라는 것이다. 산만 투입된 경우와 비교하면 1980년 기준 석회는 배출을 연간 약 2,000만 톤에서 1,500만 톤으로 줄였다. 하천 중탄산염 기록에 따르면 1900–2015년 석회로 약 4억 톤(±0.9억 톤)의 CO₂가 제거되어 이론적 최대치(4.4억 톤)의 약 90%가 실현되었고, 토양 내 양이온 교환과 지하수 체류시간(약 10년) 때문에 수십 년의 지연이 있었다. 이 결과는 온실가스 인벤토리가 석회가 아니라 산 투입을 배출원으로 다뤄야 함을 보여준다. 다만 일반적인 시비량의 석회는 추가적인 탄소 제거로 인정하기 어렵고, 다른 지역이나 강산성 토양에 그대로 적용하려면 별도의 검증이 필요하다. title: Heat and the mind: what we know about climate change and mental health
description: A summary of the umbrella review by Radua et al. (2024) in World Psychiatry: which links between heat, extreme weather, air pollution and mental health hold up, how large they are, why even young and healthy people should care, and what the evidence cannot yet say.
tags: climate change mental health heat health public health
text: When we talk about the health effects of heatwaves and cold surges, we usually mean the body: heat stroke, heart attacks, hospital admissions among older people. These effects are well documented. Many young and healthy people therefore conclude that extreme weather is not their problem. They stay indoors, turn on the air conditioner, and wait for it to pass. But heat also acts on the mind, and the mind shapes everything we do. Picture a pitcher on a scorching afternoon. The arm may be fine while judgment and temper are not. This side of climate change is harder to measure than mortality or crop yields, and it is less well understood. An umbrella review by Joaquim Radua and colleagues in World Psychiatry is one of the best attempts so far to sort out what we actually know (Radua et al. 2024). This post summarizes it. A pitcher on a hot day The baseball example is not hypothetical. Larrick and colleagues analyzed 57,293 Major League Baseball games and asked when pitchers hit batters (Larrick et al. 2011). After controlling for other factors, the probability of a hit batter rose sharply at high temperatures when more of the pitcher’s own teammates had been hit earlier in the game. The authors suggest that heat makes people more likely to read hostility into others’ actions and lowers their inhibitions against retaliating. Note what this study shows and what it does not. It shows that heat changes behavior that depends on judgment and self-control, in skilled, healthy, highly motivated professionals. It does not show that fastballs get slower on hot days because of mental state; I know of no study that separates the mental and physical sides of pitching performance in the heat. That gap is typical of the whole field. Why mental health is hard to put numbers on Mental health outcomes range from a bad mood to suicide, and most of them never appear in any database. Researchers therefore rely on what is recorded: suicides, hospital admissions, emergency visits, diagnoses, or survey scales. Individual studies often disagree. One finds that fine particulate matter is linked to depression, another with a larger sample finds no link; one finds that hot days raise suicide mortality, another does not replicate it. Even meta-analyses contradict each other. An umbrella review goes one level up. Radua and colleagues collected every systematic review with meta-analysis on air pollution or climate change hazards and mental health published up to June 2023: 32 meta-analyses covering 284 individual studies and 237 exposure–outcome associations. Most associations (195) concerned air pollution; 42 concerned climate hazards, and 35 of those were about temperature. They then graded each association with standard credibility criteria. To be “convincing” (class I), an association needs more than 1,000 cases, a p-value below 10⁻⁶, no sign of small-study effects or excess significance bias, a prediction interval that excludes the null, low heterogeneity, and a significant result in the largest study. “Highly suggestive” (class II) relaxes some of these requirements. Most associations failed even the weaker tests (Figure 1). Figure 1. Credibility of the 237 associations between air pollution or climate change hazards and mental health outcomes. Only one reached class I (convincing) and eleven class II (highly suggestive); more than half were not statistically significant. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Radua et al. (2024). What holds up: heat and suicide The strongest climate findings concern short-term heat, meaning temperature over days to weeks (Figure 2a). For every 1°C increase in temperature: deaths from suicide or mental disorders rise by 2.4%; suicidal behavior (deaths, attempts, ideation or self-harm) rises by 1.2%; hospital admissions or emergency visits for suicidal behavior or mental disorders rise by 1.1%, and for mental disorders alone by 0.9%. Apparent temperature, which combines air temperature with humidity to express how hot it feels, shows a similar link with suicidal behavior (1.0% per 1°C). All five reach class II, and all five survive a sensitivity analysis restricted to longitudinal studies, in which the exposure clearly comes before the outcome. One climate hazard besides temperature also reached class II: people more recently exposed to a cyclone had more severe post-traumatic stress symptoms. That finding rested only on cross-sectional studies, however, and did not survive the longitudinal analysis. Figure 2. (a) Increase in the risk of five mental health outcomes per 1°C rise in short-term temperature, with 95% confidence intervals; all are class II associations. (b) The mortality estimate scaled with land warming since the pre-industrial period, as in the paper’s complementary analysis. The paper estimates about 5% today and about 7% by 2050; the markers sit where the curve reaches those values. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Radua et al. (2024). Small effects, large numbers A 1–2% increase per degree sounds small. The authors’ point is that it applies to the whole population on every hot day. To show what this could mean, they combined the mortality estimate with the rise in global land temperature since 1750–1799. By their calculation, deaths from suicide or mental disorders are already about 5% higher than in a pre-industrial climate, and will be about 7% higher by 2050 (95% CI 4.2–9.7%) if land temperatures keep rising at the recent rate (Figure 2b). This projection should be read as an illustration, not a forecast. It applies a risk estimated for day-to-day temperature swings to a slow rise in the annual mean, and it assumes the relationship is linear and that people do not adapt. Each of those assumptions could be wrong in either direction. Not only the vulnerable The review does not analyze age, but other studies speak directly to young and healthy people. In the summer of 2016, researchers followed 44 university students in the Boston area, with a mean age of 20, through a heatwave (Cedeño Laurent et al. 2018). Twenty lived in buildings without air conditioning, where indoor temperatures averaged 26.3°C; the others lived in air-conditioned buildings at 21.4°C. During the heatwave, the students without air conditioning took 13.4% longer to respond on a color-word attention test and 13.3% longer on simple arithmetic, relative to the air-conditioned group. On the attention test, performance was best at indoor temperatures of 22–23°C. Staying indoors only protects you if the indoor air is cool, and buildings designed to keep heat in during winter can stay hot long after a heatwave passes. Climate change also affects young people’s minds through worry rather than heat. In a survey of 10,000 people aged 16–25 in ten countries, 59% said they were very or extremely worried about climate change, and more than 45% said their feelings about it negatively affected their daily life and functioning (Hickman et al. 2021). The review mentions this kind of distress (eco-anxiety, ecological grief, solastalgia) but could not grade it, because no meta-analyses of it existed yet. What the review cannot tell us The authors are frank about the limits, and they are worth repeating: The underlying evidence is weak. Every one of the 32 meta-analyses was rated low or critically low in methodological quality, mostly for poor handling of heterogeneity and incomplete reporting. Association is not causation. Exposures such as heat and air pollution occur together, and age, sex and income may confound or modify the links. The review could not separate them. Cold is an open question. No association with cold reached high credibility, but the authors note that this does not rule out harm from extreme cold, which has been reported in Northern Europe. For cold surges, the evidence is thinner than for heat. Thresholds are unknown. Effects were analyzed per degree. Whether risk rises sharply above some temperature, as it does for physical health, was not tested. Air pollution, the other half of the review, produced the only convincing association: long-term exposure to solvents is linked to 14% higher odds of dementia or cognitive impairment. Class II links included carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides with dementia, particulate matter during pregnancy with postpartum depression, and sulfur dioxide with schizophrenia relapse. What a hydrometeorologist takes from it Humidity matters for the mind, too. Apparent temperature, which depends on humidity, carried a link with suicidal behavior as strong as air temperature. Heat warnings based on air temperature alone may miss humid days that feel worse than they read. Indoor climate is part of exposure. Weather stations measure outdoor air, but people experience the indoor temperature of their homes, classrooms and offices. Linking urban climate and building data to health records would sharpen these estimates a great deal. Heat warnings could include mental health. Heat-health warning systems already target older people and outdoor workers. The evidence here suggests that mental health services and suicide prevention belong in those plans as well. Bottom line The umbrella review confirms that climate change affects mental health, not only physical health. The most credible link is between hot days and suicide, deaths from mental disorders, and psychiatric hospital visits: roughly 1–2.4% more per 1°C. The effects are small for any one person but apply to everyone, every hot day, and they reach young and healthy people too, through slower thinking, shorter tempers and worry about the future. The evidence base is still weak, and questions such as cold, thresholds and causation remain open. Mental health deserves a place in how we measure the human cost of a warming climate. Questions to think about In the pitcher study, the heat effect was tied to provocation. What does that suggest about how heat interacts with stress at work or at home? How would you design a study to separate the mental and physical effects of heat on athletic performance? Korean summers are hot and humid, and winters bring cold surges. Which data would you need to test whether cold affects mental health outcomes in Korea? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 폭염과 한파가 신체 건강에 미치는 영향은 잘 알려져 있지만, 정신 건강에 미치는 영향은 수치로 다루기 어렵고 아직 잘 이해되지 않았다. Radua 등(2024)은 2023년 6월까지 발표된 메타분석 32편(개별 연구 284편, 연관성 237개)을 모아 증거의 신뢰도를 평가했다. 가장 엄격한 기준을 통과한 연관성은 12개(5%)뿐이었고, 기후 관련 결과 중에는 단기 기온 상승의 영향이 가장 확실했다. 기온이 1°C 오를 때마다 자살 및 정신질환 관련 사망은 2.4%, 자살 행동은 1.2%, 자살 행동이나 정신질환으로 인한 병원 방문은 1.1% 늘었고, 습도를 반영한 체감온도도 비슷한 결과를 보였다. 한 사람에게는 작은 효과지만 모든 사람에게 더운 날마다 적용되므로, 저자들은 산업화 이전에 비해 이미 관련 사망이 약 5% 늘었고 2050년에는 약 7%에 이를 것으로 추정했다. 젊고 건강한 사람도 예외가 아니다. 미국 프로야구 5만7천여 경기를 분석한 연구에서는 더운 날 동료 타자가 맞은 뒤의 보복성 몸에 맞는 공이 크게 늘었고, 폭염 동안 에어컨 없는 기숙사에 산 대학생은 인지 반응 속도가 약 13% 느려졌으며, 16–25세 1만 명 조사에서는 45% 이상이 기후변화에 대한 걱정이 일상에 영향을 준다고 답했다. 다만 포함된 메타분석의 질은 모두 낮았고, 연관성이 곧 인과관계는 아니며, 한파의 영향과 임계 온도는 아직 밝혀지지 않았다. title: A short history of AI, part 3: transformers and large language models (2017–2026)
description: The last of three posts on how artificial intelligence developed: pre-training, the scaling era, ChatGPT and the assistants that followed, models that reason and act, AI for weather and floods, and where things stand in late 2026.
tags: artificial intelligence history of science large language models deep learning
text: Part 1 followed AI from Alan Turing to Deep Blue, and Part 2 from Deep Blue to the Transformer, the attention-based network that Google researchers proposed in June 2017. This last part covers the nine years since then. They contain more change than the previous eighty: language models grew from a research curiosity into tools used by more than a billion people, and from tools into agents that write and run code on their own. It ends with the models of late 2026, including Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon. After this, the blog turns back to the Earth for a while. Figure 1. Milestones in AI from 2017 to 2026, discussed in this post. Rows are evenly spaced rather than drawn to scale in time. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on the sources cited below. Pre-training: learning language by predicting words (2017–2019) The Transformer was built for translation, but its real impact came from a different use. In 2018 OpenAI trained a Transformer on a large collection of books simply to predict the next word in a sentence, and then fine-tuned it on specific tasks; this “generative pre-training” (the GPT in ChatGPT) improved results on most of the language-understanding tasks the authors tried (Radford et al. 2018). A few months later Google’s BERT learned by filling in randomly hidden words using the context on both sides, and set new records on a wide range of benchmarks (Devlin et al. 2019). The idea behind both is that predicting text well requires knowing a lot about the world the text describes. Nobody labels the data: the next word is its own answer, so any text on the internet becomes training material. GPT-2, trained on millions of web pages, could write passages of startling fluency and perform some tasks it had never been trained on, simply because they appeared in its training text (Radford et al. 2019). The scaling era (2020–2022) In January 2020 a group at OpenAI reported that the error of a language model falls as a smooth power law as the model, the data and the computing budget grow, with some trends holding over more than seven orders of magnitude (Kaplan et al. 2020). For a field used to unpredictable progress, this was a remarkable finding: it said that bigger would reliably be better, and by how much. Four months later GPT-3, with 175 billion parameters, showed what that meant in practice. Given just a few examples of a task in its prompt, without any further training, it could translate, answer questions or write simple code (Brown et al. 2020). The race that followed is visible in Figure 2. Model size grew about 2,500-fold in five years, reaching 540 billion parameters with Google’s PaLM (Chowdhery et al. 2022). Then DeepMind showed that most of these models had been trained on too little data for their size: Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters but four times more training text, outperformed models several times larger (Hoffmann et al. 2022). The recipe changed from “make it bigger” to “balance size and data.” Figure 2. Number of parameters of landmark language models, as reported in the papers that introduced them. Green points are models deliberately trained on more data relative to their size. From 2023 most developers of frontier models stopped publishing model size, so the recent models cannot be plotted. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Vaswani et al. (2017), Devlin et al. (2019), Radford et al. (2019), Brown et al. (2020), Chowdhery et al. (2022), Hoffmann et al. (2022) and Touvron et al. (2023). The empty right side of Figure 2 is itself part of the history. As language models became products, the information that would let outsiders judge them (size, training data, compute) largely disappeared from public view. The GPT-4 technical report, for example, gives no parameter count (OpenAI 2023). Since then, most of what we know about frontier models comes from benchmarks, which, as my post on vibe coding discussed, have their own problems. From predicting text to answering people (2022–2023) A model trained only to continue text is not an assistant. Asked a question, it may continue with more questions. The step that turned language models into assistants was fine-tuning them on human preferences: people wrote examples of good answers and ranked the model’s outputs, and the model was then trained to produce the kind of answers people preferred, a method known as reinforcement learning from human feedback. In OpenAI’s InstructGPT study, people preferred the answers of a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained this way to those of the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 (Ouyang et al. 2022). On 30 November 2022 OpenAI released ChatGPT, a conversational model trained with the same methods, as a free research preview (OpenAI 2022). An analyst note estimated that it reached 100 million monthly users by January 2023, which would make it the fastest-growing consumer application recorded at the time (Hu 2023). Within a year the field had changed shape: GPT-4 (14 March 2023) handled images as well as text and, according to OpenAI, scored around the top 10% of test takers on a simulated bar exam (OpenAI 2023). Claude, Anthropic’s first public model, was released the same day (Anthropic 2023). LLaMA (February 2023) and Llama 2 (July 2023) from Meta made capable models available as open weights, and Llama 2 was free for research and commercial use (Touvron et al. 2023; Meta 2023). An ecosystem of open models grew around them. Gemini (December 2023) was Google’s first model designed from the start to work with text, images, audio and video together (Google 2023). Thinking longer, and acting (2024–2025) Researchers had noticed that language models solve harder problems when prompted to write out their reasoning step by step, a technique called chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022). In September 2024 OpenAI’s o1 built this into training: the model was trained with reinforcement learning to produce a long internal chain of reasoning before answering, and it performed far better on mathematics and programming problems (OpenAI 2024). In January 2025 the Chinese company DeepSeek released R1, a reasoning model trained in a similar way, with its weights openly available; its Nature paper reported that the reinforcement-learning stage cost about US$294,000 in rented computing time, although that excludes the much larger cost of training the base model it started from (Guo et al. 2025). Reasoning was no longer the preserve of a few companies. The next step was to let models act. Instead of answering a question, an agent is given a goal and tools (a terminal, a browser, a code editor) and works toward the goal over many steps, checking its own results. Anthropic released Claude Code, an agent that reads, writes and runs code in a developer’s own environment, for general use in May 2025 (Anthropic 2025), and similar tools followed from other companies. METR’s measurements, discussed in my earlier post on writing and coding with LLMs, suggest that the length of task such agents can complete on their own has been doubling every few months (Kwa et al. 2025). The vibe coding of my previous post is a direct product of this period. AI for science, and for the Earth The same years brought AI into the natural sciences, in ways that matter more to a hydrology lab than any chatbot. AlphaFold 2 predicted the three-dimensional structure of proteins from their amino-acid sequences with accuracy competitive with experiments, solving a problem that had been open for fifty years (Jumper et al. 2021). In 2024 the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went half to David Baker for computational protein design and half to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction, and the Nobel Prize in Physics to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for foundational work that enabled machine learning with artificial neural networks (Nobel Prize Outreach 2024a, 2024b). Weather forecasting was transformed next. GraphCast, trained on decades of reanalysis data, produced ten-day global forecasts in under a minute and outperformed the world’s leading operational deterministic forecast on 90% of 1,380 verification targets (Lam et al. 2023). Its probabilistic successor GenCast beat the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts’ ensemble on about 97% of 1,320 targets (Price et al. 2025). Hydrology moved too. A single LSTM network trained on 531 catchments at once outperformed conceptual models calibrated for each catchment individually, and learned catchment similarities that matched hydrological understanding (Kratzert et al. 2019). In 2024 Grey Nearing and colleagues showed that a global AI model could predict extreme floods in ungauged basins up to five days ahead with reliability similar to or better than the current global system’s same-day nowcasts, and the model now feeds a free public flood-warning service in more than 80 countries (Nearing et al. 2024). The question that Hsu, Gupta and Sorooshian raised in 1995, which Part 1 described, is now being asked of operational systems. Where things stand in late 2026 The pace has not slowed. In June 2026 Anthropic released Claude Fable 5, which it described as state-of-the-art on nearly all the benchmarks it tested (Anthropic 2026a). On 22 September came Claude Opus 5.5, which Anthropic says performs at the level of its top model, Claude Fable 5.1, on most work while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5 (Anthropic 2026b). On 30 September Google announced Gemini 4 Argon, its new frontier model, reporting a state-of-the-art score on the DeepSWE software-engineering benchmark; it reached the Gemini app on 13 October (Google 2026). OpenAI’s GPT-5 family continued in parallel, and in August 2026 OpenAI described ChatGPT as having more than a billion weekly active users (OpenAI 2026). All of these claims come from the companies themselves, and none of the models’ sizes, training data or full evaluations are public. That is the honest summary of where the story stands: the systems are more capable than ever, more widely used than any previous technology of their kind, and harder for outsiders to examine than at any point in this history. What ninety years teach Turing’s question has not gone away. In 1950 Turing replaced “can machines think?” with a test of behavior. Today’s models pass versions of that test daily, and the argument has moved, exactly as it did after Deep Blue, to what passing the test does and does not show. Rules lost to learning, but not completely. The learning tradition that began with McCulloch, Pitts and Rosenblatt won decisively. Yet the most useful systems of 2026 are learned models that use rule-based tools: they call calculators, run tests and follow procedures. The two traditions of Part 1 have merged. Data and computing power decided the timing. Almost every key idea in this series was older than the moment it worked. What changed, again and again, was the amount of data and computing power available to make it work at scale. Measurement is the bottleneck. From the imitation game to ImageNet to today’s agent benchmarks, each era has had to invent a way to measure progress, and each measure has eventually been outgrown or gamed. For hydrologists, who have argued about model evaluation for decades, this is familiar ground, and it is where our field can contribute. Bottom line From 2018, pre-training on large amounts of text, with no labels, became the basis of language AI. Scaling laws (2020) made progress predictable; models grew about 2,500-fold in five years until Chinchilla showed that data mattered as much as size. Fine-tuning on human preferences turned language models into assistants; ChatGPT (2022) brought them to the public, followed by GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA and Gemini in 2023. Reasoning models (2024–2025) and coding agents (2025) extended what the models can do on their own. AI transformed protein science and weather forecasting and is entering operational flood forecasting; the 2024 Nobel Prizes recognized both the methods and their scientific use. In late 2026 the frontier includes Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, but most of what we know about such models comes from their developers. Questions to think about Predicting the next word turned out to require a great deal of knowledge about the world. Is predicting tomorrow’s streamflow from yesterday’s weather the same kind of problem? What would a “pre-trained” hydrological model learn? Model developers stopped publishing model sizes in 2023. What would you need to know about an AI model before trusting it in an operational flood warning system? Looking back over the three parts of this series, which idea do you think took longest to go from proposal to practical use, and why? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 인공지능 역사 연재의 마지막 편으로, 트랜스포머 이후 지금까지(2017–2026)를 다룬다. 2018년부터 다음 단어를 예측하도록 대량의 텍스트로 미리 학습시키는 방식(GPT, BERT)이 언어 AI의 기반이 되었다. 정답 라벨이 필요 없어 인터넷의 모든 글이 학습 자료가 되었다. 2020년 스케일링 법칙은 모형 크기, 데이터, 계산량이 늘수록 오차가 예측 가능하게 줄어든다는 것을 보였고, 언어모형은 5년 만에 약 2,500배 커졌다. 그러다 친칠라가 데이터의 양이 크기만큼 중요하다는 것을 보였고, 2023년부터는 대부분의 개발사가 모형 크기를 공개하지 않게 되었다. 사람의 선호로 미세조정하는 방법(RLHF)이 언어모형을 대화형 비서로 바꾸었고, 2022년 11월 ChatGPT가 공개된 뒤 2023년 GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA, Gemini가 잇따랐다. 2024–2025년에는 답하기 전에 길게 추론하는 모형(o1, DeepSeek-R1)과 스스로 코드를 쓰고 실행하는 에이전트(Claude Code)가 나왔다. 같은 시기 AI는 단백질 구조 예측(알파폴드, 2024년 노벨 화학상)과 날씨 예보(GraphCast, GenCast)를 바꾸었고, 미계측 유역의 홍수를 5일 앞서 예측해 80여 개국에 무료 경보를 제공하는 수준에 이르렀다. 2026년 9월에는 Claude Opus 5.5와 Gemini 4 Argon이 나왔지만, 이런 성능 주장은 대부분 개발사 자체 발표이고 모형의 크기와 학습 자료는 공개되지 않고 있다. 90년의 역사가 남긴 교훈은 튜링의 질문이 여전히 유효하다는 것, 규칙과 학습의 두 전통이 결국 합쳐졌다는 것, 아이디어가 실현되는 시점을 정한 것은 데이터와 계산 능력이었다는 것, 그리고 발전을 어떻게 측정할 것인가가 여전히 가장 어려운 문제라는 것이다. title: A short history of AI, part 2: data, GPUs and deep learning (1997–2017)
description: The second of three posts on how artificial intelligence developed: the turn to statistical learning, the return of neural networks, ImageNet and AlexNet, AlphaGo, and the attention mechanism that set the stage for today's language models.
tags: artificial intelligence history of science machine learning deep learning
text: Part 1 ended in May 1997, with IBM’s Deep Blue beating Garry Kasparov through brute-force search and hand-tuned rules. This part covers the next twenty years, in which the opposite idea won: instead of telling the machine how to solve a problem, show it enough examples and let it work out the method itself. By 2017 that approach had overtaken human performance on a standard image benchmark, mastered the game of Go without human help, and produced the network architecture behind every large language model in use today. Part 3 will pick up from there. After Deep Blue: learning from data (1997–2006) By the late 1990s the center of the field had moved from logic to statistics. The most successful methods of the decade were not neural networks but algorithms with solid mathematical foundations that worked well on modest data sets: support vector machines, which find the boundary between two classes that leaves the widest possible margin (Cortes & Vapnik 1995), and random forests, which average the votes of many randomized decision trees (Breiman 2001a). In the same year, the statistician Leo Breiman described a split between two “cultures”: one that starts by assuming a model of how the data were generated, and one that treats the process as unknown and judges a model only by how well it predicts (Breiman 2001b). Hydrologists will recognize the debate. It is the same tension between conceptual and data-driven models that the 1995 rainfall-runoff network in Part 1 raised. Neural networks were out of fashion, but two ideas from this period proved decisive later. The first was the convolutional network. Yann LeCun and colleagues trained networks whose layers scan an image with small, shared filters, and used them to read handwritten digits; a check-reading system built on this approach was deployed commercially (LeCun et al. 1998). The second was memory. Ordinary recurrent networks, which process sequences one step at a time, forget quickly: the error signal used to train them shrinks with every step it is passed back through time. Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber designed the long short-term memory (LSTM) unit, a cell with gates that decide what to keep, what to add and what to forget, so that information can survive many steps (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber 1997). Figure 1. Why LSTM networks can remember. If a signal is multiplied by a constant factor at every step, a plain recurrent network with an effective factor of 0.8 keeps almost nothing of an input from 30 steps back, while an LSTM cell whose forget gate stays open (factor 0.99) keeps most of it. The factors are chosen for illustration; in real networks they are learned and change over time. Figure by Daeha Kim; illustrative, no data. For hydrologists, Figure 1 is more than an abstraction. A catchment’s response today depends on rain that fell weeks ago and on snow that fell months ago. A model that forgets after a few days cannot represent that memory; one with a learned, gated store can, which is why LSTM networks later became the workhorse of machine learning in hydrology. Deep learning returns (2006–2012) The revival began with a trick for training networks with many layers. Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues showed that a deep network could be trained one layer at a time, each layer learning to represent the output of the layer below, and then fine-tuned as a whole (Hinton et al. 2006; Hinton & Salakhutdinov 2006). The word “deep,” meaning many layers, entered the field’s vocabulary. Two other ingredients arrived at the same time. The first was computing power from an unexpected source: graphics processing units (GPUs), built to render video games, turned out to be very good at the matrix arithmetic that neural networks need, and training on them was dramatically faster than on ordinary processors (Raina et al. 2009). The second was data. Fei-Fei Li and colleagues built ImageNet, a database of millions of photographs labeled by thousands of crowd workers according to a hierarchy of object categories (Deng et al. 2009). From 2010 its annual challenge asked programs to classify images into 1,000 categories after training on about 1.2 million labeled examples (Russakovsky et al. 2015). Not every headline of the period came from deep learning. In 2011 IBM’s Watson won the quiz show Jeopardy! against two of its strongest champions, using a large pipeline of many different language-processing and retrieval methods rather than a single learned network (Ferrucci et al. 2010). But in speech recognition, four research groups reported in 2012 that deep neural networks had overtaken the methods that had dominated the field for decades (Hinton et al. 2012). 2012: the year the benchmark broke The turning point came at the 2012 ImageNet challenge. A deep convolutional network built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Hinton, trained for several days on two consumer graphics cards, cut the top-5 error (the share of images whose correct label was not among the program’s five best guesses) to 16.4%, about ten percentage points ahead of the next-best entry (Krizhevsky et al. 2017; Russakovsky et al. 2015). The previous year’s winner had scored 25.8%. Within two years almost every competitive entry was a deep network. Figure 2. Top-5 classification error of the winning entry in the ImageNet challenge, 2010–2017. Gray bars are methods based on hand-designed image features; blue bars are deep convolutional networks. The dashed line is the error of one trained human annotator on 1,500 test images; a second annotator with less training scored 12.0%. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Russakovsky et al. (2015), He et al. (2016) and Hu et al. (2018). The error kept falling. In 2015 a residual network, which adds shortcut connections so that a network can be more than a hundred layers deep and still train, reached 3.57% (He et al. 2016). That was below the 5.1% measured for one carefully trained human annotator, and the result was widely reported as “superhuman.” The more careful statement is narrower: on this benchmark, with these 1,000 categories, the machine made fewer top-5 errors than one expert who had practiced for the task. A second annotator with less practice scored 12.0% (Russakovsky et al. 2015). By 2017 the winning error was 2.25%, and the challenge ended (Hu et al. 2018). The pattern will look familiar from my post on vibe coding: a public benchmark drives rapid progress, and then the meaning of the score becomes the hard question. Learning by playing (2013–2017) Deep networks next learned to act. DeepMind combined a convolutional network with reinforcement learning, in which a program learns from rewards rather than labeled examples, and trained a single system to play 49 Atari video games from the screen pixels and the score alone, reaching a level comparable to a professional games tester (Mnih et al. 2015). Then came Go, a game with far too many possible positions for Deep Blue’s brute-force search. AlphaGo used two deep networks, one to suggest promising moves and one to evaluate positions, trained first on records of human games and then by playing against itself, and combined them with tree search. It beat the European champion Fan Hui 5–0 (Silver et al. 2016), and in March 2016, in Seoul, it beat Lee Sedol, one of the strongest players of the previous decade, by four games to one. For many people in Korea that match, more than any paper, marked the moment AI became real. A year later AlphaGo Zero learned the game from the rules alone, with no human games at all, and beat the version that had defeated Lee Sedol by 100 games to 0 (Silver et al. 2017). The contrast with Part 1 is the clearest summary of these twenty years. Deep Blue’s strength came from its builders’ knowledge of chess, encoded by hand. AlphaGo Zero’s came from the rules of the game and an enormous amount of self-play. Language: from word vectors to attention (2013–2017) Language was harder, because meaning depends on context. A first step was to represent each word as a list of numbers learned from the contexts it appears in, so that words with similar meanings end up close together; word2vec made this fast enough to train on billions of words (Mikolov et al. 2013). Next, sequence-to-sequence models used one LSTM to read a sentence and another to write its translation (Sutskever et al. 2014). Their weakness was that the whole input sentence had to be squeezed into a single fixed-length summary. The fix, called attention, let the translating network look back at every word of the input and decide which ones mattered for the word it was writing (Bahdanau et al. 2015). In the same period, generative adversarial networks showed that two networks trained against each other could produce convincing new images (Goodfellow et al. 2014). By 2015 the change was large enough for LeCun, Yoshua Bengio and Hinton to summarize it in a review in Nature (LeCun et al. 2015); the three later shared the 2018 Turing Award. And in June 2017 a team at Google proposed a translation model that dropped recurrence altogether and was built from attention alone. Because it processed all the words of a sentence at once rather than one at a time, it could be trained far more efficiently on GPUs. They called it the Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017). Part 3 begins with what happened when people made it very large. Hydrology catches up Our field followed with a short delay. In 2018 Frederik Kratzert and colleagues showed that LSTM networks trained on daily meteorological data could simulate streamflow in hundreds of catchments in the United States with skill comparable to a well-established conceptual model, and that the network’s internal memory cells behaved in some ways like the snow and soil storages of a conceptual model (Kratzert et al. 2018). In the same year, Chaopeng Shen reviewed what deep learning could offer water resources science (Shen 2018). The question Hsu, Gupta and Sorooshian had raised in 1995, whether a network that predicts well can also teach us something, had come back in a stronger form. What changed in twenty years Three ingredients arrived together. The ideas behind deep learning (multilayer networks, backpropagation, convolution, LSTM) were mostly older than 2006. What changed was the arrival of large labeled data sets and cheap parallel computing, which finally made those ideas work at scale. Part 1 showed promises running ahead of data and computing power; Part 2 shows what happened when they caught up. Learning replaced hand design, even for the inputs. Before 2012, image recognition relied on features designed by experts. After 2012, networks learned their own features from raw pixels. AlphaGo Zero took the same step for game knowledge. The trend is still running. Benchmarks became the engine of progress, and the arguments moved with them. ImageNet focused a whole field on one number. It also showed how easily a narrow score can be read as a broad claim. Bottom line From the late 1990s, statistical learning methods replaced hand-written rules; Breiman’s “two cultures” named the split between explaining and predicting that hydrology knows well. Two older ideas, convolutional networks and LSTM memory, became the building blocks of the deep-learning era. Deep learning returned around 2006 and took over after 2012, when a GPU-trained network cut the ImageNet error by about ten percentage points. AlphaGo (2016) and AlphaGo Zero (2017) showed that learning and self-play could beat the hand-built knowledge that powered Deep Blue. Attention (2014) and the Transformer (2017) set the stage for the large language models of Part 3; hydrology adopted LSTM networks from 2018. Questions to think about Breiman described two cultures of statistical modeling. Which one does your own research belong to, and what would you gain from the other? Why does a model of daily streamflow need memory? List the processes in a catchment that make today’s flow depend on last month’s weather. A network beat one trained human on ImageNet in 2015. What would it take for you to call a hydrological model “better than an expert hydrologist”? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 인공지능 역사 연재의 두 번째 편으로, 딥 블루 이후 트랜스포머가 나오기까지(1997–2017)를 다룬다. 1990년대 후반부터는 규칙을 직접 쓰는 대신 데이터로부터 학습하는 통계적 방법(서포트 벡터 머신, 랜덤 포레스트)이 주류가 되었고, 브라이먼은 자료가 생성되는 과정을 모형으로 가정하는 문화와 예측력만으로 모형을 평가하는 문화를 “두 문화”로 구분했다. 이는 수문학의 개념적 모형과 자료 기반 모형 사이의 긴장과 같다. 이 시기 합성곱 신경망과 LSTM(게이트로 무엇을 기억하고 잊을지 정하는 순환 신경망)이라는 두 아이디어가 나중의 핵심 부품이 되었다. 2006년 무렵 층별 사전학습으로 깊은 신경망이 되살아났고, 게임용 그래픽 카드(GPU)의 계산 능력과 ImageNet이라는 대규모 라벨 데이터가 더해지면서, 2012년 GPU로 학습한 합성곱 신경망이 ImageNet 오류율을 16.4%로 낮춰 2위보다 약 10%p 앞섰다. 2015년 ResNet은 3.57%로 훈련된 한 사람의 5.1%보다 낮아졌지만, 이는 특정 벤치마크에서 한 사람과 비교한 결과일 뿐이다. 이어 딥마인드의 강화학습은 화면 픽셀만으로 아타리 게임 49종을 익혔고, 알파고는 2016년 3월 서울에서 이세돌 9단을 4승 1패로 이겼으며, 이듬해 알파고 제로는 사람의 기보 없이 규칙과 자기 대국만으로 이전 알파고를 100대 0으로 이겼다. 언어 분야에서는 단어 벡터, 시퀀스-투-시퀀스 번역, 어텐션을 거쳐 2017년 어텐션만으로 이루어진 트랜스포머가 나왔다. 수문학도 2018년 LSTM이 미국의 수백 개 유역에서 기존 개념적 모형에 견줄 만한 유출 모의 성능을 보이면서 본격적으로 딥러닝을 받아들였다. 이 20년의 핵심은 오래된 아이디어에 대규모 데이터와 값싼 병렬 계산이 더해진 것, 그리고 사람이 설계하던 특징과 지식을 학습이 대신하게 된 것이다.
