title: A short history of AI, part 1: from Turing to Deep Blue (1936–1997)
description: The first of three posts on how artificial intelligence developed: Turing's machine and his test, the founding of the field, the perceptron and its limits, expert systems, two AI winters, and the chess match that closed the century.
tags: artificial intelligence history of science machine learning neural networks
text: My recent posts have been about how to use today’s AI tools well: what they do to our writing, how to catch their errors, and when vibe coding can be trusted. Several students asked a more basic question: how did we get here? This is the first of three posts on that question. This one covers the sixty years from Alan Turing’s paper machine to the computer that beat the world chess champion (1936–1997). The second will cover the turn to data and deep learning (1997–2017), and the third the transformer and the large language models of today (2017–2026). History is worth the detour for a practical reason. Many of the debates about AI in 2026 (whether a machine can think, whether rules or learning is the better path, how to tell real progress from hype, and how to measure intelligence at all) were first argued in the period covered here. Knowing how those arguments went the first time makes the current ones easier to judge. Figure 1. Milestones in AI from 1936 to 1997, discussed in this post. Rows are evenly spaced rather than drawn to scale in time. The two “AI winters,” periods of reduced funding and interest, are shown with approximate dates because historians date them differently. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on the sources cited below. A machine on paper (1936–1950) The story usually starts with a mathematician, not a computer. In 1936 Alan Turing, then 24, wanted to answer a question in logic: is there a mechanical procedure that can decide whether any given mathematical statement is provable? To make “mechanical procedure” precise, he imagined a machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape according to a short table of rules. He then showed that a single “universal” machine could imitate any other such machine if given its rule table as input (Turing 1937). That is, in essence, the idea of the stored-program computer, described a decade before one was built. Seven years later, the neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch and the logician Walter Pitts proposed that a nerve cell could be modeled as a simple logical unit that fires when the sum of its inputs passes a threshold, and that networks of such units could compute logical functions (McCulloch & Pitts 1943). Their paper is the ancestor of every neural network in use today. In 1950, after his wartime codebreaking work, Turing returned to the question of thinking machines in the journal Mind. He judged the question “Can machines think?” too vague to answer, and replaced it with a game: an interrogator exchanges typed messages with a person and a machine and tries to tell which is which (Turing 1950). Turing predicted that in about fifty years a computer with a memory of about 109 bits would play the game well enough that an average interrogator would have no better than a 70% chance of identifying it correctly after five minutes of questioning. He also suggested that the most practical route to such a machine might be to build a “child machine” and educate it rather than program it directly, an idea that anticipates machine learning by decades. Turing died in 1954 and did not see the field he had imagined take shape. Naming the field (1955–1969) The phrase “artificial intelligence” first appeared in a funding proposal dated 31 August 1955. John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon asked the Rockefeller Foundation to support a two-month summer study at Dartmouth College, based on the conjecture that every aspect of learning and intelligence could in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it. They expected that a carefully chosen group working together for one summer could make a significant advance (McCarthy et al. 2006). The workshop took place in the summer of 1956. It did not produce the advance, but it gave the field its name and its founding generation. Progress in the following years was real and quick. Allen Newell and Herbert Simon’s Logic Theorist proved theorems from Whitehead and Russell’s Principia Mathematica by searching through possible chains of reasoning (Newell & Simon 1956). Arthur Samuel’s checkers program improved by playing against itself and remembering which positions led to wins; his 1959 paper helped popularize the term “machine learning” (Samuel 1959). Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron took McCulloch and Pitts’s artificial neuron one step further: instead of having its connection weights set by hand, it adjusted them automatically from examples until it classified them correctly (Rosenblatt 1958). Rosenblatt built it in hardware, and the press coverage was enthusiastic. The most famous program of the decade was also the simplest. Joseph Weizenbaum’s ELIZA imitated a psychotherapist by matching keywords in the user’s sentences and turning them into questions (Weizenbaum 1966). It understood nothing, and Weizenbaum said so, yet many users confided in it as if it did. He was disturbed enough by this to write a book arguing that some tasks should never be handed to computers (Weizenbaum 1976). Sixty years later, the tendency he observed, our readiness to attribute understanding to fluent text, is one of the main themes of my previous post on writing with LLMs. Limits, and the first winter (1969–1980) In 1969 Minsky and Seymour Papert published Perceptrons, a mathematical analysis of what a single layer of Rosenblatt-style neurons could and could not compute (Minsky & Papert 1969). The best-known limitation is easy to draw. A single perceptron separates its inputs with one straight line (or plane), so it can learn AND and OR but not XOR, which outputs 1 when exactly one of its two inputs is 1. Adding a hidden layer of neurons solves the problem, but in 1969 nobody had a practical way to train the weights of such hidden layers. Figure 2. AND and OR can be computed by a single perceptron because one straight line separates the inputs that should give 1 from those that should give 0. For XOR no such line exists. Two hidden units, each drawing one line, solve the problem; training such hidden units became practical only in the 1980s. Figure by Daeha Kim; illustrative, no data. The book is often blamed for a decade of neglect of neural networks. Its authors doubted that multilayer networks would do much better, but what they proved concerned single-layer ones. The wider field was in trouble too. Early programs that worked on small, clean problems failed on realistic ones, because the number of possibilities to search grows explosively with the size of the problem. In 1973 the mathematician James Lighthill, asked by the UK Science Research Council to review the field, concluded that it had failed to deliver on its promises outside a few narrow areas (Lighthill 1973). Funding in the UK was cut sharply, and in the United States military funding moved toward projects with clear applications. The period of reduced support that followed, roughly the second half of the 1970s, came to be called the first “AI winter.” Expert systems, and the second winter (1980–1993) AI recovered in the 1980s by narrowing its ambition. Instead of general intelligence, researchers built “expert systems” that encoded the knowledge of specialists as hundreds or thousands of if-then rules. The best-known commercial success was R1 (later called XCON), which configured orders for Digital Equipment Corporation’s VAX computers, a task that had required experienced engineers (McDermott 1982). Companies founded AI groups, specialized “LISP machines” were sold to run AI software, and in 1982 Japan launched its ambitious Fifth Generation Computer Systems project. The boom did not last. Expert systems were brittle: they failed abruptly on cases their rules did not anticipate, and keeping thousands of rules consistent as the world changed proved expensive. Cheaper general-purpose workstations made the specialized hardware obsolete, and the market for it collapsed around 1987. The second AI winter, from the late 1980s to the early 1990s, was as much a commercial collapse as a scientific one. Meanwhile, the neural network tradition had quietly solved its 1969 problem. In 1986 David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams showed how to train networks with hidden layers by propagating the output error backward through the network and adjusting each weight in proportion to its contribution to the error (Rumelhart et al. 1986). The method, backpropagation, had been described earlier by others, but this paper made it widely known and showed that hidden units learned useful internal representations. Multilayer networks could now learn XOR and much more. Learning from data, and a chess match (1990s) In the 1990s, much of AI quietly changed character. Instead of writing rules, researchers increasingly fitted statistical models to data, and judged them by how well they predicted cases they had not seen. Hydrology was an early adopter. Kuolin Hsu, Hoshin Gupta and Soroosh Sorooshian trained a three-layer neural network to simulate daily streamflow in the Leaf River basin in Mississippi and found that it represented the rainfall-runoff relationship better than both a linear time-series model and the conceptual Sacramento soil moisture accounting model. They added that, because its components had no physical meaning, it was no substitute for conceptual watershed modeling (Hsu et al. 1995). By 2000 an ASCE task committee had written a two-part review of neural networks in hydrology (ASCE Task Committee 2000). The tension they named, between models that predict well and models we can interpret, has never left our field. The decade, and this first part of the story, ended with a symbolic victory for the older tradition. In May 1997 IBM’s Deep Blue beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov 3.5–2.5 in a six-game match. Deep Blue did not learn chess in the modern sense. Its builders credit a massively parallel computer with hundreds of special-purpose chess chips, an emphasis on deep search, a complex evaluation function and a database of grandmaster games (Campbell et al. 2002). It was a triumph of search and engineering on a problem with clear rules and a clear score, exactly the kind of problem the Dartmouth founders had in mind, forty years later than they had hoped. What the first sixty years teach Two traditions, both still alive. From the start there were two ideas of how to build intelligence: write down the rules (logic, search, expert systems) or let the machine learn them from examples (artificial neurons, perceptrons, backpropagation). The first dominated until the 1990s; the second dominates today. But today’s systems still combine them, for example when a language model is asked to call a calculator or run a test suite. Promises ran ahead of data and computing power. Both winters followed periods in which researchers and funders expected general intelligence within a decade or two. The ideas were often sound; what was missing was enough data and computing power to make them work at scale. That is worth remembering whenever a forecast about AI sounds certain, in either direction. Turing’s question is still the hard one. Turing replaced “can it think?” with “can we tell the difference?”, a test based on behavior. The benchmark debates in my recent posts are versions of the same move, and they inherit the same weakness: passing a test is not the same as having the ability the test was meant to measure. Hydrology has been here before. The 1995 neural network that beat a conceptual model, and the authors’ caution about what it could not tell us, anticipate today’s debates about machine learning in hydrology almost exactly. Bottom line Turing defined the computer (1936) and proposed a behavioral test of machine intelligence (1950), including the idea of a machine that learns. The field was named in 1955 and grew quickly, but early optimism ran into the explosion of possibilities in real problems and into the limits of single-layer perceptrons. Two AI winters followed: in the late 1970s after early promises failed, and around 1987–1993 after the expert-system boom collapsed. Backpropagation (1986) made multilayer neural networks trainable, and in the 1990s learning from data, including in hydrology, began to replace writing rules. Deep Blue’s 1997 win was a triumph of search and engineering, not of learning, and it closed the first era. Questions to think about Turing replaced “can machines think?” with a behavioral test. What would be a good behavioral test of whether an AI “understands” a hydrological model, and what could it miss? Why can one perceptron learn AND but not XOR? Try drawing it before looking at Figure 2. Hsu and colleagues found that a neural network predicted streamflow better than a conceptual model but warned that it was no substitute for one. Do you agree, thirty years later? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 인공지능의 역사를 세 편으로 정리하는 연재의 첫 편으로, 앨런 튜링부터 딥 블루까지(1936–1997)를 다룬다. 튜링은 1936년 기호를 읽고 쓰는 가상의 기계와 어떤 기계든 흉내 낼 수 있는 “보편 기계”를 제안해 컴퓨터의 개념을 세웠고, 1950년에는 “기계가 생각할 수 있는가”라는 질문을 사람과 기계를 구별할 수 있는지 묻는 행동 시험(이미테이션 게임)으로 바꾸면서 학습하는 기계라는 생각까지 내놓았다. 1955년 다트머스 연구 제안서에서 “인공지능”이라는 말이 처음 쓰였고, 논리 이론가, 스스로 배우는 체커 프로그램, 예시로부터 가중치를 조정하는 퍼셉트론, 대화 흉내를 낸 ELIZA가 잇따라 나왔다. 그러나 실제 문제에서는 탐색해야 할 경우의 수가 폭발적으로 늘었고, 1969년 민스키와 페퍼트는 단층 퍼셉트론이 XOR 같은 문제를 풀 수 없음을 보였다. 1973년 라이트힐 보고서 이후 첫 번째 “AI 겨울”이 왔고, 1980년대 전문가 시스템 붐도 규칙의 경직성과 유지 비용 때문에 무너지며 두 번째 겨울(약 1987–1993)로 이어졌다. 그 사이 1986년 역전파 알고리즘이 은닉층을 가진 신경망을 학습시킬 수 있게 했고, 1990년대에는 규칙을 쓰는 대신 데이터로 학습하는 방식이 퍼졌다. 수문학도 일찍 이를 받아들여 1995년 신경망이 강우-유출 관계를 시계열 모형과 개념적 모형보다 잘 재현했지만, 저자들은 물리적 의미가 없어 개념적 모형을 대신할 수 없다고 경고했다. 1997년 딥 블루가 체스 세계 챔피언 카스파로프를 이긴 것은 학습이 아니라 탐색과 공학의 승리였다. 규칙과 학습이라는 두 전통, 데이터와 계산 능력을 앞질러 간 기대, 그리고 지능을 어떻게 측정할 것인가라는 튜링의 질문은 지금도 그대로 남아 있다. title: Vibe coding, vibe writing, vibe working: what decides whether it works
description: Where the term vibe coding came from, how its accuracy is measured, the factors that decide whether AI-generated code is right, and how far the same approach goes for writing and for office work.
tags: llm coding writing research integrity education
text: In the previous post I looked at what we gain and lose when LLMs help us write and code. This one asks a narrower question that students in my group keep raising: when you hand a whole task to an AI and mostly look at the result, what decides whether the result is right? The practice has a name, vibe coding, and two newer cousins, vibe writing and vibe working. I wanted to know what the evidence says about each, and in particular how anyone measures their accuracy in a way that deserves to be called scientific. As before, I have tried to report every number as the original authors did and to say when a source is a preprint, a company announcement or an industry report. Several of the most useful sources here are not peer-reviewed, because the field moves faster than journals do. That is itself part of the story. Where the term came from On 2 February 2025 Andrej Karpathy, a founding member of OpenAI and former director of AI at Tesla, posted on X about a new way of programming he called “vibe coding,” in which you “fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists” (Karpathy 2025). He described speaking his requests to an AI coding tool, accepting all of its changes without reading them and pasting error messages back without comment when something broke, and said the approach was fine for throwaway weekend projects. The post was viewed around 4.5 million times, and the term spread with unusual speed: Merriam-Webster listed it as a slang and trending entry in March 2025, and Collins English Dictionary named it Word of the Year for 2025 in November (Michels et al. 2026). Collins defines it as the use of artificial intelligence prompted by natural language to assist with the writing of computer code. The definition that matters for this post came a few weeks after the original tweet. The programmer Simon Willison argued that using an LLM is not enough to make something vibe coding: if you have reviewed, tested and understood every line the model wrote, you are simply using it as a typing assistant (Willison 2025). Vibe coding, on this reading, is defined by not reading the code and judging it only by whether it seems to work. A recent review of the evidence adopts the same boundary (Michels et al. 2026), and so will I. The distinction is important because most of the questions below are about what happens when the human stops checking. The other two terms came from industry. In late September 2025 Microsoft introduced an agent mode for Excel and Word and called the shift “vibe working,” with “vibe writing” as its Word-specific form: you describe the document or analysis you want and the agent plans and carries out the steps (Microsoft 2025). Nobody has yet defined these terms as carefully as Willison defined vibe coding, so I use them loosely here: handing a writing or office task to an AI and judging mainly by the result. How accuracy is measured There are three kinds of evidence, and they answer different questions. Benchmarks with hidden tests. A benchmark gives a model a task and checks the result automatically. The first widely used one, HumanEval, had 164 short Python functions, each with unit tests; today’s frontier models solve almost all of them, so it no longer tells models apart. Its successor for agentic coding, SWE-bench, gives an agent a real issue from a real open-source repository and counts it as solved only if the repository’s own tests pass afterwards. Scores rose from under 2% on the original SWE-bench in late 2023 to 95% on its human-validated subset, SWE-bench Verified, by mid-2026 (Michels et al. 2026). That is the most compact summary of how fast coding capability has grown. Randomized trials with people. Benchmarks measure the model alone. To know what happens when a person uses the model, someone has to randomly assign people to work with and without it and measure the outcome. The METR trial discussed in the previous post is the best-known example; a field experiment with 4,867 developers in three companies found 26% more completed tasks with an AI assistant (Cui et al. 2026); and a trial run by Anthropic found that developers learning a new library with AI help scored 17 percentage points lower (50% against 67%) on a test of what they had just learned (Shen & Tamkin 2026). Telemetry and audits. Companies and researchers also measure what happens in real codebases over months: review time, bug counts, incidents and code duplication. These data are large but usually observational and often collected by vendors, so they show associations rather than causes. Each kind has known traps, and they all push in the same direction, toward overestimating accuracy. Contamination. Models may have seen the test problems during training. When OpenAI audited SWE-bench Verified in early 2026, it found that every frontier model it tested could reproduce the reference solution or verbatim details of the problem for some tasks, and among the 138 problems that its own o3 model could not solve consistently, 59.4% had defects in the tests or the problem description. It stopped reporting the benchmark in February 2026 (Michels et al. 2026). Weak tests. A patch can pass the tests and still be wrong. An audit of the top 30 agents on SWE-bench found that about one in five “solved” patches was semantically incorrect but passed weak test suites (Yu et al. 2026). Who runs the test. On the harder, contamination-resistant SWE-bench Pro, the best scores reported by model developers were around 80%, while the benchmark’s maintainer, running the same class of models itself, found about 59–61%, although it had not yet tested the newest models (Michels et al. 2026). Figure 1. The same kind of system scores very differently depending on who runs the test, what counts as correct and how much of the task must work. Left: best scores on SWE-bench Verified and on the harder SWE-bench Pro, as reported by model developers and as measured independently (Michels et al. 2026). Middle: share of solutions from one agent that were functionally correct, and correct and secure (Zhao et al. 2026). Right: share of scientific coding subproblems and of whole problems solved by the best model in the published study, o1-preview, without background information (Tian et al. 2024). The three panels come from different studies and years and should not be compared with one another. Figure by Daeha Kim. So “how accurate is vibe coding?” has no single answer. The answer depends on what is checked, by whom and how strictly. That observation turns out to be the key to the rest of this post. What decides whether the code is right Reading across the studies, I find eight factors with reasonably direct evidence behind them. They are not independent, and the first one runs through all the others. 1. Whether the result can be checked. The review by Michels and colleagues (2026) concludes that the decisive variable is not difficulty but verifiability. Where a mechanical check exists (a test suite, a compiler, a crash that can be reproduced), current systems are strong and improving fast, because they can try, fail and try again. Where no such check exists, failures are silent. The effect of a feedback loop is visible even in older work: letting a model run its code against unit tests and explain its own mistakes improved accuracy by up to 12% on benchmarks with unit tests, while on a text-to-SQL benchmark with no unit tests the gains were only 2–3% (Chen et al. 2024). The catch is that the model can also write the tests. AI-written tests usually compile and pass, but they detect real faults less well than human-written ones (Michels et al. 2026), because a model trying to pass its own tests writes tests that confirm its code rather than tests that could break it. 2. How completely the task is specified. Benchmarks give the model a complete, precise task. Real requests rarely are. When researchers removed key information from SWE-bench Verified issues, models were poor at noticing that anything was missing; but when they were allowed to ask the user questions, performance on the underspecified tasks improved by up to 74% over working without interaction (Vijayvargiya et al. 2025). A vague request is not a neutral starting point. The model fills the gaps with plausible assumptions, and nothing tells you which ones it chose. 3. How large and how old the codebase is. Scores drop sharply from short, self-contained tasks to long tasks in large repositories (the gap between SWE-bench Verified and Pro in Figure 1). The one independent trial that measured a slowdown studied experienced developers working in their own mature repositories (Becker et al. 2025). Michels and colleagues offer a testable conjecture for much of the disagreement in the literature, which no study has yet been designed to test: AI gains are real on new code and shrink or reverse in mature codebases, where years of undocumented decisions form a specification that cannot be checked. Long inputs are also a problem in themselves. In a controlled study of 18 models, performance became less reliable as input length grew, even on simple tasks whose difficulty was held constant (Hong et al. 2025). 4. How common the language and library are. Models are much better at languages with abundant training data. The largest public code corpus, The Stack v2, contains roughly 200 GB of Python but only about 2 GB of Julia and Fortran (Boruch-Gruszecki et al. 2025), and performance on low-resource languages such as R and Racket lags well behind Python and Java (Cassano et al. 2024). Library versions matter too: on 328 Python problems that required code compatible with a specific version of a library, the best commercial models succeeded only 48–51% of the time in the baseline setting (Misra et al. 2026). For hydrologists this is not abstract. Much of our legacy modeling code is in Fortran, and much of our analysis depends on fast-moving packages. 5. How much domain knowledge the task needs. General coding skill does not transfer automatically to scientific code. SciCode, built by scientists from 16 subfields of the natural sciences, splits 80 research problems into 338 subproblems. In the published study the best model, o1-preview, solved 28.5% of the subproblems but only 7.7% of whole problems, because every step has to be right for the whole to be right (Tian et al. 2024). Models have improved since, but the structure of the result has not changed: errors compound across steps, and a scientific workflow has many steps. 6. What “correct” means. Functional correctness is only one property. SusVibes gives agents 186 real feature requests from open-source projects for which human developers had originally committed vulnerable code. The best configuration produced functionally correct solutions 57% of the time, but only 11.8% were also secure, and adding security hints to the request did not fix this (Zhao et al. 2026). If you only check whether the code runs, you are measuring the easier of the two numbers. 7. The model and the tool around it. Model generation is the factor everyone notices, and it is real: the rise on SWE-bench from under 2% to 95% happened in about two and a half years. But the same model behaves differently depending on the harness: how many attempts it gets, whether it can run tests, which tools it can call. A benchmark score belongs to a model and its setup, and your setup is probably not the one on the leaderboard. 8. The person. In Anthropic’s trial, participants who relied heavily on the AI, by delegating the code to it or letting it debug for them, scored below 40% on the comprehension test, while those who asked conceptual questions or requested explanations alongside the code scored 65–86%, although these subgroups were very small (Shen & Tamkin 2026). The developers in the METR trial believed they were faster when they were slower (Becker et al. 2025). The person decides how well the task is specified, whether a check exists and whether anyone reads the output. Vibe coding, by definition, removes the last of these. Put together, the factors suggest a simple rule. Vibe coding is most accurate when the task is small, well specified, in a common language and checkable by a test you trust; it is least accurate when the task is long, vague, scientific, security-sensitive or embedded in a large old codebase. Most research code in our field falls somewhere in between. Vibe writing: how far does it go? Writing has the same factors, but the first one, verifiability, works against it. There is no compiler for an argument and no unit test for a literature review. Prose quality can be very high. In a preregistered study, writers trained in Master of Fine Arts programs and frontier models each wrote short passages in the style of 50 award-winning authors, and 28 expert readers and 516 general readers compared them blind. When the models were simply prompted, expert readers strongly preferred the human writing. When a model was fine-tuned on each author’s complete works, the result reversed: expert readers now preferred the AI text for both style and quality, and detectors flagged only 3% of the fine-tuned passages as machine-written, against 97% of the prompted ones (Chakrabarty et al. 2025). At the level of the sentence, AI writing can already pass for expert work. Facts and sources are where it fails. The detector company GPTZero scanned 4,841 of the 5,290 papers accepted at NeurIPS 2025, one of the most selective AI conferences, and confirmed at least 100 fabricated citations in about 50 papers, roughly 1% of those it scanned, each of which had passed three or more reviewers (GPTZero 2026). The figure comes from a company that sells a citation checker, but the citations it lists can be checked by anyone. Tools designed for research do better but not well enough: an audit of AI search engines and deep-research agents found that a large share of their statements were not supported by the sources they themselves cited, with citation accuracy between 40% and 80% across systems (Venkit et al. 2025). Generated documentation shows the same pattern in code: early frontier models wrote inaccurate statements in about one fifth of generated code comments, and standard automatic metrics did not detect them (Michels et al. 2026). Whole papers are possible, but rarely good ones. In 2025 Sakana AI submitted three papers written entirely by its AI Scientist system to an ICLR workshop, with the organizers’ agreement. One received an average score of 6.33, just above the acceptance threshold; the company said none of the three met its own bar for the main conference, and its internal review found citation errors (Sakana AI 2025). Later that year, Agents4Science accepted only papers with an AI as first author: of 315 submissions, 253 complete papers were reviewed by three LLM reviewers, 79 were also assessed by humans and 48 were accepted (Bianchi et al. 2025). One human reviewer, an astrophysicist, judged the papers she saw technically correct but neither interesting nor important (Hulick 2025). And plain text is still the weak spot in office benchmarks. On GDPval tasks whose deliverable was plain text, models were rated better than professionals far less often than on tasks with spreadsheets, slides or PDFs (Patwardhan et al. 2025). My reading is that vibe writing works for text whose value lies in its surface: a summary of a document you have read, a routine email, a first structure for a report. It fails for text whose value lies in its claims, because nothing in the process checks them. The previous post showed a second, quieter failure: even light editing shifts what the text says. A scientific paper is almost entirely claims. Vibe working: how far does it go? Office work sits between coding and writing: some of it has checkable outputs (a spreadsheet formula, a filled form), some does not (a recommendation, a slide narrative). The benchmarks reflect that. Figure 2. Success rates of AI agents on benchmarks of office and freelance work. Each benchmark defines success differently (accepted by a client, all checkpoints completed, cell-level accuracy, judged at least as good as an expert’s deliverable), so the rows should not be compared with one another. The SpreadsheetBench and the December 2025 GDPval figures are reported by the companies that built the products. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Mazeika et al. (2025), CAIS (2026), Xu et al. (2025), Microsoft (2025), Patwardhan et al. (2025) and OpenAI (2025). Well-defined spreadsheet tasks. Microsoft reported that its Excel agent solved 57.2% of SpreadsheetBench tasks, against a human baseline of 71.3% (Microsoft 2025). Simulated workplace. In TheAgentCompany, a simulated software company with internal websites, documents, chat and simulated colleagues, the best agent in the published version completed about 30% of 175 tasks on its own. Administrative, finance and data science tasks, which people find easy, were harder for agents than software engineering (Xu et al. 2025). Expert deliverables. On GDPval, professionals with an average of 14 years of experience judged the best model’s deliverables at least as good as an expert’s in 47.6% of comparisons in the original paper (Patwardhan et al. 2025); a model released two months later was reported at 70.9% (OpenAI 2025). These are well-specified, one-shot tasks with all the necessary files provided. Whole paid projects. The Remote Labor Index gives agents 240 real projects, mostly from freelance platforms, from architecture to data analysis to video, and asks whether the result would be accepted by a reasonable client as the commissioned work. At release in October 2025 the best agent succeeded on 2.5% (Mazeika et al. 2025). By mid-2026 the best model reached 15.8% (CAIS 2026): a sixfold increase in under a year, but still far from most projects. The spread in Figure 2 is the same pattern as in Figure 1. The more the task is specified in advance and the narrower the definition of success, the higher the number. The closer the task is to a whole job, with an underspecified brief and a client who judges the result as a whole, the lower it is. One real-world example shows the cost of forgetting this. In 2024 the payment company Klarna announced that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 customer-service agents; in 2025 its chief executive acknowledged that quality had suffered and the company began hiring people again (Michels et al. 2026). A working rule for our group The factors above can be turned into a few questions to ask before handing a task to an AI and judging it by the result. Can I check the result with something I trust and did not let the model write? A water balance that must close, an analytical solution, a published benchmark catchment, a table I can recompute by hand. If yes, vibe away and run the check. If no, read the output as if a new student wrote it. Have I said everything the task needs? Ask the model to list its assumptions or ask you questions before it starts. The evidence says it will not do this on its own, and it helps a great deal when it does. Is the task in familiar territory for the model? Python and common packages are; old Fortran code, a specific library version or a specialized hydrological model are less so. How long is the chain of steps? Errors compound. Break long work into pieces you can check one at a time. Is “it runs” the right definition of correct? For anything that handles files, credentials, other people’s data or design decisions, it is not. Is the value of the output in its claims? If so, as in a paper, a proposal or a report, every claim and every reference needs a source you have opened. Am I learning this skill right now? If so, ask for explanations, not answers. Bottom line “Vibe coding” was coined by Andrej Karpathy on 2 February 2025 and was Collins Word of the Year for 2025. What defines it is not using an AI but not reading what the AI wrote. “Vibe writing” and “vibe working” were introduced by Microsoft in September 2025. Its accuracy is measured with benchmarks, randomized trials and field data. All three tend to overestimate it, through contamination, weak tests and self-reporting. The decisive factor is whether the result can be checked. Specification, codebase size and age, language and library, domain knowledge, the definition of correctness, the tool setup and the person all matter as well. Vibe writing produces prose that can pass for expert work, but fabricated citations and unsupported claims are common, and nothing in the process catches them. Vibe working succeeds on well-defined tasks and mostly fails on whole projects, though that is changing quickly. The narrower and more checkable the task, the more you can trust the vibes. For research, that usually means building the check first. Questions to think about For the last piece of code an AI wrote for you, what was the check that told you it was right? Did the AI write that check? Take one routine task in your research and write down everything the AI would need to know to do it correctly. How much of that would you normally leave unsaid? Which parts of a scientific paper could you check mechanically, and which could only be checked by reading the sources? What does that imply for how you use AI to write? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). “바이브 코딩”은 안드레이 카파시가 2025년 2월 2일 X에 올린 글에서 처음 쓴 말로, 코드가 존재한다는 사실조차 잊고 AI에 맡기는 방식을 가리키며, 콜린스 사전의 2025년 올해의 단어로 뽑혔다. 핵심은 AI를 쓰는 것이 아니라 AI가 쓴 코드를 읽지 않는다는 데 있다. “바이브 라이팅”과 “바이브 워킹”은 2025년 9월 마이크로소프트가 엑셀·워드 에이전트를 내놓으며 붙인 이름이다. 정확도는 숨겨진 테스트가 있는 벤치마크, 사람을 무작위로 배정한 실험, 실제 현장 데이터로 측정하지만, 학습 데이터 오염, 허술한 테스트, 개발사 자체 보고 때문에 대체로 과대평가된다. 예를 들어 SWE-bench Verified에서는 95%까지 올랐지만 더 어려운 SWE-bench Pro를 독립 기관이 직접 돌리면 약 60%였고, 기능상 맞는 코드가 57%여도 보안까지 갖춘 코드는 11.8%에 그쳤다. 정확도를 가르는 가장 큰 요인은 결과를 기계적으로 검증할 수 있는가이며, 과제를 얼마나 완전하게 명시했는가(질문을 허용하면 최대 74% 향상), 코드베이스의 크기와 연식, 언어와 라이브러리의 흔한 정도, 필요한 전문 지식(과학 코딩 문제 전체 정답률 7.7%), “정답”의 정의, 도구 환경, 그리고 사람이 함께 작용한다. 바이브 라이팅은 전문가 수준으로 읽히는 문장을 만들 수 있지만(작가별로 미세조정한 모델의 글을 전문가 독자가 더 선호), 가짜 인용과 근거 없는 주장을 걸러 주는 장치가 없다(NeurIPS 2025 채택 논문의 약 1%에서 가짜 인용 확인, 딥리서치 도구의 인용 정확도 40–80%). 바이브 워킹은 잘 정의된 과제에서는 상당히 잘하지만(스프레드시트 57.2%, 사람 71.3%) 실제 유료 프리랜서 프로젝트 전체를 맡기면 대부분 실패한다(2025년 10월 2.5%에서 2026년 15.8%로 빠르게 상승 중). 결국 과제가 좁고 검증 가능할수록 맡겨도 되고, 연구에서는 AI에게 일을 맡기기 전에 믿을 수 있는 검증 기준부터 직접 만들어야 한다. title: Writing and coding with LLMs: what we gain, what we lose, and how to catch the errors
description: What the evidence says about using large language models to write and to code: where they help, where human-only work is still better, why our own sense of how well it went is unreliable, and practical ways to detect the errors.
tags: llm writing coding research integrity education
text: Large language models (LLMs) are now part of how many researchers write papers and code analyses. One large study estimates that by late 2024 up to 22% of the text in computer science papers showed signs of LLM modification (Liang et al. 2025), and more than 40% of the code submitted in one introductory programming course in 2024 was flagged as LLM-generated, up from almost none in 2022 (Baek et al. 2026). The question for a research group is no longer whether to use these tools, but how to use them without losing what makes the work ours, and how to catch the mistakes they make. In an earlier post I looked at what LLM agents can already do in hydrologic modeling; this one is about the person using them. This post collects what I consider the most useful evidence, from controlled experiments rather than opinion pieces. It is longer than usual, because the topic deserves care. I have tried to report every number as the original authors did, and to say when a study is small, preliminary or not yet peer-reviewed. One caveat applies throughout: most of these experiments used models from 2023 and 2024, and the tools have improved much faster than the evidence about them. I come back to this near the end. What LLMs do well The gains are real, and they are largest for well-defined tasks. Speed and polish on routine writing. In a preregistered experiment with 453 professionals, access to ChatGPT cut the time needed for occupation-specific writing tasks by 40% and raised the rated quality by 18% (Noy & Zhang 2023). The least skilled writers gained the most, so the gap between workers narrowed. Speed on self-contained coding tasks. In a controlled experiment with 95 developers, those using GitHub Copilot finished a small web-server task 55.8% faster (Peng et al. 2023). This was a short, clearly specified task, and the study was run by researchers at GitHub and Microsoft. Better results inside the “frontier.” In an experiment with 758 consultants at Boston Consulting Group, GPT-4 users completed 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster and with more than 40% higher quality on tasks that the model handles well. Below-average performers improved most (Dell’Acqua et al. 2023). More ideas. Writers who received ideas from an LLM produced short stories rated more novel and more useful, especially writers who were less creative to begin with (Doshi & Hauser 2024). Useful critique. When GPT-4 commented on thousands of published papers, the overlap between its points and those of human reviewers was similar to the overlap between two human reviewers (Liang et al. 2024). Structure. Asking a model to plan before it writes (outline, characters, key events, then revision of the plan) produces stories that human raters preferred in 68.5% of comparisons, although that evaluation had only 35 responses (Lewenberg et al. 2025). What is lost compared with writing it ourselves The costs are less visible, and that is what makes them dangerous. The meaning shifts, not only the style. The most striking recent study is a preprint by Abdulhai and colleagues (2026). In a randomized study, 100 people wrote an essay on “Does money lead to happiness?”, some with an LLM available. People who let the model write most of the text were far more likely to end up with no clear position at all: 67% of their essays were neutral, compared with 40% of essays written without an LLM. People who used the model only for advice or as a search tool wrote essays that looked like the human-only ones. Figure 1. Stance of essays on “Does money lead to happiness?” in a randomized study with 100 participants, by how much the writer relied on an LLM. Heavy reliance pushed essays toward neutrality; using the model only for advice or search did not. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Abdulhai et al. (2026). The same authors then asked three current LLMs to revise 86 student essays written in 2021, before ChatGPT existed, giving the models the same expert feedback the students had received. Even when told to fix only grammar, the models changed the content: they replaced far more words than the students did when revising their own drafts, cut pronouns by 40–60%, removed personal examples, made the tone more emotional and pushed every essay in the same semantic direction. In one example, a student’s cautious “perhaps America is not ready for self-driving cars” became a firmer statement. The heavy LLM users in the user study also said their essays were less creative and less in their own voice, yet they were just as satisfied with the result. In science the same effect is already visible: in peer reviews for a major machine learning conference, reviews generated by LLMs gave scores about 10% higher and judged papers by different criteria, mentioning clarity and relevance less and reproducibility and scalability more. Everyone starts to sound the same. Stories written with LLM ideas were individually better but more similar to one another (Doshi & Hauser 2024). An explainable detector of machine text found that human news articles cover a wider variety of themes and vocabulary, while newer models produce text concentrated in a narrow part of the space that human writing occupies (Liebe et al. 2026). Even teams of LLM agents become more alike when they read each other’s drafts. Interestingly, one remedy works for machines as it does for people: in “blind peer review,” each agent receives feedback but revises its own draft without seeing the others’, which preserves diversity (Li et al. 2026). The parallel with brainstorming research, where people who work alone first produce more original ideas than groups, is hard to miss. Learning suffers when the model does the thinking. In a field experiment with nearly 1,000 high school students, unrestricted access to a GPT-4 tutor raised practice scores by 48%, but on the later exam without AI those students scored 17% worse than students who never had it. A version designed to give hints rather than answers avoided the harm (Bastani et al. 2025). In a survey of 319 knowledge workers, higher confidence in AI went with less critical thinking, and the work shifted from producing to checking (Lee et al. 2025). A small EEG study reported that most essay writers who used ChatGPT could not quote a sentence from the essay they had just written (Kosmyna et al. 2025); it is a preprint with 54 participants and its methods have been criticized, so I treat it as a warning sign rather than a result. Outside the frontier, AI makes us worse. In the consultant experiment, on a task that looked similar but lay outside what GPT-4 could do well, AI users were 19 percentage points less likely to reach the correct answer than those working alone (Dell’Acqua et al. 2023). The difficulty is that the boundary is invisible: the model sounds equally confident on both sides of it. Our sense of how well it went is unreliable This, to me, is the most important finding in the whole literature. In a randomized trial with 16 experienced open-source developers working on their own large projects, allowing AI tools made them 19% slower. Before the study they expected to be 24% faster, and afterwards they still believed they had been 20% faster (Becker et al. 2025). Outside experts predicted even larger gains. Figure 2. Predicted and measured change in the time experienced developers needed to complete tasks in their own projects when AI tools were allowed. Negative values mean faster. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Becker et al. (2025). The direction is not always the same. A 2026 follow-up by the same group, with 57 developers and late-2025 tools, pointed toward a speedup rather than a slowdown, but its confidence intervals include zero and the authors themselves call the data unreliable (Becker et al. 2026). The main reason is telling: many developers declined to take part, or held back some of their tasks, because they did not want to work without AI, and the authors think this hides a larger speedup than they could measure. And in the Copilot experiment, users underestimated their gain. The lesson is not that AI always slows us down; it is that our feelings about it are not measurements. The same gap appears in security: people with an AI assistant wrote less secure code and were more likely to believe it was secure (Perry et al. 2023), and the heavy LLM users in the essay study were satisfied with essays that no longer said what they thought. How often LLM output is wrong Error rates depend on the task and the model, and they fall as models improve. But in every study I found, they are well above zero. Figure 3. Error rates of LLM output reported in published studies. Each bar comes from a different study, model, task and year (2021–2024), so the bars should not be compared with one another; newer models generally do better. The point is that none is negligible. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Walters & Wilder (2023), Kabir et al. (2024), Bastani et al. (2025), Pearce et al. (2022) and Spracklen et al. (2025). Some of these errors are easy to miss. More than half of ChatGPT’s answers to Stack Overflow questions contained incorrect information, yet in a small user study people overlooked the misinformation 39% of the time (Kabir et al. 2024). Code models invent package names that do not exist: among 576,000 code samples, at least 5.2% from commercial models and 21.7% from open-source models referred to a non-existent package (Spracklen et al. 2025). Attackers can register those names and wait for someone to install them. In writing, the classic failure is the invented citation: in 2023, 55% of the references produced by GPT-3.5 and 18% of those produced by GPT-4 did not exist, and 24% of GPT-4’s real references contained substantive errors (Walters & Wilder 2023). Industry surveys point the same way at a larger scale: the DORA 2024 survey of about 39,000 software professionals found that higher AI adoption was associated with slightly better code quality and documentation, but lower delivery stability (Google Cloud DORA 2024). One gap in the evidence should be stated plainly. I found no rigorous trial comparing the factual error rate or peer-review outcome of scientific manuscripts written with and without LLM help. We are all, in effect, running that experiment on ourselves. The evidence is older than the tools Almost every experiment above used GPT-3.5, GPT-4 or early versions of Copilot, and most were run in 2023 or 2024. The models have moved much faster than the experimental literature, so the specific numbers in this post probably understate what current models can do. The drop in invented references from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 in a single year (55% to 18%) is a small example of how quickly such figures go out of date. Two benchmarks give a sense of the pace. METR measures the length of task, in hours of skilled human work, that a model can complete on its own half of the time. This “time horizon” doubled about every seven months from 2019 to early 2025 (Kwa et al. 2025), and METR’s revised estimate puts the doubling time since 2023 at about four months (METR 2026). On GDPval, in which experienced professionals blindly compare model and expert deliverables for tasks that take an expert about seven hours, the best model in the original paper matched or beat the expert in 47.6% of comparisons (Patwardhan et al. 2025); a model released a few months later was reported at 70.9% (OpenAI 2025). The failed follow-up in the previous section points the same way: when experienced developers refuse to work without a tool, the tool is probably doing something for them. These numbers deserve the same scrutiny as any other. The METR tasks are self-contained software tasks, and METR itself notes that few of its tasks remain beyond the latest models and that the trend is somewhat sensitive to which tasks are included. GDPval was built by a model developer, and the 70.9% figure comes from that developer’s product announcement rather than a peer-reviewed paper. And on GDPval tasks whose deliverable was plain text, closest to the writing this post is about, models did worst: the experts rated the model’s deliverable better than their own in only 14% of comparisons for Claude Opus 4.1 and 23% for GPT-5 (Patwardhan et al. 2025). More importantly, benchmarks measure the model working alone. They do not test what the earlier sections are about: whether our arguments keep their strength, whether our writing stays our own, whether students still learn, and whether we notice when the model has crossed its frontier. A more capable model may even make some of these problems worse, because it is more tempting to hand it the thinking, and its errors become rarer and therefore harder to spot. I use these tools every day, and my own impression is that they have become far more useful in the past year than the studies above suggest. I think that impression is probably right. But it is also exactly the kind of evidence Figure 2 warns against, so the practical advice that follows does not change: measure, test and check. Detecting the errors None of the following is new to anyone trained in science. LLMs simply make it more necessary. For coding Write the test before you ask for the code. Decide what the correct output is, ideally with a case you can solve by hand, and run it. In hydrology that means checking that a water balance closes, that a model reproduces an analytical solution, or that it gives the published result for a benchmark catchment. Run everything, and read every line you keep. If you cannot explain a line, you do not yet own it. Check that every imported package actually exists and is the one you intended, before installing it. Work in small steps. Ask for one function at a time and inspect the change, rather than accepting a whole script. Pay extra attention to security, file handling and anything that deletes or overwrites data, where the studies above found the most problems. For writing Open every reference. Look up each DOI and confirm that the paper exists and says what the sentence claims. Never cite a paper you have not opened. Trace every number back to its source table or figure. Compare meaning, not only grammar. After an LLM edits a paragraph, compare it with your original sentence by sentence and ask whether each claim is still the one you intended, at the strength you intended. Ask for critique, not a rewrite. “What is unclear or unsupported here?” keeps your text and your argument intact. “Improve this” invites the model to replace them. Signals in the model’s own words. In a study of 30,300 classroom utterances labeled by several LLMs, wrong labels came with explanations that were five times more likely to hedge (“might,” “could”) and twice as likely to narrate the model’s own thinking (“I think,” “I realize”), and they were usually longer. Correct ones linked evidence to conclusions with words like “because” and “therefore” (Ahtisham et al. 2026). That study is about classifying text, not about code, but the rule of thumb transfers: a long, hedging, self-narrating explanation is a reason to check more carefully. Ask more than once. If you ask the same factual question several times and get different answers, the model is probably guessing. This idea underlies “semantic entropy,” which detects many confabulations from the disagreement among repeated answers (Farquhar et al. 2024). A related technique, chain-of-verification, has the model draft an answer, write its own fact-checking questions, answer them independently and then revise; in benchmark tests it cut the number of hallucinated items in list-style answers by more than three quarters (Dhuliawala et al. 2024). Both catch inconsistency, not errors the model makes consistently, so they complement rather than replace checking against sources. Detecting AI-written text is a different problem, and a risky one. Detectors of machine-written text are improving, but they wrongly flag human writing. One recent detector labeled 25% of randomly collected human news articles as machine-written (Liebe et al. 2026). A detector of LLM-generated code that was more than 99% accurate still flagged one of five reference solutions written by the course instructor (Baek et al. 2026). People are not reliable judges either: most cannot tell AI-written from human-written self-descriptions (Jakesch et al. 2023), although people who use LLMs often for writing are much better at it (Russell et al. 2025). Baek and colleagues draw a sensible conclusion for teaching: when code looks generated, ask the student a few conceptual questions about it rather than imposing a penalty. A working attitude Putting the evidence together, this is the approach I suggest to students in my group. Think first, then prompt. Decide what you want to say, or what the code must do, before you open the chat window. The essay study shows that using an LLM for advice preserves your voice and your conclusions; letting it draft does not. Use the model as a critic, a tutor or a student, not as a ghostwriter. In a small preliminary study, students who taught rhetorical strategies to an LLM playing a novice student used more of those strategies in their own essays and made fewer errors on a delayed test than after a video lecture (Miller & Bosch, in press). Explaining to the model is good for you; letting the model explain to the reader is not. Stay inside the frontier, or verify harder outside it. LLMs are most reliable on common tasks with checkable answers. The further you are from that, the more you must check. The frontier moves outward with every model generation, so test it again for your own tasks rather than relying on what was true last year. Match the checking to the stakes. A plotting script and a figure for a paper do not need the same scrutiny as a flood frequency analysis that will inform a design. Keep some work unaided. Skills that are never exercised fade. Write some first drafts, derivations and functions yourself, especially while you are still learning them. Keep the responsibility. The model is not an author. Whatever goes out under your name, you must be able to explain and defend line by line, and you should disclose how you used AI. Bottom line LLMs make routine writing and coding faster and often better, especially for less experienced people, on tasks within their competence. They also change what we say, make our writing more alike, can weaken learning, and make us worse on tasks just beyond their competence. Our own impression of how much they helped is unreliable; only measurement and checking tell us. Error rates in LLM output are well above zero. Tests for code and source checks for writing are not optional. The tools are improving faster than the evidence. Current models are probably more capable than the studies here suggest, but benchmarks measure the model, not what happens to us when we use it. Use LLMs to think better, not to think less. Questions to think about Pick a recent piece of your own writing that an LLM edited. Compare the two versions sentence by sentence. Did any claim change in strength or meaning? For the hydrological model you use most, what simple test (a water balance, an analytical case, a benchmark catchment) would tell you that AI-generated code is wrong? The developers in Figure 2 felt faster but were slower. How could you measure, honestly, whether an AI tool is helping your own research? Benchmarks say the models have improved dramatically since these studies. What evidence would convince you that your own use of them has improved as well? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). LLM은 정해진 글쓰기와 코딩 작업을 빠르고 매끄럽게 해 주며, 특히 경험이 적은 사람에게 도움이 크다(전문직 글쓰기 시간 40% 단축·품질 18% 향상, 간단한 코딩 과제 55.8% 단축). 그러나 사람이 직접 쓴 글과 비교하면 잃는 것도 분명하다. 무작위 실험에서 LLM이 글 대부분을 쓰게 한 사람들의 에세이는 67%가 입장 없는 중립으로 끝났고(직접 쓴 경우 40%), 문법만 고치라고 해도 LLM은 단어와 주장, 어조를 바꾸었다. LLM과 함께 쓴 글은 서로 비슷해지고, 답을 그대로 주는 AI를 쓴 학생들은 AI 없이 치른 시험에서 17% 낮은 점수를 받았으며, 모델이 잘하지 못하는 과제에서는 오히려 정답률이 19%p 떨어졌다. 더 중요한 것은 체감과 실제가 다르다는 점이다. 숙련 개발자들은 AI 덕분에 20% 빨라졌다고 믿었지만 실제로는 19% 느려졌다. 연구마다 차이는 있지만 LLM 출력의 오류율(가짜 인용, 틀린 답, 보안 취약점, 존재하지 않는 패키지)은 결코 0이 아니다. 다만 이 실험들은 대부분 2023–2024년 모델을 썼고, 모델의 능력은 그보다 훨씬 빠르게 늘고 있다. 모델이 혼자 끝낼 수 있는 과제의 길이는 최근 약 4개월마다 두 배가 되었고, 전문가 수준 업무 평가(GDPval)에서 최신 모델은 전문가와 같거나 나은 결과를 70% 이상 냈다는 보고도 있다. 그래서 지금의 LLM은 이 글의 수치보다 유능할 가능성이 크다. 그러나 벤치마크는 모델 혼자의 능력을 잴 뿐, 우리가 쓸 때 주장과 목소리, 배움이 지켜지는지는 재지 않으며, 순수 텍스트 과제에서는 여전히 성적이 가장 낮았다. 따라서 코드는 먼저 검증 기준(물수지, 해석해, 벤치마크)을 정하고 테스트하며, 글은 모든 인용과 수치를 원문에서 확인하고 수정 전후의 의미를 비교해야 한다. 같은 질문을 여러 번 해 답이 달라지거나 설명이 길고 얼버무리는 표현이 많으면 더 의심해야 한다. title: How much water and carbon does AI use?
description: Four recent papers on the water and carbon footprints of AI data centers: where the water goes, why most of it is hidden at the power plant, why the local picture matters more than the global one, and why transparency is the first thing to fix.
tags: artificial intelligence data centers water footprint carbon footprint water energy nexus
text: A question to a chatbot feels weightless. There is no smokestack, no pipe, nothing to see. But every answer is computed on chips that turn electricity into heat, and that heat has to go somewhere. In most data centers it leaves as water vapor, either from the building’s own cooling towers or from the power plants that supply the electricity. In other words, AI is a thermodynamic system, and thermodynamic systems drink. Four papers published this year look at this problem from different angles. Alex de Vries-Gao estimates the carbon and water footprints of AI from what tech companies report (de Vries-Gao 2026). Ana Pinheiro Privette, Ana Barros and Ximing Cai, writing in AGU Advances, focus on local water impacts and the lack of data (Privette et al. 2026). Zohar Barnett-Itzhaki reviews cooling technologies and governance in Water Research (Barnett-Itzhaki 2026). And Navid Saleh argues in Environmental Science & Technology that the next problem is not how much water, but what kind (Saleh 2026). This post reads them together. Three ways AI uses water The papers agree on three pathways. On site (direct). Servers are cooled by air or liquid, and the heat is usually rejected in evaporative cooling towers. The water that evaporates is lost to the local supply. Depending on cooling technology and climate, evaporative systems lose about 1 to 9 liters per kWh of server energy; air-cooled facilities use almost none. At the power plant (indirect). Thermoelectric plants evaporate water for cooling, and hydropower reservoirs lose water to evaporation. On average, US electricity generation consumes about 7.6 liters per kWh. In the supply chain. Chip fabrication needs large volumes of ultra-pure water; an average chip plant uses about 38 million liters per day. Two definitions matter for anyone who reads these numbers. Withdrawal is the water taken from a river, aquifer or utility; consumption is the part that is not returned, mostly because it evaporates. A once-through cooling system withdraws a lot and consumes little (but returns warmer water), while a cooling tower withdraws less and consumes most of it. Barnett-Itzhaki warns that company reports often mix the two. The industry’s efficiency metric, water usage effectiveness (WUE), is the on-site water used per kWh of IT energy; its sister metric, power usage effectiveness (PUE), is the facility’s total electricity divided by the IT electricity. How big is it? The International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that data centers consumed 460 TWh of electricity in 2024, producing about 182 million tonnes of CO₂, and 560 billion liters of water in 2023. AI is the fastest-growing part. De Vries-Gao uses estimates of AI hardware power demand, which rose from 9.4 GW at the end of 2024 to perhaps 23 GW by the end of 2025, almost half of all data center demand and approaching the average electricity demand of the United Kingdom. Combining this with average carbon and water intensities checked against company reports, he estimates that AI systems alone could emit 32.6–79.7 million tonnes of CO₂ and consume 312–765 billion liters of water in 2025. Figure 1. Estimated carbon (top) and water (bottom) footprints of AI systems in 2025, compared with the emissions of New York City and the world’s annual bottled water consumption. The gray bars show all data centers: the IEA estimates and, for water, an alternative estimate based on the water intensity of electricity reported by tech companies. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in de Vries-Gao (2026). For scale, the carbon range brackets the emissions of New York City (52.2 million tonnes in 2023), and the water range brackets the world’s entire bottled water consumption (446 billion liters per year). Readers may have seen a much larger number: that AI’s water footprint could reach 4.2–6.6 billion cubic meters a year by 2027, cited by Barnett-Itzhaki from earlier work by Li and colleagues. That is roughly ten times larger, and for 2027 rather than 2025. Much of the difference comes from definitions: the larger figure refers to water withdrawn, much of which is returned, while de Vries-Gao counts water consumed. It is a good example of why the withdrawal–consumption distinction is not pedantry. Most of the water is hidden at the power plant The most important finding in de Vries-Gao’s paper concerns the indirect water. On site, the numbers are consistent: the IEA implies a WUE of about 0.56 liters per kWh, and the tech companies’ own reports average 0.59. But for the water consumed in generating the electricity, the IEA implies only 1.04 liters per kWh. Every other estimate is three to five times higher: Meta reports 3.92 liters per kWh for its own electricity, the US data centers of Apple, Google and Meta come out at about 3.40, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory finds 4.52 for all US data centers. Figure 2. Water consumed per kWh of data center electricity, on site (blue) and at the power plants that generate the electricity (red), from different sources. The IEA’s estimate of indirect water is much lower than estimates based on company reports and US national data. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in de Vries-Gao (2026). If the companies’ 3.40 liters per kWh is applied to the IEA’s 360 TWh for 2023, data centers consumed about 1,225 billion liters of water at power plants, plus 140 billion liters on site. That is more than twice the IEA’s total. In other words, the global water footprint of data centers may be substantially underestimated, and most of it is not in the data center at all. For a hydrologist, the spread across sites is just as striking. At the US locations examined, the water intensity of the local grid ranged from 0.68 to almost 12 liters per kWh, depending on whether the electricity comes from thermoelectric plants, hydropower reservoirs or wind and solar. Where a data center is built, and which grid it draws from, can change its water footprint by more than a factor of ten. The local picture matters more than the global one Measured against national totals, data center water use looks small. US data centers account for about 0.3% of the public water supply of the contiguous United States, while agriculture accounts for about 70% of freshwater withdrawals. Privette and colleagues argue that this is exactly the wrong scale to look at. Figure 3. Data center water use as a share of the relevant supply: nationally in the United States, and in three US cities. The Mesa value is a projection for one proposed facility at full operation. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Privette et al. (2026). In 2023, one Google campus in Council Bluffs, Iowa, consumed about 3.7 billion liters, about 21% of the city’s total water use and equivalent to adding more than 4,700 residents. In The Dalles, Oregon, data center water use nearly tripled in five years to about 29% of the city’s demand in 2021. In Mesa, Arizona, one proposed data center was projected to use about two-thirds of the city’s daily supply at full operation. More than 97% of the water consumed by major operators comes from municipal drinking water systems, and since 2022 nearly two-thirds of new US data centers have been built in areas of high water stress. Barnett-Itzhaki adds a case from Mexico. In Colón, a town of 67,000 people north of Mexico City, a hyperscale campus was built during a severe drought, while the region’s reservoirs ran low and farming communities relied on trucked water. Industrial water concessions, once granted, are rarely revisited when supply shrinks. The problem there is less the technology than the water allocation rules. Cooling choices are trade-offs The technology to cut on-site water use exists. Barnett-Itzhaki compares the options: Evaporative cooling is energy-efficient but uses about 2–3 liters per kWh, roughly 25,500 cubic meters a year for each megawatt of IT load. Free-air cooling in cold climates can bring WUE below 0.3, but only works in a few regions and needs backup on hot days. Lake or sea water can bring consumption close to zero, but returns water 5–8°C warmer, which can disturb lake stratification and oxygen levels. Waterless designs (dry coolers, immersion cooling) eliminate on-site water use, but use about 10–25% more electricity, which shifts water use and carbon emissions to the power plant. Reclaimed wastewater spares drinking water but needs separate pipes and treatment. There is no free option. Saving water on site usually costs energy, energy costs carbon and water elsewhere, and the sunniest places for solar power tend to be the driest. Barnett-Itzhaki also points out an economic reason why evaporative cooling remains popular: electricity is typically 40–60% of a data center’s operating costs, while water is priced far below its scarcity value. Not only how much, but what kind of water Saleh adds a point that water engineers will recognize. As operators switch to recirculating cooling and reclaimed wastewater, the problem shifts from quantity to quality. Cooling towers lose water by evaporation and leave the dissolved salts behind. Systems typically run at three to ten “cycles of concentration,” so water that enters with about 200 mg of dissolved solids per liter can exceed 1,000 mg per liter. Scaling, corrosion, silica deposits and the disposal of the concentrated blowdown then become the limiting factors, even when there is enough water. Waterless cooling fluids raise their own questions about composition, life cycle and disposal. In Saleh’s words, water demand asks whether water is available; water compatibility asks whether it can be used sustainably. The first problem is the missing data All four papers return to the same point: we cannot manage what is not measured. None of the eleven companies that de Vries-Gao examined reports any AI-specific environmental data. Only Meta reports the water embedded in its purchased electricity. Fewer than a third of operators even track WUE. Privette and colleagues note that local governments and utilities sometimes sign non-disclosure agreements or treat a data center’s water use as a trade secret. The papers’ recommendations are consistent: report water use, WUE and PUE for each facility, separating withdrawal from consumption; include the water embedded in purchased electricity, just as greenhouse gas reporting already includes emissions from purchased electricity; assess water availability and cumulative demand before a site is approved, not after; treat AI demand as one water user among others in regional water planning. Barnett-Itzhaki goes further and proposes “digital water sobriety”: asking which AI applications justify their water use in a stressed watershed, much as we already ask which crops justify irrigation. What a hydrologist takes from it Footprints must be read at the scale of the catchment. A national total of 0.3% says little about a town where one facility uses a fifth of the supply. The right denominator is the local water budget, in the season when it is tightest. The water–energy–carbon nexus is real, and data centers sit in the middle of it. Moving water use from the cooling tower to the power plant does not make it disappear; it moves it to another basin. Any honest assessment has to track all three. This is planning work we already know how to do. Demand forecasting, drought reliability, allocation rules and environmental flow limits are the everyday tools of water resources engineering. What is new is a user that arrives fast, in large blocks, and often without disclosing its numbers. Bottom line AI systems alone may have emitted 33–80 million tonnes of CO₂ and consumed 310–770 billion liters of water in 2025, but these are estimates built on very incomplete data. Most of a data center’s water footprint is at the power plant, and global estimates of that part may be several times too low. Nationally, data centers use little water; locally, a single facility can use a fifth or more of a city’s supply. Every cooling option trades water against energy and carbon; reuse adds water quality challenges. Facility-level, standardized disclosure of water and energy use is the first step. Questions to think about A data center switches from evaporative to dry cooling and uses 20% more electricity. Under what grid mix would its total water footprint go down, and when would it go up? Why is water consumption, rather than withdrawal, the more relevant measure for a cooling tower, and the less relevant one for a once-through cooling system? If you were the water utility in a small city asked to supply a new data center, what information would you require before agreeing, and how would you test the drought reliability of your system with the new demand? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 눈에 보이지는 않지만 AI는 계산 과정에서 나오는 열을 식히기 위해 데이터센터의 냉각탑에서, 그리고 전기를 만드는 발전소에서 물을 증발시킨다. 올해 게재된 네 편의 논문을 종합하면, AI 시스템만으로 2025년에 약 3,300만–8,000만 톤의 이산화탄소를 배출했을 수 있고, 3,100억–7,700억 리터의 물을 소비했을 수 있다(뉴욕시의 연간 배출량, 전 세계 생수 소비량과 비슷한 규모). 데이터센터의 물 사용 대부분은 현장 냉각이 아니라 발전 과정에서 생기며, 기업 보고 자료로 보면 국제에너지기구(IEA)의 추정치는 이 부분을 크게 과소평가했을 가능성이 있다. 미국 전체로는 데이터센터가 공공 급수의 약 0.3%에 불과하지만, Council Bluffs, Iowa에서는 구글 캠퍼스 하나가 도시 물 사용량의 약 21%를 차지했다. 냉각 방식은 물·에너지·탄소 사이의 맞교환이며, 물을 재이용하면 농축된 염분과 같은 수질 문제가 새로 생긴다. 무엇보다 시설별로 물 취수량과 소비량, 그리고 구매 전력에 포함된 물까지 표준화해 공개하는 것이 첫 단계이며, 데이터센터를 지역 물 계획 안의 한 수요자로 다뤄야 한다.
