title: Where our CO₂ goes, and how much is left to emit
description: A hydrologist's reading of the Global Carbon Budget 2025 and two companion papers: the carbon cycle as a mass balance, why the land sink is weaker than we thought, what the remaining carbon budget means, and which sectors emit how much.
tags: carbon budget carbon cycle climate change emissions mitigation
text: Every hydrology student learns the water balance before anything else: precipitation equals evapotranspiration plus runoff plus the change in storage, and whatever does not close is the error term. The global carbon cycle can be read in exactly the same way. Each year the Global Carbon Project closes this balance for carbon dioxide, and its latest edition, the Global Carbon Budget 2025, was published this year (Friedlingstein et al. 2026b). A companion paper in Nature explains why several terms of the budget were revised (Friedlingstein et al. 2026a), and a short review by Deng and colleagues breaks down where fossil CO₂ comes from, sector by sector (Deng et al. 2025). In this post I read the three papers together and try to answer four questions. Where does the CO₂ we emit go? What changed in our understanding? What does “the remaining carbon budget” actually mean? And which sectors would have to change, and by how much? The carbon budget is a mass balance The budget has five main terms. On the source side are emissions from fossil fuels and cement (EFOS) and net emissions from land-use change, mostly deforestation (ELUC). On the receiving side are the growth of CO₂ in the atmosphere (GATM), uptake by the ocean (SOCEAN) and uptake by land ecosystems (SLAND). What is left over is the budget imbalance: BIM = EFOS + ELUC − (GATM + SOCEAN + SLAND) Hydrologists will recognize the structure. Two terms are measured well: fossil emissions come from energy statistics, and the atmospheric growth comes from direct CO₂ measurements. The other three are estimated with models and indirect data, in the same way that we often estimate evapotranspiration or groundwater storage. The imbalance is a check on the whole system. Figure 1. The global carbon budget averaged over 2015–2024. Human emissions of about 41 GtCO₂ per year (left) are balanced by the growth of CO₂ in the atmosphere and by uptake in the ocean and on land (right). Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from the decadal budget in Friedlingstein et al. (2026b), converted from carbon to CO₂ (1 GtC = 3.664 GtCO₂). Over the last decade, humans emitted about 41 GtCO₂ per year, 88% of it from fossil fuels and 12% from land-use change. Half of it stayed in the atmosphere. The ocean took up 29% and land ecosystems 21%. In 2024 alone, total emissions reached 42.4 GtCO₂, and the CO₂ concentration averaged 422.8 ppm. The preliminary estimate for 2025 is 425.6 ppm, 53% above the pre-industrial level of about 278 ppm. The long view is just as instructive. Since 1850, humans have emitted about 2,700 GtCO₂ (745 GtC). Of this, 39% is still in the atmosphere, 27% has gone into the ocean and 24% into land ecosystems. Land-use change emitted more over this period than the land sink took up, so the land as a whole has been a net source. What changed: a weaker land, a stronger ocean For years, the budget did not quite close. The 2024 edition had an imbalance of −0.4 GtC per year over the last decade, meaning that either the sources were too small or the sinks too large, and this imbalance had a trend. A budget with a trending error term is hard to interpret, just as a water balance with a drifting residual makes it hard to say whether evapotranspiration is really changing. The Nature paper fixes this by adding processes that were known but missing (Friedlingstein et al. 2026a). Three corrections stand out. Land-use emissions were too low. The models assumed that a hectare of forest always stores the same amount of carbon. In reality, forests store more today than in the past because of higher CO₂, so clearing one releases more. Accounting for this raises land-use emissions slightly. The land sink was too large. The models computed the land sink on a pre-industrial land-cover map, ignoring that about a fifth of the world’s forest area has since been lost. Forests are among the strongest sinks, so this inflated the sink. Correcting it reduces the land sink by about 0.5 GtC per year. The ocean sink was too small. Ocean models are known to underestimate uptake by about 10%, and observation-based estimates missed the effect of the thin, cool skin at the sea surface. Correcting both raises the ocean sink. One more correction is close to home for hydrologists. Human activities have increased the amount of carbon that moves from soils into rivers, lakes and reservoirs. The paper estimates that this lateral flux is now 0.54 GtC per year higher than before industrialization. Most of it is CO₂ from soil respiration that simply escapes through the water instead of the soil surface, so it does not change the land sink. But part of it is organic carbon that is lost from land ecosystems and released by inland waters, and that part does reduce the land sink. The correction is small, about 0.07 GtC per year, but it is a reminder that inland waters are not just pipes; they are an active part of the carbon cycle. After these corrections, the net land sink over 2014–2023 drops by 31%, from 2.1 to 1.4 GtC per year, and the ocean now takes up about 15% more carbon than the land does. The imbalance falls to nearly zero and its trend is no longer significant. Just as important, the revised numbers agree with two independent checks, atmospheric inversions and atmospheric oxygen measurements, which gives more confidence that the budget is now right for the right reasons. Climate change is weakening the sinks With a budget that closes, the authors could ask a sharper question: how much has climate change itself reduced the sinks? Using model runs with rising CO₂ but a constant climate, they estimate that warming and changing rainfall reduced the land sink by about 23% and the ocean sink by about 6% over the last decade. Since 1960 this has left about 30 GtC more in the atmosphere, or 8.3 ppm, which is roughly 8% of the observed CO₂ rise. The effect is largest in the tropics. The combined pressure of climate change and deforestation has turned the tropical forests of Southeast Asia and large parts of South America from sinks into sources. In South America, the main cause is now climate stress on the forest rather than clearing. The year 2024 showed what this looks like in a single year. During the 2023–2024 El Niño, the land sink dropped to 1.9 GtC, and the atmospheric CO₂ growth rate hit a record 3.7 ppm. For those of us who study droughts and evapotranspiration, this is the part of the carbon budget that is really a water story: when land ecosystems run short of water, they stop absorbing carbon. What the remaining carbon budget means Warming depends, to a good approximation, on cumulative CO₂ emissions, not on the emission rate in any one year. The Global Carbon Budget 2025 puts it simply: every additional 180 GtCO₂ adds about 0.1°C of warming. That is why we can speak of a carbon budget at all. It works less like a speed limit and more like a reservoir: what matters is the total volume released, and once it is released it stays released. From January 2026, the remaining budgets for a 50% chance of staying below each warming level are: 1.5°C: about 170 GtCO₂, roughly 4 years at the 2025 emission rate; 1.7°C: about 525 GtCO₂, roughly 12 years; 2.0°C: about 1,055 GtCO₂, roughly 25 years. Figure 2. Remaining CO₂ budgets from January 2026 for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5, 1.7 and 2.0°C. The two lighter bars are two published estimates, each updated to 2026; the dark bar is their average, used in the Global Carbon Budget 2025. The top axis converts the budgets into years at the 2025 emission rate. The dashed line marks the cumulative emissions of a straight-line path from today to net zero in 2050. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Friedlingstein et al. (2026b). Three things are worth noting. First, the estimates differ a lot, especially for 1.5°C (90 versus 250 GtCO₂), mainly because of how the warming from other gases such as methane is modeled. In an earlier post on overshoot I used a UNEP figure of 130 GtCO₂; it sits inside this range. Deng et al. (2025), using different starting points, go as far as to say that the 1.5°C budget may already be used up. Second, at today’s emission rate, warming increases by about 0.023°C every year, or about a quarter of a degree per decade. The budget does not tell us when 1.5°C will be crossed in a given year, but it does tell us how fast the long-term level is rising. Third, even a demanding plan does not fit inside the 1.5°C budget. Reaching net zero CO₂ by 2050 in a straight line would mean cutting emissions by about 1.7 GtCO₂, or 4%, every year. That is similar to the drop in 2020 during the COVID-19 lockdowns, repeated every year for 25 years. Even so, it would add about 520 GtCO₂ along the way: three times the 1.5°C budget, but just within the budget for 1.7°C. Warming stops only when net CO₂ emissions reach zero; cutting them slows warming but does not stop it. Who emits what Deng et al. (2025) use near-real-time activity data from the Carbon Monitor project to break down fossil CO₂ emissions by sector. Their total for 2024 is 36.3 GtCO₂, a little lower than the Global Carbon Project’s 37.8 GtCO₂, because the two datasets are built differently. Figure 3. Fossil CO₂ emissions by sector in 2024 from the Carbon Monitor project, as shares of the 36.3 GtCO₂ total. Land-use change emissions in 2024 from the Global Carbon Budget 2025 are shown separately for comparison; they come from a different dataset and are not part of the 36.3 GtCO₂. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Deng et al. (2025) and Friedlingstein et al. (2026b). Power generation is the largest single source at 38.7%, followed by industry at 28.5%, ground transport at 18.7% and residential use at 9.4%. Aviation and shipping together are under 5%, but international aviation grew fastest in 2024, by almost 10%. By fuel, the Global Carbon Project attributes 41% of fossil CO₂ to coal, 32% to oil, 21% to natural gas and 4% to cement. Land-use change adds roughly another 4.8 GtCO₂. How much could each sector cut? This is where I want to be careful. None of the three papers estimates how far each sector could cut its emissions. What they do provide are pieces of evidence about where cuts are already happening and where they are not. Power is where the tools already work. Deng et al. estimate that hydro, nuclear, wind and solar electricity avoided 9.8 GtCO₂ in 2024 compared with generating the same electricity from fossil fuels, with solar output up 25% in one year. Using projections from the International Energy Agency, they estimate a further 682 GtCO₂ could be avoided between 2025 and 2050, mostly by wind and solar. Stopping deforestation is the largest single lever on land. Gross emissions from deforestation are about 1.9 GtC (about 7 GtCO₂) per year, of which regrowth and afforestation offset about two thirds. Brazil, Indonesia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo account for more than half of net land-use emissions. Growth without more CO₂ is possible. Between 2015 and 2024, 35 countries cut their fossil CO₂ emissions while their economies grew, nearly twice as many as in the previous decade. Together they produce 27% of global fossil emissions. Industry and aviation are the hard part. Deng et al. point to heavy industry and aviation as sectors whose emissions are still rising; they are widely regarded as the hardest to decarbonize. For sector-by-sector potentials, the standard reference is the IPCC’s mitigation report, which concluded that options costing 100 US dollars per tonne of CO₂-equivalent or less could reduce global greenhouse gas emissions by at least half of the 2019 level by 2030 (IPCC 2022). That is a statement about what is technically and economically available, not about what is happening. What a hydrologist takes from it Closing the budget matters. The improvement in this year’s carbon budget came not from new satellites but from adding known processes and checking the result against independent data. It is the same discipline we try to teach in catchment hydrology: if the balance does not close, something is missing, and the residual is telling you what. The land sink is a water problem. The weakening of the land sink is concentrated in the tropics and shows up in drought years. Better estimates of evapotranspiration and soil moisture are not only a matter of water supply; they are part of predicting how much CO₂ stays in the air. Inland waters belong in the carbon cycle. Rivers, lakes and reservoirs emit, bury and transport carbon, and human activity has changed all three. That is a research frontier where hydrologists have something to offer. Bottom line Humans emit about 41 GtCO₂ per year. Half stays in the atmosphere; the ocean takes up 29% and land 21%. After corrections, the land sink is weaker and the ocean sink stronger than previously thought, and the budget now closes. Climate change has already reduced the land sink by about a quarter and the ocean sink by about 6%, adding about 8 ppm to atmospheric CO₂ since 1960. At current emissions, the 1.5°C budget lasts about 4 more years, the 1.7°C budget about 12 and the 2°C budget about 25. Power and industry emit about two thirds of fossil CO₂. Power has proven alternatives; industry and aviation do not yet. Questions to think about The carbon budget and the catchment water balance both have an imbalance term. In your own catchment, which water balance term would you suspect first if the balance did not close, and why? The land sink dropped sharply in the 2023–2024 El Niño. What hydrological variables would you monitor to anticipate such a drop? If every 180 GtCO₂ adds 0.1°C, how much additional warming is implied by a straight-line path to net zero in 2050? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 지구 탄소 순환은 물수지처럼 하나의 질량수지로 읽을 수 있다. 『Global Carbon Budget 2025』에 따르면 최근 10년(2015–2024) 동안 인류는 해마다 약 41 GtCO₂를 배출했고(화석연료 88%, 토지이용 변화 12%), 그중 절반은 대기에 남고 29%는 해양이, 21%는 육상 생태계가 흡수했다. 함께 발표된 『Nature』 논문은 그동안 빠져 있던 과정(현재 산림의 더 높은 탄소 밀도, 줄어든 산림 면적, 하천·호수로의 탄소 유출, 해수면 냉피층 효과)을 반영해 육상 흡수원은 이전 추정보다 약하고 해양 흡수원은 더 강하다는 것을 보였고, 그 결과 수지가 거의 맞게 되었다. 기후변화가 없었을 경우와 비교하면, 최근 10년 동안 육상 생태계는 약 23%, 해양은 약 6% 적게 CO₂를 흡수했다. 1960년 이후 이렇게 덜 흡수된 CO₂가 쌓여 대기 CO₂ 농도를 약 8 ppm 더 높였다. 2026년 초부터 남은 탄소예산(50% 확률)은 1.5°C 기준 약 170 GtCO₂로 현재 배출 속도로 약 4년, 1.7°C는 약 12년, 2°C는 약 25년 분량이다. 화석 CO₂ 배출의 부문별 비중(2024)은 발전 38.7%, 산업 28.5%, 도로 수송 18.7%, 가정 9.4% 순이다. 발전 부문은 재생에너지라는 검증된 대안이 있고 산림 파괴를 멈추는 것도 큰 감축 수단이지만, 산업과 항공은 아직 어렵다. 세 논문은 부문별 감축 가능량을 직접 추정하지 않으며, 이는 IPCC 보고서의 몫이다. title: Does living through extreme weather make people act on climate?
description: A new Registered Report in Nature Climate Change linked 1,451 Americans' real carbon choices to the extreme weather recorded in their counties. Party affiliation shaped what people paid attention to; the weather itself did not, unless people read it as climate change.
tags: climate action extreme weather risk perception climate communication
text: After every major flood or heatwave, someone says it: this time people will finally take climate change seriously. I have heard it in Korea after the Seoul floods of 2022 and the Osong underpass disaster of 2023. The idea is appealing to those of us who study water, because it suggests that the hazards we measure will do the persuading for us. If extreme weather is becoming more frequent, then more people will experience it, and experience will turn into action. A new paper in Nature Climate Change by Annika Wyss, Emmanuel Guizar Rosales and colleagues at the universities of Bern, Basel and Lüneburg tests this idea more carefully than most (Wyss et al. 2026). Their answer is uncomfortable but useful: in the United States, what people experienced mattered much less than how they interpreted it, and political affiliation shaped both what people looked at and what they chose. How the study was done Two features of the design make this paper worth reading closely. First, it is a Registered Report. The authors submitted their hypotheses, methods and analysis plan to the journal before collecting any data, and the journal accepted the study in principle on that basis (the Stage 1 protocol was accepted in July 2025). The data were collected in August and September 2025. Because publication did not depend on the results, the paper reports its null findings as plainly as its positive ones. This matters here, since several of the main hypotheses turned out not to be supported. Second, the choices were real, and the researchers could watch how people made them. About 2,000 US adults, quota-matched to the population by party, age, sex and region, completed 30 trials of a “Carbon Emission Task.” In each trial they chose between two options: one paid a larger bonus but caused more carbon emissions, the other paid less but emitted less. On average a bonus was about 60 US cents and the emissions about 20 pounds (9 kg) of CO₂. One trial was picked at random and carried out: the bonus was paid, and emission certificates were bought and retired to match the emissions. The information was hidden behind boxes that opened only when the cursor hovered over them, so the researchers could measure how long each person looked at the money and how long at the carbon. After strict quality checks, 1,451 participants remained. Each participant’s county was then matched to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Storm Events Database. A person counted as exposed if at least one episode of excessive heat, drought, wildfire, flash flood, coastal flood, hail, strong wind or tornado was recorded in their county in the 30 days before the study. Participants also reported which events they had experienced themselves, and how strongly they believed that extreme weather is caused by climate change (their subjective attribution). Finding 1: party shapes attention, not only choice Democrats made more pro-climate choices than Republicans, with roughly twice the odds of choosing the low-carbon option (odds ratio 2.06). That part is not surprising. The new result is that the difference already appears before the choice, while people are gathering information. Democrats spent a larger share of their looking time on the carbon numbers, about four percentage points more than Republicans. One obvious explanation can be ruled out. Republicans might simply distrust emission certificates. They did not: both groups rated the certificates as equally effective (4.13 and 4.10 on a five-point scale). The partisan gap is in where attention goes, not in beliefs about whether the mechanism works. Finding 2: recorded extreme weather did not change the picture The authors expected recent exposure to extreme weather to widen the partisan gap, as some earlier studies had found. It did not. Exposure did not increase attention to carbon, and it did not change the difference between Democrats and Republicans. The result held across event types and across exposure windows from one to twelve months, and the authors also report equivalence tests for these null results. Something else in the data is telling. In the final sample, Republicans were slightly more likely to have been exposed to a recorded event (48.2% against 43.4%). Yet Democrats reported having experienced more extreme weather. The same kind of storm record was turned into different memories by different people. Figure 1. Three steps between a storm and a belief, by party, for the 1,451 participants in the final sample. Panel 1 shows extreme weather recorded in each participant’s county by NOAA. Panel 2 shows the extreme weather participants said they had experienced (a log-transformed count). Panel 3 shows how strongly they attributed extreme weather to climate change. Republicans were slightly more often exposed, yet Democrats reported more experience and linked it to climate change more strongly. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from group values reported in Wyss et al. (2026). The authors put it in a phrase I find helpful: political affiliation may act as a perceptual filter that shapes how environmental experiences are encoded in memory. Finding 3: interpretation is what matters Subjective attribution, the belief that extreme weather is caused by climate change, was linked to more attention to carbon and more pro-climate choices, over and above party. Two interactions refine the picture. The partisan gap grew with attribution. It was largest among people who most strongly attributed extreme weather to climate change. Exposure helped only among people who did not already make the link. For people with low attribution, recent extreme weather was associated with more attention to carbon. For people with high attribution, it was associated with less. The authors offer two explanations: people who already care may have no more attention to give (a ceiling effect), or they may turn away from threatening information (avoidance). The study cannot tell which. The hypothesis that tied all three factors together, that exposure would widen the partisan gap most among strong attributors, was not supported. Figure 2. Odds ratios, with 95% confidence intervals, for choosing the low-carbon option, as reported in the paper. Values above 1 mean a higher chance of the pro-climate choice. The first five rows come from the models that include subjective attribution, so the exposure row is the effect of recorded extreme weather for a person with average attribution. The last row comes from a separate exploratory model with self-reported experience. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Wyss et al. (2026). Figure 2 summarizes the choice results. Party and attribution push toward the low-carbon option. Self-reported experience does too. Recorded exposure, for a person with average attribution, does not: if anything it goes the other way. What I take from it as a hydrologist A gauge record is not an experience. In hydrology we describe a flood by its peak discharge and its return period. Those numbers are what our infrastructure is designed for, and they are the right numbers for that purpose. But people do not experience a 100-year flood; they experience a flooded street, a closed road, or a news report, and they file it under an explanation they already hold. This study is a reminder that the hazard we measure and the experience that shapes behavior are different quantities. The link between them runs through interpretation. Event attribution is part of the service, not an extra. Climate science can now say, within days of an event, how much more likely or intense climate change made it. This study, together with earlier work, suggests that this kind of information is where the leverage lies. In the United Kingdom, flood experience predicted support for mitigation only among people who attributed the floods to climate change (Ogunbode et al. 2019). In California, wildfire exposure increased pro-environment voting only in Democratic areas (Hazlett & Mildenberger 2020). A survey of nearly 72,000 people in 68 countries found the same pattern: attributing extreme weather to climate change was linked to support for climate policy, while exposure to most types of extreme weather was not (Cologna et al. 2025). For those of us who provide climate services, for example drought information for farmers, explaining why an event happened may be as important as reporting that it happened. Do not wait for disasters to do the persuading. People’s sense of “normal weather” also adapts quickly: a study of social media posts found that the reference point is set by the weather of only the past few years, so repeated anomalies soon stop being remarkable (Moore et al. 2019). Put together with this paper, the hope that more frequent extremes will eventually convince everyone looks weak. It is the same lesson as in my earlier post on the Atlantic overturning circulation: by the time the evidence is felt directly, much is already locked in. Limits worth keeping in mind The study is careful, but its scope is narrow. One country, two parties. US politics is unusually polarized on climate. Independents were asked which party they lean toward and classified accordingly. The results may not carry over to Korea or Europe, where views on climate may be less tied to party identity. Small stakes. Each choice involved cents and a few kilograms of CO₂. That is far from the decisions that matter most, such as buying a car, voting, or supporting a flood-defense levy. Attribution was measured, not manipulated. The study shows that attribution is associated with attention and choice; it does not show that changing someone’s attribution would change their behavior. County-level exposure is a proxy. A storm recorded somewhere in a large county may never touch a given resident, which could dilute any real effect of exposure. About a quarter of the sample was excluded under the pre-registered quality rules, although analyses with the full sample gave similar conclusions. Bottom line Political affiliation shapes not only what people choose but what they look at while choosing. Recent extreme weather recorded in people’s counties did not, by itself, increase attention to carbon or pro-climate choices, and it did not widen the partisan gap. What mattered was interpretation: people who see extreme weather as a consequence of climate change paid more attention to carbon and chose the low-carbon option more often. For scientists and engineers, the practical message is that hazard data need a story that connects them to their causes. Exposure alone is unlikely to do the work. Questions to think about Republicans in this sample were more often exposed to recorded extreme weather, yet reported less of it. What could explain the difference between a recorded event and a remembered one? A flood frequency analysis treats a 100-year flood as the same event wherever it occurs. What would a “perceived return period” look like, and how could it differ between two communities hit by the same flood? If you were designing a drought early-warning bulletin for farmers, how would you include attribution information without making the bulletin feel political? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 극한기상을 직접 겪으면 사람들이 기후행동에 나설까? 스위스·독일 연구진은 미국 성인 1,451명에게 실제 탄소배출이 걸린 선택 실험을 했다(Nature Climate Change 등록보고서). 참가자는 보너스를 더 받는 대신 탄소를 더 배출하는 선택지와, 보너스를 덜 받는 대신 탄소를 덜 배출하는 선택지 중 하나를 골랐다. 연구진은 이 선택을 각자가 사는 카운티에 최근 30일간 기록된 극한기상(NOAA 자료)과 연결해 분석했다. 민주당 지지자는 공화당 지지자보다 돈을 덜 받더라도 탄소배출이 적은 쪽(저탄소 선택)을 고르는 경우가 뚜렷이 많았다. 그 차이는 선택하기 전 정보를 살펴보는 단계에서부터 나타나, 민주당 지지자가 탄소 정보를 더 오래 들여다보았다. 반면 실제로 기록된 극한기상 노출은 탄소 정보에 대한 주의도, 저탄소 선택도 늘리지 않았고 당파 간 차이도 키우지 않았다. 오히려 공화당 지지자가 극한기상에 조금 더 자주 노출되었는데도, 겪었다고 보고한 경험은 민주당 지지자가 더 많았다. 결정적인 것은 해석이었다. 극한기상을 기후변화의 결과로 받아들이는 사람일수록 탄소 정보에 더 주의를 기울이고 저탄소 선택을 더 많이 했다. 관측된 재해와 사람들이 경험하는 재해는 서로 다른 양이다. 재해가 저절로 사람들을 설득해 주기를 기다리기보다, 사건의 원인(기후변화 기여도)을 함께 설명하는 기후서비스와 소통이 중요하다. title: Will the Atlantic overturning tip, and how fast would we feel it?
description: A check-up on the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation based on two new papers: what the observations show, why the models are probably too optimistic, why the speed of emissions matters, and whether a collapse would be sudden or slow.
tags: amoc ocean circulation tipping points climate change sea level
text: Every few months, a headline warns that the Gulf Stream is about to “shut down.” Many readers picture the film The Day After Tomorrow, where New York freezes in a week. The real science is less cinematic but no less serious. Two recent papers from the Utrecht group of Henk Dijkstra and René van Westen give a good picture of where things stand. The first is a review of how likely a collapse is this century (Dijkstra & van Westen 2026). The second is a new modeling study showing that the speed of warming may matter more than its final level (van Westen, Börner & Dijkstra 2026). In this post I read the two papers as a diagnosis: what we know about the patient now, what could go wrong, and above all how fast. When students ask me about this topic, the question behind the question is usually: is this something sudden, or something people would only feel slowly over a long time? The short answer is that it is both, on different clocks. The rest of this post explains what that means. What the AMOC is, and why a hydrologist should care The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is the large loop of the Atlantic Ocean in which warm, salty surface water flows north, gives up its heat to the atmosphere, becomes dense enough to sink in the northern North Atlantic, and returns south at depth. Its strength is measured in sverdrups (1 Sv = one million cubic meters per second). At about 17 Sv, it moves roughly fifteen times the combined discharge of all the world’s rivers. At 26°N it carries about 1.5 petawatts of heat northward, which is a large part of the reason north-western Europe is so mild for its latitude. The reason the AMOC can “tip” is a feedback any water engineer will recognize as a positive feedback loop. The overturning brings salt north. If the northern Atlantic becomes fresher (from more rain, river runoff, sea-ice melt or Greenland meltwater), the surface water becomes lighter, sinks less, and the weaker circulation delivers less salt. This freshens the surface further. Beyond a critical point, the loop can run away and the circulation settles into a much weaker state. Physicists call this the salt-advection feedback, and it is why the AMOC can have two stable states rather than one. Diagnosis 1: what the observations say Direct, continuous measurements are surprisingly recent. The RAPID array at 26°N has been running only since 2004. Over 2004–2024 it shows a mean strength of about 16.9 ± 1.2 Sv, with a decline from 2005 to 2012 and a partial recovery afterwards. Arrays further north (OSNAP at 53–57°N and NOAC at 47°N) give similar values of about 17 Sv. Longer records are indirect, and they do not agree with one another: A sea-surface temperature “fingerprint” (the cold patch south of Greenland, which has warmed less than the rest of the ocean) suggests the AMOC has weakened by about 3 Sv since 1950. Proxy records suggest it may now be at its weakest in more than a thousand years. Hydrographic sections show no long-term decline over 1982–2016. A recent reconstruction from air–sea heat fluxes finds no weakening at 26°N since the 1960s. Verdict: there is no clear observational evidence that a collapse has started. There is also no evidence that would rule one out. Twenty years of direct data is a short record for a system whose natural variability spans decades. Diagnosis 2: what the models say, and why they are probably too optimistic The IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report projects that the AMOC will weaken during this century under every emission scenario, with most CMIP6 models giving a 34–45% decline by 2100. It also states, with medium confidence, that there will be no abrupt collapse before 2100. The review explains why that reassurance should be read carefully. The climate models used by the IPCC have well-known biases that make their AMOC too stable. The most important is the freshwater carried by the overturning across 34°S, a quantity called FovS. Its sign is a useful indicator of whether the AMOC sits in the regime where a collapsed state is possible. Observations and ocean reanalyses put FovS in that regime, but very few CMIP6 models reproduce both the observed FovS and the observed AMOC strength. Many also have overturning cells that are too shallow and carry too little heat. The Utrecht group’s own model illustrates the problem. To make the AMOC collapse in their version of the Community Earth System Model (CESM), they had to add freshwater at about 65 times the present-day melt rate of the Greenland Ice Sheet. They interpret this not as a sign that the real AMOC is safe, but as a sign that the model is biased. In their words, the real AMOC is probably closer to a tipping point, and the extra freshwater should be thought of as a bias correction. What about the probability of a collapse? The honest answer from the review is that no adequate estimate exists yet. One widely reported statistical study put the onset of collapse at 2057, with a 90% range of 2025–2095 (Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen 2023), but other researchers have shown that the temperature data used to reconstruct the AMOC carry uncertainties too large for such a prediction. Early-warning indicators based on rising variance are known to give false alarms. A simple box model gives a probability of about 15% for a noise-driven transition, but only within that model. The review makes one more point that engineers will appreciate: because the impacts are so large, even a probability as small as 10−4 matters. We design dam spillways for floods with an annual probability of 1 in 10,000. A climate system with a similar chance of a severe failure deserves the same seriousness. Diagnosis 3: it is the speed, not only the level The commonly cited warming threshold for an AMOC collapse is about +4°C, with a range of 1.4–8°C. The new Nature Climate Change paper argues that this number may not mean much, because the AMOC’s stability depends on how fast the climate is forced, not on a fixed temperature. The authors increased CO₂ in the CESM linearly at three rates, all the way to four times the pre-industrial level: at +0.5 ppm per year, the AMOC stayed strong even when global warming reached +5.5°C; at +2.5 and +5.0 ppm per year, it began to collapse at about +2.0°C. For comparison, CO₂ at Mauna Loa rose by about +2.6 ppm per year on average in 2015–2025. In this model, today’s rate falls on the wrong side of the line. Figure 1. Global warming at which the AMOC began to collapse in three CO₂-ramp experiments with one climate model (CESM, with a freshwater bias correction of 0.45 Sv). Under the slowest ramp the AMOC did not collapse, even at +5.5°C. The dashed line marks the observed rate of CO₂ increase. The bar on the right is the commonly cited warming threshold and its range. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in van Westen, Börner & Dijkstra (2026). Why should the rate matter? When the forcing is slow, the deep ocean has time to adjust together with the surface. In a warmer climate, evaporation over the Atlantic increases and there is less North Atlantic sea ice, so less meltwater is released into the sinking region. Both effects make the Atlantic saltier and help keep the circulation going. When the forcing is fast, the surface water becomes lighter much faster than the interior can follow, the pathways by which water sinks shut down, and the circulation collapses before these stabilizing effects can act. Hydrologists know this logic well. The same storm total can produce no runoff when it falls as gentle rain over a week, and a flood when it falls in an hour, because infiltration cannot keep up. It is the intensity, not only the depth, that decides. The same model under standard emission scenarios tells a consistent story. Under a low-emission pathway (RCP2.6) the AMOC weakens and then recovers. Under moderate emissions (RCP4.5) collapse begins around 2110, at +2.2°C. Under high emissions (RCP8.5) it begins around 2060, at +2.8°C. The authors combine these results with CMIP6 analyses and estimate a critical warming rate of about 0.29°C per decade. This lies within the 0.27–0.36°C per decade projected for the coming decades. Their conclusion is direct: cutting emissions quickly is what reduces the risk. What a collapse would do The cleanest way to study the impacts is to collapse the AMOC in a model run without global warming, so that the AMOC signal is not mixed with everything else. In the CESM, the results include: North-western Europe gets much colder. Sea-surface temperatures near western Europe drop by as much as 10°C. Over a broad region, annual-mean air temperature falls by more than 1°C per decade, and several European cities cool by 5–15°C. Arctic sea ice in March extends as far south as about 50°N, and the extra ice reflects more sunlight, amplifying the cooling. The Southern Hemisphere warms. Less heat is carried north, so the two hemispheres move in opposite directions (the “bipolar seesaw”). Sea level rises along Atlantic coasts. A weaker circulation changes the slope of the sea surface, and some coastal regions see more than 70 cm of additional dynamic sea-level rise, on top of the global rise from warming. Tropical rain belts shift south. The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) moves southward and the Northern Hemisphere Hadley cell strengthens. In the Amazon, the dry season and the wet season trade places. In a warming world, part of the European cooling would be offset by greenhouse warming, so the temperature numbers above are an upper picture. The sea-level signal, however, looks similar regardless of when the collapse happens. Outside Europe, the review notes that significant changes appear mainly in particular months, not across the whole year. For East Asia, including Korea, the regional details are still model-dependent, so I will not pretend to more precision than the papers give. From a water perspective, the ITCZ shift is the part that worries me most. The tropical rain belt feeds some of the world’s largest rivers and supports the agriculture of hundreds of millions of people. A shift of the seasons, rather than a change in the annual total, is exactly what our reservoir rules, irrigation calendars and flood seasons are not designed for. It would also mean that the statistics we use to design infrastructure would stop describing the future, a problem hydrologists summarize as “stationarity is dead.” So, sudden or gradual? Three clocks Here is my answer to the students’ question. An AMOC collapse runs on three clocks with very different speeds. Figure 2. Timescales involved in a possible AMOC collapse. The gray rows show the short observational record and a contested statistical estimate of collapse onset. The colored rows show one climate model (CESM, bias-corrected) under three emission scenarios: triangles mark collapse onset, the fading bars show the decline over about a century, and the solid bars show the persistent weak state. This is a schematic of published numbers, not a forecast. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on Dijkstra & van Westen (2026), van Westen, Börner & Dijkstra (2026) and Ditlevsen & Ditlevsen (2023). Clock 1: the trigger (now to the next few decades). Whether a collapse starts is decided by what we emit, and how fast, over the next few decades. In the one model that has been pushed hardest, onset comes in the second half of this century or early next. The IPCC considers an abrupt collapse before 2100 unlikely, but that judgment rests on models that are probably too stable. Nobody can yet give a reliable probability. Clock 2: the fall (about a century). Once a collapse begins, the circulation declines over roughly a hundred years. That rules out the Day After Tomorrow picture. Nothing freezes overnight, and from one year to the next the change would be smaller than ordinary weather variability. Yet by the standards of climate it is fast. A cooling trend of more than 1°C per decade in north-western Europe is about four times faster than today’s global warming, and in the opposite direction. People would not feel a shock, but over a working career they would see a clear trend, much as we see global warming today. A child born this year could live through most of the decline. Clock 3: the memory (centuries). A collapsed AMOC does not come back when emissions stop. In the CESM runs, the AMOC is still very weak in 2500, and the authors note that even if it eventually recovered, its impacts would last for at least about 300 years. Conceptual models suggest an asymmetry: a collapse can be set off relatively quickly, but recovery needs the North Atlantic to be slowly made saltier again. On any human timescale, a collapse would be permanent. There is one more, uncomfortable timing problem. Because the direct record is short and natural variability is large, we would probably recognize a collapse only after it was well under way, and by then it would already be locked in. The decision has to be made before the evidence is conclusive. It is the same lesson as in my earlier post on overshooting 1.5°C: the consequences arrive long after the causes, so waiting for certainty is itself a choice. Bottom line Current state: the AMOC is about 17 Sv, with no clear sign that a collapse has begun, but only about 20 years of direct data and conflicting indirect evidence. Risk: probably underestimated, because the models used by the IPCC tend to make the AMOC too stable. No reliable probability exists, and even small probabilities matter. Main control: the rate of warming. In one model, the current rate of CO₂ increase is fast enough to cause a collapse at about +2°C, while a much slower rise does not cause one even at +5.5°C. Timescale: decades to the trigger, about a century to fall, centuries to recover. A collapse would be gradual enough to feel like a trend, fast enough to outrun adaptation, and lasting enough to be permanent for us. Questions to think about The salt-advection feedback is a positive feedback. Can you name a positive feedback in a catchment or a river channel, and what keeps it from running away? Why might the same total amount of warming be safe when it is slow and dangerous when it is fast? Try explaining it using infiltration-excess runoff. If you were designing a coastal drainage system on the US East Coast with a 100-year design life, how would you treat a low-probability, high-impact scenario such as an extra 70 cm of dynamic sea-level rise? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 대서양 자오선 순환(AMOC)은 현재 약 17 Sv로, 붕괴가 시작되었다는 뚜렷한 관측 증거는 없지만 직접 관측 기록은 20년 남짓에 불과하다. IPCC는 2100년 이전의 급격한 붕괴 가능성을 낮게 보지만, 기후모델들은 AMOC를 실제보다 안정적으로 모의하는 경향이 있어 위험이 과소평가되었을 가능성이 크다. 최신 연구에 따르면 붕괴 여부는 도달하는 온도보다 온난화 속도에 좌우된다: 한 모델에서 CO₂가 연 0.5 ppm씩 오르면 +5.5°C에서도 버텼지만, 연 2.5 ppm 이상(현재는 연 2.6 ppm)에서는 약 +2°C에서 붕괴가 시작되었다. 붕괴하면 북서유럽이 10년에 1°C 이상 냉각되고, 대서양 연안 해수면이 최대 70 cm 이상 추가로 오르며, 열대 강우대가 남쪽으로 이동해 아마존의 건기와 우기가 뒤바뀐다. 시간 규모로 보면 붕괴가 시작될지는 향후 수십 년의 배출이 결정하고, 붕괴 자체는 약 100년에 걸쳐 진행되며(하룻밤에 일어나는 일은 아니지만 한 사람의 일생 동안 분명히 느낄 만큼 빠르다), 그 영향은 수백 년간 지속된다. 관측으로 확인될 즈음에는 이미 되돌리기 어려울 가능성이 크므로, 확실한 증거를 기다리기보다 배출을 빨리 줄이는 것이 핵심이다. title: From chatbot to coworker: three years of LLMs in hydrology
description: Re-reading a 2023 editorial on ChatGPT in hydrology next to two new papers and a book on AI: what LLMs could not do then, what agents can do now, and why most research has not switched yet.
tags: llm ai agents hydrologic modeling calibration education
text: In September 2023, Water Resources Research published an editorial by Foroumandi and colleagues titled “ChatGPT in Hydrology and Earth Sciences: Opportunities, Prospects, and Concerns.” It was one of the first careful attempts by our community to say what these tools were good for and where they should be kept away. Three years and several model generations later, it is worth reading again next to two recent hydrology papers and Christopher Summerfield’s book These Strange New Minds. Together they show how quickly the question has changed: from “can it write a correct loop?” to “can it run a 531-basin experiment overnight, and should we let it?” 2023: a useful but unreliable writing partner The 2023 editorial was balanced, and most of its observations held up. ChatGPT was good at beginner-to-intermediate coding (reading and cleaning data, explaining syntax, translating between languages, adding comments), at polishing prose for non-native writers, and at summarizing text. The problems began with anything harder: Complex code. In one test, after several rounds of error messages, the model “fixed” a shape mismatch in a deep-learning script by inserting an array of zeros. The code ran, and the answer was meaningless. Unstable physics. Asked how shortwave radiation affects precipitation in humid regions, it gave one plausible explanation, then reversed itself as soon as the authors said it was wrong. Invented references. All three citations it supplied for that answer turned out not to exist. Arguing a bad case. When asked to help convince a reviewer that an uncalibrated model was valid, it obliged with persuasive talking points. Frozen knowledge. It had no internet access and knew nothing after its training cutoff. The authors’ conclusion was that ChatGPT was a compiler rather than an author, and their recommendations followed from that: never use it as the sole source of information, disclose its use, keep teaching programming so researchers can check AI-written code, and redesign assignments around critical thinking. One recommendation aged badly. AI-text detectors were suggested for screening manuscripts, but they proved unreliable; OpenAI withdrew its own classifier in 2023 because of low accuracy. The rest still reads as sound advice, and some of it has become more important, not less. What changed: from answering to acting The biggest change since 2023 is not that models know more hydrology, although they do. It is that they can now act. Current assistants search the web, read and write files, run code, see the errors, and try again. Open standards such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP) let a model call external tools in a structured way. “Agentic” coding tools can take a goal, plan the steps, edit a whole project and test the result with little hand-holding. I built this website that way, by describing what I wanted and reviewing what came back. The market has changed too. ChatGPT is now one of many: Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen and Moonshot’s Kimi compete closely, and several strong models have openly released weights. Competition has moved from raw capability toward cost. By one industry index, frontier token prices in late 2026 are about 85% below their March 2023 level, and open-weight models are typically far cheaper than proprietary ones, although the newest frontier models have become more expensive again over the past year. For agents, which can consume more than a million tokens per task, cost per task now matters as much as cost per token. The figure below summarizes how the role of the LLM has shifted across the three hydrology papers discussed here. Figure 1. How the role of the LLM changed across three studies. In 2023 the human did all the running and checking. In the GRL study, the LLM proposed parameters inside a loop built by the researchers. In the Journal of Hydrology study, agents planned, coded, ran and debugged entire modeling workflows within an expert-designed process. Original schematic by Daeha Kim, based on Foroumandi et al. (2023), Zhu et al. (2026) and Li et al. (2026). 2025: the LLM inside the calibration loop Zhu et al. (2026, Geophysical Research Letters) asked whether an LLM could replace the optimization algorithm in calibrating the VIC model for a sub-basin of the Yangtze. Judging from the models tested (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-V3 and two Llama models) and the submission date of October 2025, the experiments reflect LLMs of roughly mid-2025. The researchers wrote a Python program that ran VIC, computed NSE, RMSE and bias, and sent the results and hydrograph to the LLM, which proposed the next parameter set. The LLM never ran or imitated the model; it only made the decisions that SCE-UA or NSGA-III would normally make. The result was mixed in an informative way. DeepSeek-R1 reached an NSE of about 0.89 within roughly 200 iterations and matched SCE-UA’s best NSE using fewer model runs. It also focused early on the parameters hydrologists know to be sensitive, such as infiltration shape and soil depth. The other four models did worse than the standard algorithms. One basin, one model and six parameters is a small test, and “fewer iterations” says nothing about API cost or about whether the result repeats on a second run. But it showed that a reasoning model could act like a sensible, if inexperienced, calibrator. 2026: agents that build the whole workflow Li et al. (2026, Journal of Hydrology), submitted in May 2026, used the next generation of models: GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2 and Qwen-Plus. Their system, HydroAIM, uses several cooperating agents connected through MCP. Given a task, the agents prepare the data, write and run the training code, read the error messages, fix them and evaluate the result, all without a human in the loop. Three findings stand out. It works most of the time. Across 125 modeling tasks with five different LLMs, 92.8% of runs succeeded. On 531 CAMELS basins, the agent-built models reached a median NSE of 0.58 for basin-by-basin LSTMs (close to the 0.61 of the calibrated SAC-SMA benchmark) and 0.73 for a single LSTM trained on all basins, which is in line with published LSTM benchmarks. Planning, not knowledge, is the bottleneck. When the researchers removed the expert-designed workflow and let the agents organize the task themselves, the success rate fell to 0%. Agents declared victory after one sub-step, looped on the same tool calls, or lost track of file paths after their context was summarized. Experts are still needed. In one run, weak performance turned out to come from a data-loading error that withheld same-day weather inputs. When prompts pushed the agents toward “bigger” architectures, they switched to models that performed worse. Newer versions of some models also had to be used partway through the study, which makes exact reproduction harder. The cost appendix of the same paper makes the price competition concrete. A successful end-to-end run used between half a million and two million tokens, and the price of that run differed by a factor of 25 to 45 depending on the model, even though all five models completed the tasks at similar rates. Figure 2. API cost of one representative successful run for each LLM and each of five task types. Data from Table A1 of Li et al. (2026); plotted by Daeha Kim. Costs reflect list prices at the time of the study and will change. Checking a book’s predictions Christopher Summerfield, a cognitive neuroscientist, wrote These Strange New Minds in 2024. His closing chapter makes a few claims that are easy to check against what has happened since. He argued that LLMs are not minds like ours: they have no body, no friends and no motivation of their own, and so no built-in curiosity about the world. Nothing in the papers above contradicts that. In both studies, the question, the data, the success criterion and the judgment of what counts as physically plausible all came from people. He identified two engineering limits, short memory and weak long-term planning, and expected both to be solved soon. That has partly happened. Assistants now remember across conversations and agents routinely complete multi-step tasks. But the 0% result without an expert workflow shows that open-ended, long-horizon scientific work still breaks down unless someone gives the agent a structure to follow. He predicted that we would drift gradually toward AI that acts rather than merely answers, starting with simple, well-defined tasks. That is exactly the path we have seen. Software was first, because code can be run and tested automatically. Scientific modeling, with its many judgment calls, is following more slowly. He also cited early evidence that AI help lifts the least-skilled workers the most and could act as a leveller. In research, the early picture points the other way. In a 2026 survey of 1,260 social scientists, 81% had used AI chatbots for research, but only 20% used coding agents weekly. Use was concentrated among economists, doctoral students and researchers at top universities. That sample was self-selected, so the true share is probably lower, and I know of no equivalent survey for hydrology. My impression matches it: agentic workflows are still rare in our field. Finally, he warned that forecasts about AI replacing professionals have often been wrong. His example was the 2016 prediction that we would soon stop training radiologists, which has not come true. The hydrology papers suggest a similar story for us. The agents did not replace the hydrologist; they moved the hydrologist’s work from writing code to designing workflows, checking assumptions and judging results. Why most research has not switched yet Agentic tools have spread quickly in software development but slowly in research. I think the reasons are specific to science. Verification costs time. A program that runs is not a program that is right. The zero-array “fix” from 2023 and the missing-forcing bug from 2026 are the same kind of error at different scales. Reproducibility is harder. The same prompt can give different code from day to day, and model versions change underneath you. Li et al. recommend recording model identifiers, prompts, tool definitions and execution logs; few groups do this yet. Costs are real. A single agentic run is cheap, but sensitivity analyses across hundreds of basins add up, and frontier models can cost tens of times more than open ones. You still need to know the craft. To supervise an agent, you need enough coding and enough hydrology to recognize a wrong answer. Ironically, this keeps the people who would benefit most from the tools from trusting them. What I tell students now The 2023 editorial ended with the advice to use AI as a tool for problem-solving, but never to let it solve the problem by itself. In 2026 I would phrase it slightly differently: treat the agent as a fast, tireless junior colleague whose work you must check. Do let agents handle the plumbing: downloading data, reformatting files, plotting, writing tests and rerunning experiments. Do use them to run more checks than you could by hand, such as sensitivity tests, additional basins or alternative model structures. Do not let them choose your research question, your success criterion or your interpretation of the physics. Do not report a number you cannot reproduce. Record the model and version, the prompt and the code that was actually run. Keep learning to code and keep learning hydrology. In 2023 that was needed to fix the AI’s mistakes. In 2026 it is needed to notice them. Questions to think about The GRL study accepted parameter sets based on NSE alone. What could go wrong if an agent optimizes only one metric for you? Why might an agent that cannot plan on its own still succeed when given an expert workflow? What does that suggest about the value of writing down your own modeling procedures? If a cheap model and an expensive model both succeed 90% of the time, what else would you want to know before choosing one for a 500-basin study? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 2023년 WRR editorial은 ChatGPT를 저자가 아니라 편집 도구로 보고, 복잡한 코드, 물리적 설명, 인용에서 믿을 수 없다고 경고했다. 그로부터 3년이 지난 2026년 10월 현재, LLM은 보정(calibration) 루프 안에서 직접 매개변수를 결정하고(GRL), 여러 에이전트가 531개 유역의 LSTM 모형을 처음부터 끝까지 만들어 낼 정도로 발전했다(J. Hydrol.). 하지만 전문가가 직접 설계한 절차가 없으면 성공률은 0%로 떨어졌고, 데이터 오류를 잡아낸 것도 여전히 사람이었다. 연구 현장에서 LLM을 에이전트 방식으로 사용하는 경우가 아직 드문 이유는 검증, 재현성, 비용, 그리고 결과를 판단할 전문성 때문이다. 에이전트 방식의 사용은 앞으로 늘어나겠지만, 학생들에게 필요한 것이 코딩과 수문학에 대한 탄탄한 이해라는 사실은 변함이 없다. 바다 위에서 정확한 방향을 잡도록 도와주는 것은 출렁거리는 파도가 아니라 위치가 변하지 않는 북극성이다. title: Approaching 1.5°C from above
description: What UNEP's Limiting Overshoot report says about exceeding 1.5°C, why every five years of delay costs about 0.1°C, and what a temperature that rises and then falls means for water engineering.
tags: overshoot climate change carbon budget water resources adaptation
text: For most of my career, 1.5°C was a line we were trying not to cross. That framing is about to expire. Human-induced warming is now close to 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels and rising by roughly a quarter of a degree per decade. The United Nations Environment Programme’s new report, Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return (UNEP 2026), starts from a blunt premise: 1.5°C will be exceeded within the next few years. The question is no longer whether we cross it, but how far past it we go, how long we stay there, and whether we can come back. The report’s short answer is that the goal stays the same, but we now have to approach it from above. Here are the messages I think matter most, followed by what they mean for those of us who design and manage water systems. 1. Overshoot is a pathway with stages, not a single event The report describes an “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway in four stages: exceedance (warming passes 1.5°C), peak (warming stops rising once net CO₂ emissions reach zero), decline (warming falls slowly, only if the world removes more CO₂ than it emits for decades), and stabilization. Matching these, it proposes three overlapping response phases: Immediate response: cut emissions fast, especially methane and other short-lived pollutants, and protect the most vulnerable people and ecosystems now. Coping and containment: reach at least net-zero emissions to stop the rise, and manage severe impacts while temperatures peak. Long-term resilience: sustain net-negative CO₂ emissions to bring temperatures down, and adapt where losses have become permanent. The report stresses that this is not a preferred or acceptable pathway. It is simply the best option still on the table. There are no benign scenarios above 1.5°C. 2. Every five years of delay adds about 0.1°C to the peak The most quantitative message is also the simplest. Warming scales almost linearly with cumulative CO₂ emissions, so the peak temperature is set by how much CO₂ we emit before reaching net zero. The report puts the remaining budget for a 50% chance of 1.5°C at only about 130 GtCO₂ from 2026, against current emissions of about 40 GtCO₂ per year. At that rate the budget is gone in roughly three years. Staying within it would require emissions to fall in a straight line to zero in just over six years. Because about 220 GtCO₂ produces 0.1°C of warming (the IPCC best estimate), every five years of emissions at today’s level adds roughly 0.1°C to whatever peak we eventually reach. The figure below is my own back-of-the-envelope version of that arithmetic. It is not a figure from the report. Figure. (a) Three idealized CO₂ pathways that all take 30 years to fall from 40 GtCO₂ per year to net zero, starting in 2026, 2031 or 2036. The dashed line is what staying within the 1.5°C budget would require. (b) The resulting peak warming, computed as 1.5°C plus the warming from CO₂ emitted beyond the 130 GtCO₂ budget, using the IPCC AR6 transient climate response to cumulative emissions (best estimate 0.45°C per 1000 GtCO₂; bars show the likely range of 0.27–0.63). Non-CO₂ gases and CO₂ removal are held fixed, so this is an illustration of the budget logic, not a projection. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on numbers reported in UNEP (2026). Even the prompt-start case peaks at about 1.7°C. That is consistent with the report’s estimate that full implementation of every current national pledge and net-zero target still implies a peak of around 1.8°C. Each delay of five years pushes the peak up by another tenth of a degree. 3. Coming back down is slow, limited and uncertain Returning below 1.5°C requires the world to become net-negative: removing more CO₂ than it emits, for decades. The report is sober about how hard that is: Even optimistic scaling of carbon dioxide removal is unlikely to lower temperatures by more than a few tenths of a degree this century. At today’s scale, afforestation and forest management would take over a century to reverse just 0.1°C of warming, and that assumes zero residual CO₂ emissions. Geological storage is finite. Merely maintaining net-zero CO₂ could use up the estimated storage capacity of sedimentary basins by around 2200. Once the peak exceeds about 1.8°C, a return to 1.5°C within this century becomes increasingly difficult. The conclusion is that removal is needed in addition to deep emission cuts, never instead of them. The cheapest tenth of a degree is the one we never emit. 4. Some damage does not reverse when the temperature does Bringing temperatures down helps, but the climate system has long memory. Glaciers could lose more than a quarter of their mass by 2100, and glacier loss will continue for centuries even if warming stabilizes. Sea level keeps rising long after the peak. Even so, a pathway that declines rather than stabilizing at a higher level could reduce sea-level rise by almost half a meter by 2300. Species extinctions and some ecosystem shifts, such as the loss of coral reefs, may not be undone at all. The report’s message to decision-makers is that the legacy of the peak is inherited by every stage that follows. What this means for water Reading the report as a hydrologist, three points stand out. Our design assumptions have a new shape. Almost twenty years ago, Milly and colleagues argued that “stationarity is dead,” meaning that we can no longer design water infrastructure as if the past climate will repeat. Overshoot adds a twist. The climate we design for is not just moving. It may rise, peak and then partly fall within the lifetime of a single dam, levee or water supply system. A reservoir rule curve or design flood that is right for the peak may be wrong for the decline. The report explicitly calls for infrastructure that favors robustness and safety margins over optimization, and for forward-looking stress tests instead of planning from the historical record. Water availability can change non-linearly. In glacier-fed basins, meltwater first rises as glaciers shrink, then falls as they disappear. A study cited in the report suggests that if temperatures decline after the peak and glaciers partly regrow, downstream runoff could drop further still, into what the authors call “trough water.” For communities that rely on seasonal meltwater, the decline stage is not automatically a recovery. Adaptation has to be iterative. Because the path, the peak and the timing are all uncertain, the report argues that adaptation must be revisited repeatedly rather than designed once. This is the reasoning behind the decision-centric and scenario-neutral approaches my group has used to assess dams and river basins: start from the thresholds at which a system fails, then ask how plausible those conditions are under many possible futures, instead of betting on a single projection. The bottom line The report closes on a point worth repeating: overshoot is an argument for urgency, not resignation. Every fraction of a degree avoided and every year by which overshoot is shortened reduces risk to people, ecosystems and the infrastructure we build. For students thinking about a career in hydrology and water resources, this is the problem your generation will manage: water systems built for one climate, operated through another and possibly handed on in a third. Questions to think about If a 100-year design flood is estimated for the peak-warming period, how should it be revised during the decline stage? Which water infrastructure in Korea has a design life that will span exceedance, peak and decline? Using the budget arithmetic in the figure, how much later could emissions start to fall if the target were a 1.8°C peak instead? 한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). 지구 온난화는 몇 년 안에 1.5°C를 넘어설 전망이며, UNEP 보고서는 이제 1.5°C 목표에 “위로부터” 접근해야 한다고 강조한다. 감축이 5년 늦어질 때마다 최고 기온은 약 0.1°C 높아지고, 대기 이산화탄소를 흡수해 저장하는 제거(CDR) 기술로 되돌릴 수 있는 온도는 이번 세기 안에 수십 분의 1°C 정도에 그친다. 기후가 오르고, 정점을 찍고, 다시 내려가는 과정 전체를 견딜 수 있도록 기후관련 인프라를 설계하고 적응 전략을 지속적으로 수정해 나가야 한다. Reference United Nations Environment Programme (2026). Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return. Nairobi. https://doi.org/10.59117/20.500.11822/49857 Milly, P. C. D., et al. (2008). Stationarity is dead: Whither water management? Science, 319, 573–574. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1151915 The figure is an original illustration.
